subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
stem:
A state vocational rehabilitation program provides paid medical leave for workers injured in program-sponsored training. The program excludes leave for disabilities arising from pregnancy-related complications. An employee brings a federal Equal Protection claim against the exclusion but offers no evidence that the state adopted the exclusion because of sex stereotypes. 

(A) Equal Protection requires every state benefit program to cover all medical conditions without exception.

(B) The exclusion automatically receives intermediate scrutiny because pregnancy is always a sex classification under the Equal Protection Clause.

(C) The Equal Protection claim does not automatically trigger intermediate scrutiny on pregnancy status alone.

(D) Strict scrutiny applies because pregnancy implicates bodily autonomy.
call: Which statement is most accurate?
distilled_core_question: A state disability-benefit program excludes pregnancy-related conditions; the plaintiff brings only an Equal Protection claim and offers no proof of sex-stereotyping purpose. What level of scrutiny applies?
review_truth: A pregnancy-based exclusion from a state benefit program does not automatically constitute a sex classification triggering intermediate scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause.

choices.text: Equal Protection requires every state benefit program to cover all medical conditions without exception.
choices.student_label: EP demands universal coverage — too broad
choices.c3_signal: The choice claims EP requires ALL programs to cover ALL conditions. No standard of review in EP mandates universal coverage. Cut on overbreadth.
choices.why_attractive: Students overgeneralize Equal Protection's protective reach, assuming it mandates universal coverage without exceptions.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: EP does not require universal coverage; the state may rationally draw lines among benefit categories.
choices.future_cue: Replace the 'all/all' instinct with the rational-basis rule: the state need only have a legitimate reason for treating groups differently.

choices.text: The exclusion automatically receives intermediate scrutiny because pregnancy is always a sex classification under the Equal Protection Clause.
choices.student_label: Pregnancy = sex classification → automatic intermediate scrutiny
choices.c3_signal: The choice says pregnancy is ALWAYS a sex classification under EP. Geduldig Gold Key needed. Without it, the pull is strong: students know pregnancy is sex-linked and mechanically jump to heightened scrutiny.
choices.why_attractive: Pregnancy is obviously sex-linked, and students are trained to associate sex classifications with intermediate scrutiny — the mechanical chain feels automatic.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Under Geduldig v. Aiello, pregnancy classification is NOT automatically a sex classification under constitutional EP. The word 'always' overclaims. This is the dominant trap.
choices.future_cue: Memorize Geduldig: pregnancy classification ≠ automatic sex classification constitutionally. The word 'always' in a choice about EP scrutiny is a red flag.

choices.text: The Equal Protection claim does not automatically trigger intermediate scrutiny on pregnancy status alone.
choices.student_label: The accurate statement of the law
choices.c3_signal: The correct answer — pregnancy alone ≠ automatic intermediate scrutiny under EP.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: See the preserved right-answer explanation above.

choices.text: Strict scrutiny applies because pregnancy implicates bodily-autonomy concerns.
choices.student_label: Strict scrutiny via bodily autonomy — wrong framework
choices.c3_signal: The choice smuggles a substantive-due-process bodily-autonomy argument into an EP question. The stem provides no support for strict scrutiny. Cut on framework misfit.
choices.why_attractive: Bodily autonomy is a real constitutional value (Due Process/privacy), and students may instinctively upgrade to strict scrutiny for anything touching on bodily integrity.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Strict scrutiny under EP requires a suspect or quasi-suspect classification. Bodily autonomy invokes Due Process, not EP, and pregnancy alone is not a suspect class under Geduldig.
choices.future_cue: Separate the frameworks: EP strict scrutiny requires suspect/quasi-suspect classification; bodily autonomy is a Due Process concern. The stem's EP-only framing controls.

remediation_card.title: Pregnancy ≠ Sex Classification on Constitutional EP
remediation_card.trigger_signal: State program excludes pregnancy conditions; claim is EP-only; no stereotyping evidence
remediation_card.student_move: When the stem says 'only an Equal Protection claim' and 'no evidence of sex stereotypes,' map to Geduldig: pregnancy classification alone does not trigger intermediate scrutiny. Rational basis applies.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Pregnancy-alone ≠ automatic sex classification → rational basis, not intermediate scrutiny. Gold Key: Geduldig distinvid.
remediation_card.trap: B (automatic intermediate scrutiny)

gold_keys.statement: A pregnancy-based classification is not automatically a sex-based classification under the constitutional Equal Protection Clause. (Geduldig v. Aiello, 417 U.S. 484 (1974)). Intermediate scrutiny applies only when the classification is genuinely sex-based or when sex-stereotyping purpose is proven.
gold_keys.trigger: Any MBE question where a state program excludes pregnancy conditions and the claim is constitutional EP only (no Title VII / PDA), with no showing of sex-stereotyping purpose
gold_keys.authority: Geduldig v. Aiello, 417 U.S. 484 (1974)

silver_keys.statement: When two choices survive the CUT and one says 'always/never' while the other is hedged ('does not automatically'), look up the Geduldig distinction — the hedged answer is usually correct in EP classification questions.
silver_keys.trigger: EP classification question with a pregnancy or sex-classification tension where one option uses absolute language and the other is qualified

drill_seeds.prompt: A state university's health plan excludes coverage for gender-affirming surgical procedures. A student brings an Equal Protection claim. What level of scrutiny applies, and why is this different from Geduldig?
drill_seeds.answer: Gender-affirming care exclusions classify based on transgender status, which the Supreme Court in Bostock (via Title VII) and emerging case law treats as sex-based. This is a sex classification triggering intermediate scrutiny — unlike Geduldig's pregnancy-alone rule, because the classification is facially sex-based (transgender status = sex-linked), not pregnancy-linked.

drill_seeds.prompt: Explain why Geduldig v. Aiello (1974) reached the opposite result from the Pregnancy Discrimination Act (1978) on the same underlying facts.
drill_seeds.answer: Geduldig held that pregnancy exclusion is not a constitutional sex classification under EP (rational basis applies). Congress then passed the PDA, amending Title VII to statutorily define pregnancy discrimination as sex discrimination. The PDA is a statutory override — it does not change the constitutional rule, but it provides a statutory cause of action that reaches what Geduldig left untouched.

drill_seeds.target_skill: Absolute vs. hedged language in EP questions
drill_seeds.prompt: You see two choices: (A) 'The classification always triggers intermediate scrutiny' and (B) 'The classification does not automatically trigger intermediate scrutiny.' The stem involves a state program excluding a sex-linked condition with no evidence of discriminatory intent. Which do you pick and why?
drill_seeds.answer: Pick B. The word 'always' is a structural red flag in EP classification questions. Without proof of sex-based purpose or a facial sex classification, the Geduldig rule applies: the classification is reviewed rationally. The hedged 'not automatically' language signals the accurate statement.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
stem: Congress enacts a valid federal rule governing interstate shipments of portable Christmas-pageant lighting rigs sold by private vendors. To administer that shipment rule, Congress creates a federal serial-number portal for those rigs. Lydia, who ships the rigs through Barnabas Pageant Supply, argues that the portal is unconstitutional because federal inspectors could enforce the shipment rule by using paper invoices instead.
call: Which answer best states the constitutional result?
distilled_core_question: Congress validly regulates interstate shipments and adds an administrative portal to help run that regulation. Is the portal invalid merely because it is not indispensable?
review_truth: Necessary and Proper means useful or appropriate to executing an enumerated power, not absolutely indispensable and not freestanding.

choices.text: The portal may be valid if it is a proper means rationally related to carrying out the valid commerce regulation.
choices.c3_signal: keeps both links: valid underlying power and a connected means
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A is the only answer that is both valid-result and power-linked.

choices.text: The portal is invalid because federal tracking portals are never proper.
choices.c3_signal: the word 'never' bans a whole category of administrative means
choices.why_attractive: A student may distrust federal tracking systems and treat the answer as a principled limit on federal power. The breaker is the categorical word 'never,' which overclaims the rule.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer overclaims by saying federal tracking portals are never proper.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer bans an entire category without a trigger.

choices.text: The portal is invalid unless it is absolutely indispensable to the shipment rules.
choices.c3_signal: the phrase 'absolutely indispensable' is stronger than the Gold Key allows
choices.why_attractive: A student may translate 'necessary' into ordinary-language indispensability. The breaker is the Gold Key that Necessary and Proper does not require the only possible means.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer overclaims by requiring absolute indispensability.
choices.future_cue: Replace 'only possible' with 'appropriate means connected to the power.'

choices.text: The portal is valid even if it has no connection to any enumerated power.
choices.c3_signal: it cuts the required link to an enumerated power
choices.why_attractive: A student may see the word 'valid' and stop reading before the reason. The breaker is that Necessary and Proper still needs an enumerated-power connection.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer removes the required enumerated-power connection.
choices.future_cue: Check whether the reason preserves the enumerated-power hook.

remediation_card.title: Necessary means useful, not indispensable
remediation_card.signal: The stem says Congress could have used another method.
remediation_card.student_move: Reject indispensability language; check for enumerated-power connection.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Useful/proper means plus enumerated-power hook survives.
remediation_card.trap: Turning necessary into only possible.

gold_keys.statement: Necessary and Proper does not mean absolutely indispensable; Congress may use appropriate means connected to executing an enumerated power.
gold_keys.trigger: challenger says Congress could have used another administrative method
gold_keys.authority: McCulloch v. Maryland; United States v. Darby; United States v. Comstock

gold_keys.statement: The Necessary and Proper Clause is not freestanding; the means must execute an enumerated or otherwise vested federal power.
gold_keys.trigger: answer says valid even with no enumerated-power connection
gold_keys.authority: Kinsella v. United States ex rel. Singleton

silver_keys.statement: In a 2-valid/2-invalid constitutional array, do not stop at the result word; read the reason after it and keep the answer that preserves both required links.
silver_keys.trigger: two answers say valid and two say invalid

drill_seeds.prompt: Congress uses an administrative method to run a valid commerce regulation. The challenger says another method would work. Does the method have to be indispensable?
drill_seeds.answer: No. It must be an appropriate means connected to executing the enumerated power.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two choices say valid and two say invalid. What must you read next?
drill_seeds.answer: The reason after the result word.

drill_seeds.prompt: Classify: 'Federal tracking portals are never proper.'
drill_seeds.answer: NOT_TRUE, tiered_absolute.

drill_seeds.prompt: Classify: 'Valid even with no connection to an enumerated power.'
drill_seeds.answer: NOT_TRUE, flat_misstatement.

subject: CONTRACTS
stem:
Mary, a professional puzzle designer, agreed to design and run a “Road to Emmaus” puzzle quest for Daniel’s private Bible-themed birthday party for a fee of $12,600. Mary completed the entire puzzle quest, including the final resurrection-clue round. Comparable event designers would reasonably have charged $20,400 for the same work. Daniel refuses to pay. Mary sues for $20,400, arguing that she relied on the contract by doing puzzle-design work worth that amount.

What is Mary’s proper contract recovery?
call:
Call lock: proper contract recovery.

Adjacent-call trap: Do not answer, “Is reliance the right label?” Answer the recovery amount.

Prediction: Start with the agreed fee because the contract gives the number and Mary fully performed.
distilled_core_question: A service provider fully performs a fixed-price services contract; reasonable value is higher; the other side refuses to pay. What recovery?
review_truth: Full performance plus an unpaid fixed contract price points to the bargain price; reasonable value is not a bigger reliance recovery.

choices.text: $7,800, the difference between the reasonable value of the work and the agreed fee.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees two dollar figures and tries to do bar-exam arithmetic. The breaker is that no rule in this call asks for the difference between value and price.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A invents a spread recovery from two stem numbers. The call asks for proper contract recovery, not a market-value-minus-price calculation.
choices.future_cue: Ask which number the contract itself makes legally operative.

choices.text: Nothing, because once Mary fully performed, reliance damages are unavailable.
choices.why_attractive: The student correctly senses that reliance is not the winning remedy label. The breaker is that the answer skips the contract-price recovery and therefore answers the wrong subquestion.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B reacts to the bad reliance label but skips the contract-price recovery that remains.
choices.future_cue: After rejecting reliance, identify the affirmative recovery still available.

choices.text: $12,600, the agreed fee, because Mary fully performed and the expectation measure is readily fixed.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Mary fully performed under an enforceable services contract with a definite agreed fee. The call asks for her proper contract recovery, and that recovery is the agreed fee: $12,600.

Gold Key: When the plaintiff fully performs and the only thing left is the defendant’s payment of a definite contract price, the recovery is the bargain price. Do not relabel a higher market value as “reliance” to get more.

Silver Key: Read this answer set as a remedy-measure menu. The numbers are not random; they are contract price, reasonable value, zero, and the spread. Lock the call to “proper contract recovery,” then pick the number supplied by the bargain.

choices.text: $20,400, because reliance damages always use the reasonable value of services.
choices.why_attractive: The student wants to award the higher value because Mary gave work worth more than the bargain. The breaker is the Gold Key: after full performance, fixed contract price controls over reasonable-value bait.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: D overclaims with 'always' and misuses reasonable value as a higher reliance measure.
choices.future_cue: Apply the bargain-price Gold Key when fixed price and full performance appear together.

remediation_card.title: Bargain price beats reasonable-value bait
remediation_card.signal: Full performance + agreed price + higher reasonable value
remediation_card.student_move: Start with the bargain number before considering reliance or restitution labels.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: If the contract price is fixed and fully earned, recover that price.
remediation_card.trap: Picking the higher market value or the spread.

gold_keys.statement: Full performance plus an unpaid fixed contract price means the bargain price is the recovery. Do not relabel higher reasonable value as reliance or restitution to get more.
gold_keys.trigger: The stem gives both a fixed contract price and a higher reasonable value after full performance.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 344, 347, 349, 373(2).

silver_keys.statement: When the choices are all dollar amounts, classify the menu before choosing: contract price, market value, zero, or spread.
silver_keys.trigger: The stem supplies two dollar amounts and the choices recombine them.

drill_seeds.prompt: A fully performing painter agreed to $9,000. The work was worth $14,000. The owner refuses to pay. Choices are $9,000, $14,000, $5,000, or $0. Which number starts as the anchor?
drill_seeds.answer: $9,000, the contract price.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut this answer: '$14,000, because reliance damages always use reasonable value.'
drill_seeds.answer: Cut as tiered_absolute; 'always' overclaims and reasonable value is not automatic reliance.

drill_seeds.target_skill: Separate bad label from proper recovery.
drill_seeds.prompt: Why is 'nothing, because reliance is unavailable' not responsive when the plaintiff fully performed?
drill_seeds.answer: Because the call asks proper recovery; the contract price remains available.

drill_seeds.prompt: State the tiny rule for fixed price + full performance + higher market value.
drill_seeds.answer: Recover the fixed contract price; do not use higher reasonable value to exceed it.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
stem:
Two members of the same congregation, Peter and Lydia, got into a heated disagreement over the use of the church basement for a weekday tutoring program. Peter claimed Lydia had promised him exclusive use of the basement on Tuesday evenings; Lydia denied making any such promise. Peter sued Lydia in federal court for breach of contract, seeking $14,000 in damages. Both Peter and Lydia are citizens of the same state. The case proceeded through an answer, discovery, and a pretrial conference. One week before trial, the federal judge reviewed the file and realized the complaint asserted only a state-law contract claim between two nondiverse parties, with no basis for federal-question or supplemental jurisdiction. Neither Peter nor Lydia had ever raised a subject-matter-jurisdiction objection.



A. Proceed to trial, because the parties' failure to raise the issue before trial constitutes a waiver of the subject-matter-jurisdiction defect.

B. Proceed to trial, because only a party Section  not the court Section  may raise a challenge to subject matter jurisdiction.

C. Dismiss the action, because a court must dismiss whenever it determines it lacks subject matter jurisdiction, regardless of the stage of the proceedings.

D. Transfer the action to an appropriate state court, because the federal court should not dismiss when a state court of competent jurisdiction is available.
call: What should the court do?
distilled_core_question: A federal court realizes one week before trial that the case involves only state-law claims between nondiverse parties and no supplemental-jurisdiction anchor. Neither party has objected. What must the court do?
review_truth: Subject matter jurisdiction cannot be waived by delay, agreement, or silence Section  a court must dismiss whenever it determines it lacks subject matter jurisdiction.

choices.text: Proceed to trial, because the parties' failure to raise the issue before trial constitutes a waiver of the subject-matter-jurisdiction defect.
choices.student_label: The 'waiver-by-delay' trap Section  SMJ is non-waivable
choices.c3_signal: The word 'waiver' in an SMJ question is always wrong. Rule 12(h)(3) says the court must dismiss Section  no waiver possible.
choices.why_attractive: Students know that most defenses can be waived by delay or failure to raise them. This choice weaponizes that general intuition and applies it to SMJ Section  it feels like a natural extension of the waiver rules they have just learned.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Choice A says SMJ is waived by delay. Rule 12(h)(3) says SMJ is non-waivable. The word 'waiver' in an SMJ answer is always wrong.
choices.future_cue: Re-read the Gold Key for Rule 12(h)(3). SMJ is non-waivable. Cut any choice with 'waiver' in it.

choices.text: Proceed to trial, because only a party Section  not the court Section  may raise a challenge to subject matter jurisdiction.
choices.student_label: The 'only a party can raise it' trap Section  the court has an independent duty
choices.c3_signal: The word 'only' is the tell. Rule 12(h)(3) says the court must dismiss Section  the duty is the court's, not the parties'.
choices.why_attractive: In most of civil procedure, the parties drive the litigation Section  the court does not inject defenses the parties have not raised. Personal jurisdiction, for example, is waived if the defendant does not raise it. This choice exploits that pattern and makes it feel like SMJ works the same way.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Choice B says only a party can raise SMJ. Rule 12(h)(3) says the court must dismiss on its own motion. The word 'only' is the tell Section  the rule says the opposite.
choices.future_cue: Recall the Silver Key: Rule 12(h)(3) places the duty on the court, not the parties. Cut B.

choices.text: Dismiss the action, because a court must dismiss whenever it determines it lacks subject matter jurisdiction, regardless of the stage of the proceedings.
choices.student_label: Correct Section  the court must dismiss under Rule 12(h)(3)
choices.c3_signal: Rule 12(h)(3) mandates dismissal whenever the court determines it lacks SMJ. The late stage does not cure the defect.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
Gold Key: Rule 12(h)(3) Section  the court's independent, non-waivable duty.

Under FRCP 12(h)(3), lack of subject matter jurisdiction is one of the three defenses that can never be waived. A court has an independent obligation to notice and act on its own lack of subject matter jurisdiction at any stage Section  even after trial, even on appeal. Neither party silence nor procedural delay creates federal adjudicatory power that does not exist. The court must dismiss.

Here, the federal court has only state-law claims between nondiverse parties and no supplemental-jurisdiction anchor. The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction. Under Rule 12(h)(3), the court must dismiss Section  the one-week-before-trial posture is irrelevant.

choices.text: Transfer the action to an appropriate state court, because the federal court should not dismiss when a state court of competent jurisdiction is available.
choices.student_label: The 'transfer instead of dismiss' trap Section  wrong remedy for SMJ
choices.c3_signal: Transfer is a venue remedy (Section  1406), not an SMJ remedy. Rule 12(h)(3) says 'dismiss,' not 'transfer.'
choices.why_attractive: This choice appeals to common sense and fairness. Dismissing a case that could be heard in state court seems wasteful Section  why not just send it where it belongs? The word 'transfer' sounds like a reasonable judicial remedy.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Choice D proposes transfer as the remedy. Transfer is a venue remedy under Section  1406, not an SMJ remedy. Rule 12(h)(3) mandates dismissal.
choices.future_cue: Recall that transfer is a venue remedy under Section  1406, not an SMJ remedy. Rule 12(h)(3) mandates dismissal. Cut D.

remediation_card.title: SMJ Is Non-Waivable Section  The Court's Independent Duty
remediation_card.signal: A federal court discovers it lacks SMJ at any stage, and neither party has objected.
remediation_card.student_move: Cut any answer that says SMJ is waived or that only a party can raise it. The court must dismiss under Rule 12(h)(3).
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Rule 12(h)(3): The court must dismiss whenever it determines it lacks SMJ Section  at any time, on its own motion.
remediation_card.trap: Confusing SMJ with personal jurisdiction (which IS waivable) or venue (which can be transferred).

gold_keys.statement: Rule 12(h)(3) places the duty to dismiss on the court itself Section  not the parties. Subject matter jurisdiction can never be waived by delay, silence, or agreement.
gold_keys.trigger: Any answer choice that says SMJ is waived or that only a party can raise it
gold_keys.authority: FRCP 12(h)(3); Wright & Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure Section  1350

silver_keys.statement: When you see 'waiver,' 'only a party,' or 'transfer' in an SMJ question, cut that choice immediately Section  Rule 12(h)(3) says the court must dismiss, and nothing else.
silver_keys.trigger: Any choice that frames SMJ as a party-controlled or waivable defense

drill_seeds.prompt: True or False: Subject matter jurisdiction can be waived if neither party raises it before trial.
drill_seeds.answer: False. Rule 12(h)(3) requires dismissal whenever the court determines it lacks SMJ Section  at any time, on its own motion.

drill_seeds.prompt: Compare the waiver rules for personal jurisdiction (Rule 12(h)(1)) and subject matter jurisdiction (Rule 12(h)(3)). What is the key difference?
drill_seeds.answer: Personal jurisdiction is waivable Section  if not raised in the responsive pleading, it is waived. Subject matter jurisdiction is non-waivable Section  the court must dismiss whenever it determines it lacks SMJ, regardless of party action.

drill_seeds.prompt: A federal court lacks subject matter jurisdiction. What is the proper remedy: dismissal or transfer?
drill_seeds.answer: Dismissal. Rule 12(h)(3) mandates dismissal. Transfer under Section  1406(a) cures venue defects, not SMJ defects.

subject: TORTS
subtopic: Warranty Theory — Implied warranty of merchantability; UCC § 2-316 disclaimer
tension_axis: AS-IS disclaimer controls over IWM-definitional fact, dealer's opinion, and household privity
stem: Joseph went to Daniel’s farm-equipment resale lot on the edge of town and bought a used 14-horsepower riding lawn tractor for $1,850 to help Hannah mow their long gravel drive and back pasture. The bill of sale Daniel gave Joseph included, in capital letters at the top, the line: "TRACTOR SOLD AS IS — NO IMPLIED WARRANTIES." When Joseph asked Daniel how the tractor ran, Daniel said, "I believe this tractor is in good working order." Hannah used the tractor to mow that Saturday, and after about two hours the engine seized. The repair bill was $720.
call: If Hannah asserts a claim for damages against Daniel on the grounds that Daniel breached the implied warranty of merchantability, the court should find for:
distilled_core_question: A used-goods sales contract contains a conspicuous 'AS IS' clause, the seller says 'I believe the goods are in good condition,' the buyer's household member uses the goods, and the goods turn out to be unfit; in an IWM claim by the household member, who wins?
review_truth: A conspicuous 'as is' clause in a sales contract disclaims the implied warranty of merchantability.

choices.text: Hannah, because the tractor was unfit for ordinary use.
choices.c3_signal: The choice proves a fact (unfit for ordinary use) that defines an IWM breach — but the IWM was disclaimed. The reason does not answer a disclaimed-warranty claim.
choices.why_attractive: A student reads the IWM definition (fit for ordinary purposes), sees that the tractor seized mid-mow, and concludes the IWM was breached. The breaker is the Gold Key: a conspicuous AS-IS clause under UCC § 2-316(3)(a) disclaims the IWM, so the fitness finding is not the verdict.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice proves a fact (unfit for ordinary use) that defines an IWM breach, but the IWM was disclaimed by a conspicuous AS-IS clause. The fact is real; it does not answer a disclaimed-warranty claim. This is the dominant trap.
choices.future_cue: Ask: 'Did the contract disclaim the IWM?' If yes, the fitness finding is not the verdict.

choices.text: Daniel, because the bill of sale included the phrase "TRACTOR SOLD AS IS — NO IMPLIED WARRANTIES."
choices.c3_signal: The answer pairs the right party (Daniel) with the right reason (AS-IS clause disclaimed the IWM that Hannah is suing on).
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: True and responsive to the IWM-claim call: Daniel wins because the AS-IS clause in the bill of sale disclaimed the IWM that Hannah is suing on.

choices.text: Hannah, because Daniel told Joseph that he believed the tractor was in good working order.
choices.c3_signal: The choice asserts that a seller's positive statement is an express warranty. The student skipped UCC § 2-313(2) (opinion does not create a warranty).
choices.why_attractive: A student assumes any positive statement by a seller becomes a warranty. The breaker is UCC § 2-313(2): a statement purporting to be merely the seller's opinion or commendation does not create a warranty. 'I believe' is opinion, not affirmation of fact.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice asserts that a seller's 'I believe' statement is an express warranty. Under UCC § 2-313(2), a statement purporting to be merely the seller's opinion or commendation does not create a warranty. Even if it had risen to an express warranty, the AS-IS clause under § 2-316(1) would be construed to negate or limit it.
choices.future_cue: Ask: 'Is this an affirmation of fact, or a statement of opinion or value?' Opinion is not an express warranty.

choices.text: Daniel, because he did not enter into any contractual relationship with Hannah.
choices.c3_signal: The choice imports a contract-privity rule. The student skipped UCC § 2-318 (Alt. A) — seller's warranty extends to natural persons in the buyer's family or household.
choices.why_attractive: A student reflexively reaches for a contract-privity rule because Hannah was not the buyer. The breaker is UCC § 2-318 (Alternative A): a seller's warranty extends to natural persons in the buyer's family or household. The no-privity answer is not a true defense to an IWM claim by a household member.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice imports a contract-privity rule. Under UCC § 2-318 (Alternative A), a seller's warranty extends to natural persons in the buyer's family or household. The no-privity answer is not a true defense to an IWM claim by a household member.
choices.future_cue: Ask: 'Is the plaintiff a member of the buyer's household?' If yes, the IWM claim is permitted; the no-privity answer is not a true defense.

remediation_card.title: AS-IS disclaimer controls IWM
remediation_card.signal: A sales contract for goods contains a conspicuous 'AS IS' clause and the claim is breach of the implied warranty of merchantability.
remediation_card.student_move: Lock the contract terms first. The IWM-definitional fact is real but not the verdict.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Under UCC § 2-316(3)(a), conspicuous 'as is' language in a sales contract disclaims all implied warranties.
remediation_card.trap: Treating 'unfit for ordinary use' as automatic liability without checking for an AS-IS disclaimer.

gold_keys.statement: Under UCC § 2-316(3)(a), expressions like 'as is' or 'with all faults' in a sales contract for goods, and other language which in common understanding calls the buyer's attention to the exclusion of warranties, disclaim all implied warranties, including the implied warranty of merchantability. A finding that the goods were unfit is not enough to win an IWM claim once the IWM has been validly disclaimed.
gold_keys.trigger: the sales contract contains a conspicuous 'as is' clause and the claim is breach of the implied warranty of merchantability

silver_keys.statement: When the contract says 'AS IS' and the claim is IWM, the disclaimer controls the answer. Lock the contract terms before reaching for the IWM-definitional bait.
silver_keys.trigger: an answer choice proves the goods were unfit, but the contract contains an AS-IS clause and the claim is IWM

drill_seeds.prompt: A sales contract for a used lawn tractor says 'TRACTOR SOLD AS IS — NO IMPLIED WARRANTIES' in capital letters at the top, and the tractor's engine seizes. The buyer sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Which answer is suspect: 'the buyer, because the tractor was unfit for ordinary use'?
drill_seeds.answer: Suspect; the AS-IS clause under UCC § 2-316(3)(a) disclaims the IWM, so the fitness finding is not the verdict.

drill_seeds.prompt: A seller says 'I believe this used refrigerator is in good working order' and the refrigerator fails. The buyer sues for breach of express warranty. Which answer is suspect: 'the buyer, because the seller said the refrigerator was in good working order'?
drill_seeds.answer: Suspect; under UCC § 2-313(2), a statement of opinion or commendation does not create a warranty.

drill_seeds.prompt: A husband buys a used riding mower from a dealer, the contract says AS IS, the mower fails, and the husband's spouse sues the dealer for breach of the IWM. Which answer is suspect: 'the dealer, because he did not enter into any contractual relationship with the spouse'?
drill_seeds.answer: Suspect; under UCC § 2-318 (Alt. A), a seller's warranty extends to natural persons in the buyer's family or household, so the no-privity answer is not a true defense to an IWM claim by a household member.

subject: CONTRACTS
stem: Ruth, who makes handbound prayer journals, and Timothy, who runs a Christian bookstore, signed a written contract for Timothy to buy 160 journals for an upcoming discipleship conference. Before signing, they orally agreed that the price would be $38 per journal. During final drafting, the price line was accidentally omitted from the writing, and neither Ruth nor Timothy noticed before signing. Ruth later sued Timothy for breach of the contract.
call: In deciding the action, the court should
distilled_core_question: A written goods contract states the quantity, the parties orally agreed on price, and the writing accidentally omits the price. In a breach action, may the court hear oral evidence of the agreed price?
review_truth: When both parties agreed on a price but accidentally left it out of their written goods contract, the court may use oral evidence to reform the writing to reflect the agreed price.

choices.text: refuse to enforce the contract if it is one that the Statute of Frauds required to be in writing.
choices.c3_signal: This treats the missing price line as if the whole writing fails.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees a missing price in a goods contract and reaches for the writing requirement. The breaker is that UCC 2-201 does not make a quantity-sufficient writing fail merely because an agreed price is omitted.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The Statute of Frauds does not make a goods writing insufficient merely because an agreed price term is omitted.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the writing is missing quantity or merely missing another agreed term.

choices.text: disregard the writing because it omits an essential term of the bargain.
choices.c3_signal: This jumps from one omitted line to throwing away the whole contract.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats a missing price line as a missing-contract failure. The breaker is that reformation and Article 2 both resist throwing away a bargain when intent and quantity are clear.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The writing is not disregarded merely because it accidentally omits the price.
choices.future_cue: Look for whether the parties actually agreed on the omitted term.

choices.text: admit oral testimony to establish the price Ruth and Timothy intended.
choices.c3_signal: This is the only answer that uses the agreed-price fact.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Only C treats the price as agreed but omitted from the writing.

choices.text: conclude that the contract calls for payment of a reasonable price at the time of delivery.
choices.c3_signal: This answers the question for a price never settled, not a price omitted from the writing.
choices.why_attractive: The student remembers the UCC reasonable-price gap filler and sees a blank price line. The breaker is that the stem says the parties had already agreed on a price.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The reasonable-price rule answers a different case, where price was not settled.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the price was open or merely omitted from the written expression.

remediation_card.title: Blank price line is not always open price
remediation_card.signal: The stem says the parties agreed on price before the writing.
remediation_card.student_move: Choose the answer that proves the intended price, not the answer that supplies a new reasonable price.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Agreed-but-omitted price points to reformation evidence.
remediation_card.trap: open-price gap filler

gold_keys.statement: When a writing omits an agreed term by mutual mistake, reformation lets the court use relevant extrinsic evidence to make the writing reflect the parties' actual agreement.
gold_keys.trigger: the stem says the parties orally agreed on price but accidentally omitted it from the writing
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 155; OneBeacon America Insurance Co. v. Travelers Indemnity Co. of Illinois; UCC sections 2-201 and 2-305

silver_keys.statement: When two answers fight over intended price versus reasonable price, mark whether the stem says the parties agreed on price; an omitted written term is not the same as no agreement.
silver_keys.trigger: blank price line plus oral agreement on price

misconception_tags: reasonable price always fills a blank price line
oral evidence is always barred by a writing

drill_seeds.target_skill: distinguish agreed-but-omitted price from open price
drill_seeds.prompt: The writing omits price, but the stem says both parties orally agreed to $20 each. Open price or reformation evidence?
drill_seeds.answer: Reformation evidence.

drill_seeds.prompt: A signed goods writing lists quantity but omits price. Is it automatically insufficient under UCC 2-201?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Omitted agreed terms other than quantity do not automatically make the writing insufficient.

drill_seeds.prompt: What remedy fits when the parties' writing accidentally omits a term both sides agreed to?
drill_seeds.answer: Reformation, with extrinsic evidence of the intended term.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
tension_axis: specific Property Clause source vs wrong constitutional labels
stem: In an effort to improve the position of United States companies in the world mobile-disaster-relief catering market, Congress voted to sell twelve surplus federal field-kitchen trailers nicknamed 'manna wagons' to Lydia's Ark Logistics, Inc., for $7 each. If Timothy Relief Systems, a competitor of Lydia's Ark Logistics, challenges the constitutionality of the congressional action in an appropriate proceeding, the sale will probably be found:
call: If a competitor challenges the constitutionality of the congressional sale, the sale will probably be found:
distilled_core_question: Congress sells surplus federal property to one private company at a nominal price. A competitor challenges. Is the sale valid because Congress has constitutional power to dispose of United States property?
review_truth: Federal property plus congressional disposal points to the Property Clause.

choices.text: invalid as a bill of attainder.
choices.c3_signal: The stem gives a sale/benefit, not a punishment.
choices.why_attractive: A student sees Congress favoring one company and reaches for a severe constitutional label. The breaker is that bill-of-attainder analysis needs punishment, and the stem gives a sale.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer invokes a punishment doctrine, but the stem gives a sale/benefit and no punishment fact.
choices.future_cue: Ask: what was imposed on the alleged target, a burden or a benefit?

choices.text: valid under the Property Clause of Article IV.
choices.c3_signal: Actor + object + action match Congress + federal property + disposal.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. The challenged action is Congress selling property that belongs to the United States. Gold Key: when the stem gives federal property and Congress is disposing of it, lock the Property Clause as the power source before chasing fairness, punishment, or general police-power answers. Article IV, Section 3, Clause 2 gives Congress power to dispose of and regulate United States territory or other property, and official Constitution Annotated materials state that this clause covers “Territory or other Property belonging to the United States.” ([Congress.gov][1])

Silver Key: this is a four-doctrine-home array. Do not debate whether the sale is wise or fair. Match actor + object + action: Congress + federal property + sale.

choices.text: invalid as a denial of equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment.
choices.c3_signal: Federal Congress fact does not match Fourteenth Amendment state-action source.
choices.why_attractive: A student sees unequal treatment between competitors and reaches for equal protection. The breaker is that this answer names the Fourteenth Amendment even though the actor is Congress.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer names a state-action source while the actor in the stem is Congress.
choices.future_cue: Ask: is the answer's amendment aimed at this actor?

choices.text: valid under the general police powers of Congress.
choices.c3_signal: The answer gives broad federal police power instead of a named enumerated power.
choices.why_attractive: A student likes the valid result and accepts the broad power label. The breaker is that Congress has no general police power, so the source must be a specific enumerated power.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer gives the right result but relies on a nonexistent general federal police power.
choices.future_cue: Replace generic power labels with the specific enumerated power that matches the facts.

remediation_card.title: Property Clause source match
remediation_card.signal: Congress disposes of property belonging to the United States.
remediation_card.student_move: Name the actor, object, and action; match them to the specific power source.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Federal property + dispose/sell = Property Clause.
remediation_card.trap: Policy/fairness answers distract from the source of power.

gold_keys.statement: When Congress sells or otherwise disposes of property belonging to the United States, the Property Clause is the power source.
gold_keys.trigger: Congress + federal property + sell/dispose
gold_keys.authority: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 3, cl. 2

gold_keys.statement: A bill of attainder requires legislative punishment of an identified person or group without judicial trial.
gold_keys.trigger: Answer says bill of attainder but stem gives no punishment
gold_keys.authority: Nixon v. Administrator of General Services, 433 U.S. 425

gold_keys.statement: The Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause is the state-action source; do not use it as the direct source for Congress.
gold_keys.trigger: Congress/federal actor + Fourteenth Amendment answer
gold_keys.authority: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1

gold_keys.statement: Congress has enumerated powers, not a general police power; find the specific federal power that fits.
gold_keys.trigger: Answer says general police powers of Congress
gold_keys.authority: United States v. Lopez, 514 U.S. 549

silver_keys.statement: For a Con Law source-choice array, match actor + object + action before debating policy.
silver_keys.trigger: Congress + federal property + sale

drill_seeds.prompt: Congress sells surplus federal equipment to a private buyer. What power source should you check first?
drill_seeds.answer: Property Clause.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says bill of attainder, but the stem gives a subsidy or sale. What fact is missing?
drill_seeds.answer: Punishment.

drill_seeds.prompt: The actor is Congress and the answer says Fourteenth Amendment equal protection. What is the mismatch?
drill_seeds.answer: The Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause is the state-action source.

drill_seeds.prompt: An answer says a congressional act is valid under general police powers. What is the recovery move?
drill_seeds.answer: Find the specific enumerated power; Congress lacks a general police power.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
subtopic: Rational basis — sexual orientation / federal law / equal dignity
tension_axis: Equal-protection classification purpose vs benefit-entitlement frame
stem: A federal statute provides that, for every federal tax, employee-benefit, grant, and insurance program, the word 'spouse' means only a husband or wife of the opposite sex, and 'marriage' means only a legal union between one man and one woman. Stephen and Barnabas, who run a little gospel-poster shop called Loaves & Pages, are legally married under their state’s law. After Stephen takes a federal park-service job, he tries to enroll Barnabas for spousal health coverage available to opposite-sex spouses of federal employees. The agency denies the enrollment solely because Barnabas is not an opposite-sex spouse. Stephen and Barnabas challenge the statute under the Equal Protection component of the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause.
call: Under Equal Protection analysis, how should a court evaluate the federal statute’s refusal to recognize their state-law marriage for federal benefits?
distilled_core_question: A federal law defines marriage/spouse as opposite-sex only and denies a federal benefit to a same-sex spouse who is lawfully married under state law. Under Equal Protection, does the federal definition survive?
review_truth: A federal marriage-recognition law cannot deny federal benefits to state-law same-sex spouses when the operative purpose/effect is to demean their lawful marriage status.

choices.text: The statute is subject to strict scrutiny because it discriminates against gay and lesbian persons on the basis of sexual orientation, which is a suspect classification.
choices.c3_signal: Gold Key needed: Windsor invalidates the law without making sexual orientation a suspect class.
choices.why_attractive: Strict scrutiny feels like the strongest answer for a law affecting same-sex couples. The breaker is that Windsor did not expressly make sexual orientation a suspect classification.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice overpromotes Windsor into strict scrutiny based on suspect-class status.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the controlling case actually declared suspect-class status.

choices.text: The statute survives rational basis review because Congress has a legitimate interest in using one uniform definition of marriage across federal programs and preserving the traditional definition of marriage.
choices.c3_signal: Gold Key needed: uniformity/tradition do not save the federal definition when the operative purpose/effect is to demean state-law same-sex marriages.
choices.why_attractive: Rational basis plus tradition and uniformity sounds like ordinary Con Law deference. The breaker is the Windsor/Romer Gold Key that bare animus or dignity injury is not legitimate.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice treats uniformity and tradition as sufficient rational-basis interests even under Windsor/Romer bare-animus facts.
choices.future_cue: Check whether the stated interests mask a purpose/effect to demean an identifiable group.

choices.text: The statute survives because Congress controls federal benefit programs, and there is no constitutional right to receive a spousal federal benefit.
choices.c3_signal: The call asks Equal Protection classification. This choice answers Congress’s benefits authority and freestanding entitlement.
choices.why_attractive: Congress’s control over federal benefit programs sounds like a powerful threshold answer. The breaker is that the call asks Equal Protection classification, not entitlement to the benefit.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice answers benefits authority and entitlement, not the Equal Protection classification question.
choices.future_cue: Restate the call as Equal Protection classification and ask why the line was drawn.

choices.text: The statute fails Equal Protection review because denying federal recognition to lawfully married same-sex couples serves only to demean their status, and a bare desire to harm an identifiable group is not a legitimate governmental interest under any level of scrutiny.
choices.c3_signal: Matches the Windsor/Romer Gold Key: bare desire to demean or harm is not legitimate.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
D is the best answer. Gold Key: A federal marriage-recognition law that denies federal benefits to same-sex spouses who are lawfully married under state law fails when its purpose and effect are to impose a separate, lesser status on those marriages. Silver Key: Do not let “Congress controls benefits” or “no one has a right to a benefit” answer the wrong question. The call is Equal Protection: why did the government draw this line?

The statute denies federal recognition to a marriage the state has made lawful. The answer does not need to promote sexual orientation to suspect-class status. It also does not ask whether federal benefits exist as a free-standing right. It asks whether this classification may be justified. Under the controlling Windsor/Romer line, a bare desire to demean or injure an identifiable group is not a legitimate governmental interest.

remediation_card.title: Federal benefits + state-law same-sex marriage
remediation_card.signal: Federal law refuses to recognize a same-sex spouse whom state law recognizes.
remediation_card.student_move: Lock the Equal Protection call; avoid both strict-scrutiny overpromotion and benefits-entitlement wrong frame.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Bare animus/equal-dignity injury is not a legitimate interest.
remediation_card.trap: Rational-basis deference plus tradition language.

gold_keys.statement: When a federal marriage-recognition law denies federal benefits to same-sex spouses who are lawfully married under state law for the purpose/effect of marking those marriages as lesser, it fails Fifth Amendment equal-protection principles; bare animus is not a legitimate interest.
gold_keys.trigger: Federal definition of spouse/marriage excludes state-law same-sex spouses from federal benefits.
gold_keys.authority: United States v. Windsor, 570 U.S. 744 (2013); Romer v. Evans, 517 U.S. 620 (1996).

gold_keys.statement: Do not turn Windsor into a strict-scrutiny/suspect-classification answer; Windsor invalidated DOMA without expressly making sexual orientation a suspect classification.
gold_keys.trigger: Answer says sexual orientation is a suspect classification under Windsor-style facts.
gold_keys.authority: United States v. Windsor, 570 U.S. 744 (2013).

silver_keys.statement: When the call is Equal Protection, do not answer whether the benefit exists as a free-standing right; answer whether the government may draw this line.
silver_keys.trigger: Answer talks about Congress’s benefits power or no constitutional right to a benefit.

drill_seeds.prompt: Federal law denies federal recognition to a same-sex spouse lawfully married under state law. What tiny anchor decides the item?
drill_seeds.answer: Bare animus/equal-dignity injury is not a legitimate governmental interest; Windsor/Romer controls.

drill_seeds.prompt: The call asks Equal Protection, but one answer says Congress controls federal benefits. What is the cut?
drill_seeds.answer: NOT_RESPONSIVE misfit: benefits authority does not answer whether the classification violates Equal Protection.

drill_seeds.prompt: An answer says Windsor requires strict scrutiny because sexual orientation is a suspect class. What is the recovery move?
drill_seeds.answer: Do not overpromote Windsor; it invalidated DOMA without expressly declaring suspect-class status.

subject: TORTS
stem:
Lydia operated Road to Emmaus Puzzles, a for-profit Bible-themed puzzle-room business. She leased a narrow mural breezeway behind the shop as the exit path for paying teams. For six years, teams had used the breezeway at night without fights, robberies, threats, or similar security incidents. After Esther finished a paid puzzle session and walked through the breezeway, an unknown stranger entered the breezeway and attacked her. Esther sued Lydia for negligence, claiming Lydia should have posted security guards at the breezeway.

Which duty analysis is most accurate?
call: The call asks for the most accurate duty analysis. Prediction: the guard-duty claim needs a fact making stranger crime foreseeable. Six quiet years points away from guard duty.
distilled_core_question: A paying customer is randomly attacked by an unknown stranger in a business exit area after years with no similar trouble. Did the business have a duty to post security guards?
review_truth: A business is not an insurer against random third-party crime; guard duty needs a foreseeability trigger beyond mere customer status.

choices.text: Lydia owed a duty because Esther had just finished a paid puzzle session.
choices.why_attractive: It notices that Esther was a paying participant, so it feels like the premises relationship is solved. The breaker is that the call asks for a guard-duty trigger, and paid status alone does not make a random attack foreseeable.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Uses a real status fact but does not answer the security-guard duty trigger.
choices.future_cue: Ask: what fact made guards necessary before the attack?

choices.text: Lydia owed a duty because every business must prevent all crimes on its premises.
choices.why_attractive: It converts the broad idea of business safety into a simple protective rule. The breaker is the absolute wording: every business and all crimes turns premises liability into insurance.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Every business/all crimes is an absolute insurance duty.
choices.future_cue: Circle every/all and test whether the law is really absolute.

choices.text: Lydia likely had no duty to post security guards because the random attack was not made foreseeable by prior similar incidents, a created danger, or another guard-duty trigger.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is the best answer.

Silver Key: Lock the exact duty. The question is not “was Esther a paying customer?” It is “did these facts trigger a duty to post security guards against a random third-party attack?”

Gold Key: A business is not an insurer against random third-party crime. Customer status matters, but a guard/security duty needs a foreseeability trigger: prior similar incidents, created risk, imminent danger, or comparable notice.

The stem gives six quiet years, an unknown stranger, and no created danger. That makes C the only answer tied to the duty the lawsuit actually claims.

choices.text: Lydia owed a duty because exit breezeways are inherently dangerous as a matter of law.
choices.why_attractive: It sounds lawyerly because it declares a category dangerous as a matter of law. The breaker is that no stem fact supports automatic danger for every exit breezeway.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Invents an inherent-danger category for exit breezeways.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer names a real trigger or merely labels a location dangerous.

remediation_card.title: Customer status is not guard-duty by itself
remediation_card.signal: A business customer is attacked by an unknown stranger, and the answer says duty exists merely because the person was a customer.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask what specific duty is claimed. If it is guards/security, look for prior similar danger, created risk, imminent danger, or comparable notice.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Status opens the premises-duty lane; foreseeability triggers the security-guard duty.
remediation_card.trap: Treating invitee/customer status as automatic insurance against crime.

gold_keys.statement: A business is not an insurer against random third-party crime. Customer status matters, but guard/security duty needs a foreseeability trigger such as prior similar incidents, created risk, imminent danger, or comparable notice.
gold_keys.trigger: A customer is attacked by an unknown third party and sues for missing security guards.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 344 cmt. f; Restatement (Second) of Torts § 314A business-invitee principles, lawyer-confirmation only.

silver_keys.statement: Lock the exact duty before reading the choices: the question is not whether Esther was a customer, but whether these facts triggered a guard-duty against a random third-party attack.
silver_keys.trigger: A choice says duty exists merely because the plaintiff bought or completed something at the business.

drill_seeds.prompt: A business must prevent all crimes on its premises.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: tiered_absolute.

drill_seeds.prompt: Duty exists because the plaintiff had just paid for the service.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: status fact only; not guard-duty trigger.

drill_seeds.prompt: No prior similar incidents; unknown stranger attack; guard-duty claim.
drill_seeds.answer: No guard duty absent foreseeability trigger.

subject: EVIDENCE
tension_axis: communication substance and confidentiality vs medium/refusal traps
stem: In a later federal proceeding, the government subpoenas Ruth to authenticate and read a folded prayer-card she alone found while packing her personal study Bible for Naomi’s Psalms class. Daniel, Ruth’s husband, had tucked the card into the Bible during their marriage, and the card said, “I slid the silver coins into the olive-wood nativity crate.” Daniel asserts the marital communications privilege.
call: How should the court rule?
distilled_core_question: A husband privately leaves his wife a written note during marriage. The government later subpoenas the wife to read it. Does marital communications privilege protect it despite written format?
review_truth: A confidential marital communication can be written; the privilege follows the private spouse-to-spouse communication, not the medium or the witness spouse’s refusal.

choices.text: Sustain the objection only if Ruth refuses to testify.
choices.c3_signal: The answer turns on Ruth’s refusal, but the stem says Daniel asserts protection for the communication.
choices.why_attractive: The student remembers that a spouse may have a refusal-to-testify privilege and imports that neighbor rule. The breaker is that Daniel asserts the communication privilege over the message itself.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This answers the witness-spouse refusal frame rather than Daniel’s communication-privilege objection.
choices.future_cue: Separate communications privilege from testimonial refusal.

choices.text: Overrule the objection, because the prayer-card is a document rather than a communication.
choices.c3_signal: The choice says document status defeats communication status; the Gold Key says the document can embody the communication.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees a physical prayer-card and treats the card’s format as the legal object. The breaker is that a document can embody the protected confidential communication.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This treats document status as defeating communication status.
choices.future_cue: Name the protected object before naming the medium.

choices.text: Sustain the objection, because a confidential written message between spouses during marriage can be a protected marital communication.
choices.c3_signal: Matches the call and the trigger facts: written, confidential, spouse-to-spouse, during marriage.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: C is correct. The prayer-card is written, but that does not defeat the privilege. Gold Key: marital communications privilege protects the confidential spouse-to-spouse communication made during marriage; the protected object is the confidential communication, not the medium. Silver Key: when the answers fight over “spoken words,” “document,” and “refuses to testify,” sort the array by object: communication object beats evidence format and witness-choice bait.

choices.text: Overrule the objection, because the privilege protects only spoken words.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'only' creates a restriction the Gold Key rejects.
choices.why_attractive: The student equates marital communications with spoken conversation. The breaker is the invented oral-only limit.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This invents an oral-only limitation.
choices.future_cue: Treat 'only spoken words' as an invented restriction.

remediation_card.title: Privilege Object, Not Medium
remediation_card.signal: The answer says a writing, text, card, email, or document is not a communication.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the object contains a confidential spouse-to-spouse communication.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Written can still be communication.
remediation_card.trap: format/object confusion

gold_keys.statement: Marital communications privilege protects a confidential communication between spouses during marriage; the communication can be written or electronic, not only spoken.
gold_keys.trigger: private written message between spouses during marriage
gold_keys.authority: FRE 501; SEC v. Lavin; Wolfle v. United States; Trammel v. United States

silver_keys.statement: When privilege answers fight over spoken words, document format, and refusal to testify, ask what object the privilege protects.
silver_keys.trigger: one answer says document; one says spoken; one says spouse refuses

drill_seeds.prompt: A husband privately emails his wife during marriage. Is the email excluded from privilege merely because it is written?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Written can still be a confidential marital communication.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says: 'not privileged because the note is a document.' Name the trap.
drill_seeds.answer: Format/object confusion.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice turns on whether the witness spouse refuses to testify. What call did it answer?
drill_seeds.answer: Adverse spousal testimony, not confidential marital communication.

subject: CONTRACTS
tension_axis: objective commercial performance vs subjective personal dislike
stem:
To stock her private Bible-conference booth, Lydia leased from Stephen a portable printer that made Scripture-verse cards. The lease made rent due only if Lydia was “satisfied that the printer produces 3,200 finished cards per hour.” Before payment came due, Naomi timed three runs; each run produced 3,360 finished cards per hour. Lydia then refused to pay, saying she was honestly dissatisfied because she disliked the printer’s purple case.

Which statement best describes the parties’ rights?
call:
Call: best statement of the parties’ rights.
Adjacent-call trap: whether Lydia honestly disliked the printer.
Prediction: rent is due. The condition is about output, and the output metric was met.
distilled_core_question: A rent condition depends on satisfaction that equipment meets a measurable output rate; the equipment exceeds that rate, but the renter honestly dislikes a nonperformance feature. Must the renter pay?
review_truth: A satisfaction clause about measurable commercial performance uses an objective standard; meeting the metric satisfies the condition despite an honest personal gripe.

choices.text: Stephen can recover only in restitution because the express condition failed.
choices.why_attractive: It sounds precise because it gives Stephen a fallback remedy after a supposed failed condition. The breaker is that the performance metric was met under the commercial-utility Gold Key, so the condition did not fail.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice assumes the express condition failed; under the commercial-output standard, the output metric was met.
choices.future_cue: Apply the Gold Key, then compare 3,200 required to 3,360 actual.

choices.text: Lydia’s satisfaction is judged by an objective commercial standard, and the rent condition is satisfied if the printer met the required commercial performance.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is correct. The clause asks whether Lydia is satisfied that the printer produces a stated commercial output. That is a measurable performance target, not a personal-aesthetic taste term. Gold Key: a satisfaction clause about commercial utility or mechanical performance is judged objectively when a reasonable-person test is practicable. Silver Key: underline what the party must be satisfied *about* before honoring “I was not satisfied.” Here, the target is 3,200 finished cards per hour, and the printer produced 3,360. The rent condition is satisfied.

choices.text: Lydia may refuse rent because any satisfaction clause gives unlimited subjective discretion.
choices.why_attractive: It sells the broad student myth that satisfaction words always make the buyer the judge. The breaker is the absolute any/unlimited language, which collapses a measured-performance clause into personal whim.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The words any and unlimited make the choice structurally overbroad.
choices.future_cue: Mark any/unlimited as the tell.

choices.text: Lydia may refuse rent if she honestly dislikes any aspect of the printer.
choices.why_attractive: It sells a familiar honesty idea: if Lydia truly dislikes the printer, satisfaction sounds absent. The breaker is the wrong frame; this clause asks about output, not personal taste.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice answers a personal-taste satisfaction question, not the measurable-output condition in the stem.
choices.future_cue: Ask: satisfied about what?

remediation_card.title: Satisfaction About What?
remediation_card.signal: A party says 'I was not satisfied' after a measurable performance condition was met.
remediation_card.student_move: Underline the object of satisfaction, then compare it to the facts.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Commercial/mechanical satisfaction is objective; personal taste is subjective.
remediation_card.trap: honest-dislike wrong frame

gold_keys.statement: When a satisfaction condition concerns commercial utility, mechanical fitness, or measurable performance, use an objective reasonable-person standard if practicable. Honest personal dissatisfaction controls only taste/aesthetic satisfaction clauses.
gold_keys.trigger: satisfaction clause tied to a measurable output or performance metric
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 228; commercial/mechanical utility cases applying objective reasonableness.

silver_keys.statement: Before honoring 'not satisfied,' underline what the clause says the party must be satisfied about. If the object is a measurable output, match the answer to the metric, not the buyer's mood.
silver_keys.trigger: satisfaction clause plus test results

drill_seeds.prompt: A satisfaction clause asks whether equipment produces 900 units per hour; tests show 940; buyer dislikes the color. Which standard governs?
drill_seeds.answer: Objective commercial standard.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut the phrase: 'any satisfaction clause gives unlimited subjective discretion.'
drill_seeds.answer: tiered_absolute; NOT_TRUE.

drill_seeds.prompt: Before accepting 'I was not satisfied,' what do you underline?
drill_seeds.answer: What the contract says the party must be satisfied about.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: ownership/title vs possession-only vs lawful custody
splitting_fact: Paul signed bills of sale transferring ownership.
stem:
At a private Christian music expo, Lydia tells Paul, a collector of antique chapel handbell sets, that she is the purchasing manager for a well-known Christian retreat center and is buying seven handbell sets for its chapel choir. Relying on that statement, Paul signs bills of sale transferring ownership of all seven sets to Lydia and accepts Lydia’s personal check. Lydia is not affiliated with the retreat center, the check is drawn on a closed account, and she has no intention of paying. She loads the handbells into her van and leaves with the signed bills of sale.

Of which crime is Lydia most likely guilty?

The original row is BARMATRIX Q# 19263, a Criminal Law and Procedure / Property Crimes item keyed to false pretenses.
call:
Predict before choices: this is not “was there fraud?” It is “which theft label fits the transfer?” The fact to hunt is what Paul transferred.

Prediction: if ownership/title moved because of a present-fact lie, the crime is false pretenses.
distilled_core_question: A buyer lies about current status, the seller signs a bill of sale passing ownership, and the buyer leaves intending not to pay. What theft crime?
review_truth: Title or ownership by a knowingly false present-fact lie is false pretenses; possession-only deception is larceny by trick; lawful custody then conversion is embezzlement.

choices.text: Embezzlement, because Lydia was entrusted with the handbells in a private sale for a Christian music program.
choices.why_attractive: It sees a transaction and turns that into an entrustment story. The breaker is that Paul transferred ownership because of Lydia's lie, not lawful custody for later conversion.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Embezzlement is the neighboring lawful-custody frame; the stem gives ownership transfer by deception.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether Lydia first had lawful custody or whether ownership moved because of fraud.

choices.text: False pretenses, because Lydia obtained ownership of the handbell sets by a knowingly false representation of a present fact.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. Lydia’s false statement was about a present fact: her current role as purchasing manager for a retreat center. Paul relied on that statement and signed bills of sale transferring ownership of the handbell sets.

Gold Key: In property-crime taxonomy, title or ownership by a knowingly false present-fact representation points to false pretenses.

Silver Key: Do not start with “there was deception.” Start with what Paul handed over: ownership/title, possession only, or lawful custody.

choices.text: Larceny by trick, because Lydia used fraudulent misrepresentations to obtain the handbells.
choices.why_attractive: It sees deception and reaches for the familiar deception crime. The breaker is the bill of sale transferring ownership, which moves the case off the possession-only lane.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Larceny by trick is the neighboring possession-only frame; the bill of sale makes ownership the split.
choices.future_cue: Find whether Paul transferred ownership or only possession.

choices.text: False pretenses, because Lydia’s check was drawn on a closed account, constituting a false promise of future payment.
choices.why_attractive: It notices the closed-account check and treats that as the false-pretense basis. The breaker is that the check is intent evidence while the operative present-fact lie is Lydia's claimed role.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The bad check supports intent but does not supply the operative present-fact representation.
choices.future_cue: Separate intent evidence from the present-fact lie that caused the transfer.

remediation_card.title: Property-crime taxonomy: title, possession, custody
remediation_card.signal: Choices name larceny by trick, embezzlement, and false pretenses.
remediation_card.student_move: Find what the victim transferred.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Title/ownership by deceit = false pretenses; possession-only by deceit = larceny by trick; lawful custody then conversion = embezzlement.
remediation_card.trap: Students stop at the visible lie instead of classifying the transfer.

gold_keys.statement: False pretenses is the theft lane for title or ownership obtained by a knowingly false present or past fact. Larceny by trick is possession-only deception; embezzlement is lawful possession followed by conversion.
gold_keys.trigger: deception plus bill of sale/title/ownership transfer
gold_keys.authority: Cornell Wex false pretenses and larceny-by-trick entries; official BarMatrix explanation.

silver_keys.statement: In a theft-taxonomy array, ask what moved first: title/ownership, possession only, or lawful custody. That axis picks the crime before the bad-check fact distracts you.
silver_keys.trigger: multiple property-crime labels in the answer choices

drill_seeds.prompt: Seller signs a bill of sale after a buyer lies about current status. Which lane?
drill_seeds.answer: False pretenses.

drill_seeds.prompt: Borrowed by lie versus sold by lie: classify each.
drill_seeds.answer: Borrowed by lie = larceny by trick; sold by lie = false pretenses.

drill_seeds.prompt: A bad check appears in a false-pretenses stem. What does it usually do?
drill_seeds.answer: It supports fraudulent intent; it does not replace the present-fact lie.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
topic: Judgment as a Matter of Law
stem: In a federal jury trial, Daniel sues Lydia, a private event planner, claiming she breached an agreement to reserve a rented community hall for his Christmas carol banquet. Daniel rests after telling the story of the banquet, but he introduces no evidence that Lydia ever agreed to make the reservation. Lydia moves for judgment as a matter of law on the agreement element. No witness, message, receipt, or admission supports Daniel on that element.
call: What standard should the court apply?
distilled_core_question: After a plaintiff has been fully heard at trial and has no evidence on a required element, what Rule 50 standard governs JMOL?
review_truth: Rule 50 JMOL turns on whether a reasonable jury has a legally sufficient evidentiary basis on the targeted issue, not sympathy, bad faith, or automatic jury submission.

choices.text: Grant JMOL only if Lydia proves Daniel filed the complaint in bad faith.
choices.c3_signal: The choice says 'only if' and shifts from trial evidence to filing motive.
choices.why_attractive: The choice borrows a seriousness screen from filing or sanctions language, so it sounds like a gatekeeping standard. The breaker is that the motion targets trial evidence on one element, not the plaintiff's motive for filing.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice invents a bad-faith filing threshold for a motion that targets evidentiary sufficiency at trial.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the motion attacks filing conduct or trial evidence on the target element.

choices.text: Deny JMOL automatically because any civil case that reaches trial must go to the jury.
choices.c3_signal: Automatically and any civil case are absolute words that erase the procedural gate.
choices.why_attractive: The choice flatters the jury-trial instinct that once evidence starts, everything belongs to the jury. The breaker is the absolute word automatically, because Rule 50 is the trial tool for legally insufficient evidence.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice overclaims that any civil case reaching trial must automatically go to the jury.
choices.future_cue: Mark automatically and any civil case, then recall that Rule 50 is the evidence gate.

choices.text: Grant JMOL if no reasonable jury would have a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find for Daniel on the agreement element.
choices.c3_signal: This is the only choice that talks about a reasonable jury, legally sufficient evidence, and the exact agreement element.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Only C is true and responsive under the Rule 50 anchor and the stem’s no-evidence trigger.

choices.text: Deny JMOL if the judge personally thinks Daniel’s carol banquet is sympathetic.
choices.c3_signal: The choice uses personal sympathy instead of a legal or evidentiary standard.
choices.why_attractive: The choice turns a sympathetic Christian event into a reason to keep the case alive. The breaker is that sympathy is not evidence on the targeted element.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice substitutes sympathy for evidence on the targeted element.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the reason supplies evidence a jury could use.

remediation_card.title: JMOL = evidence gate, not moral gate
remediation_card.signal: Party rests; motion targets one element.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the record contains evidence a reasonable jury could use on that element.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No evidence on an essential element means no legally sufficient jury basis.
remediation_card.trap: Bad faith, sympathy, or jury-autopilot standards.

gold_keys.statement: JMOL asks whether, after a party has been fully heard on an issue, a reasonable jury would have a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find for that party on that issue.
gold_keys.trigger: Party rests; opponent moves for JMOL on a specific element.
gold_keys.authority: Fed. R. Civ. P. 50(a)(1)

silver_keys.statement: On a JMOL motion, stay on trial evidence for the targeted element; do not drift to sympathy, filing conduct, or automatic jury submission.
silver_keys.trigger: Call asks what standard the court should apply to JMOL.

drill_seeds.prompt: A plaintiff rests with no evidence on causation. Defendant moves for JMOL. Cut an answer saying JMOL turns on plaintiff bad faith.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut as fabricated_rule / procedural_frame.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says JMOL must be denied automatically because all civil trials go to the jury. What is the mold?
drill_seeds.answer: tiered_absolute.

drill_seeds.prompt: State the JMOL standard after a party has been fully heard on an issue.
drill_seeds.answer: Whether a reasonable jury would have a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find for that party on that issue.

drill_seeds.prompt: A judge thinks the plaintiff is sympathetic, but the record has no evidence on an element. Does sympathy supply a jury basis?
drill_seeds.answer: No.
