subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
tension_axis: prejudice-only curative measures vs intent-based severe sanctions
splitting_fact: The record shows no deliberate plan to keep the notes from Ruth.
stem: Mary owns Five Loaves Press, a private company that prints Bible-verse memory-card kits for homeschool groups. Ruth sues Five Loaves Press in federal court over a ruined Lent-season print run. Before the complaint was filed, Five Loaves Press knew litigation was likely and its lawyer told the company to preserve project records. The company kept using a project-board app that automatically erased production notes every 14 days. Several 'manna batch' notes about the disputed print run disappeared and cannot be restored from backups or replaced through other discovery. Ruth shows that losing the notes prejudices her proof about when the print run failed. The record shows careless preservation, but not a deliberate plan to keep the notes from Ruth in the lawsuit.
call: Which sanction framework should the court use?
distilled_core_question: ESI that should have been preserved was lost, cannot be restored, and caused prejudice, but there was no intent to deprive. What sanction track applies?
review_truth: Prejudice from lost ESI without intent gets cure-only measures; intent is the gate for adverse inference and case-ending sanctions.

choices.text: The court must instruct the jury that the missing project-board notes were unfavorable to Five Loaves Press.
choices.c3_signal: The stem gives prejudice but removes deliberate deprivation. This answer jumps to the harsher track.
choices.why_attractive: A student sees lost notes and wants the jury to assume the worst. The breaker is the missing intent gate for unfavorable-inference sanctions.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This applies an intent-based jury-inference sanction when the stem gives prejudice but no intent.
choices.future_cue: Ask: prejudice-only track or intent-based track?

choices.text: The court may do nothing because electronically stored project-board notes are not discoverable.
choices.c3_signal: The answer creates a broad category that says electronic project notes are not discoverable.
choices.why_attractive: A student may treat electronic project-board notes as informal and outside discovery. The breaker is that the answer invents a categorical ESI exclusion.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This fabricates a categorical rule that electronic project-board notes are not discoverable.
choices.future_cue: Treat broad 'not discoverable' statements as suspect unless a named rule supports them.

choices.text: The court may order measures no greater than necessary to cure the prejudice caused by the missing notes.
choices.c3_signal: It matches the stem's prejudice/no-intent lane.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It is the only answer calibrated to prejudice without intent.

choices.text: The court must enter a case-ending sanction whenever any electronically stored information is lost.
choices.c3_signal: The words 'must' and 'whenever any' turn a calibrated rule into an automatic penalty.
choices.why_attractive: A student may think spoliation always deserves the harshest punishment. The breaker is the automatic wording: must, whenever any.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This makes a case-ending sanction automatic whenever any ESI is lost.
choices.future_cue: Replace automatic punishment with calibrated sanction ladder.

remediation_card.title: Lost ESI sanction ladder
remediation_card.signal: ESI lost after preservation duty, prejudice shown, no intent.
remediation_card.student_move: Choose cure-the-prejudice measures; cut adverse inference and case-ending sanctions.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Prejudice cures; intent punishes.
remediation_card.trap: Treating lost evidence as automatically unfavorable.

gold_keys.statement: Lost ESI has a sanction ladder: prejudice without intent allows only curative measures no greater than necessary; adverse inference, presumption, dismissal, or default requires intent to deprive.
gold_keys.trigger: lost ESI + prejudice + no deliberate deprivation

silver_keys.statement: Read the choices by sanction severity keyed to mental state: no intent in the stem pushes you away from unfavorable-presumption and case-ending answers.
silver_keys.trigger: one answer cures prejudice; two answers punish as if intent existed

drill_seeds.prompt: Lost ESI, prejudice, no intent. What sanction lane?
drill_seeds.answer: Measures no greater than necessary to cure prejudice.

drill_seeds.prompt: The court must enter default whenever any ESI is lost.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: automatic case-ending sanction overclaim.

drill_seeds.target_skill: sanction severity keyed to mental state
drill_seeds.prompt: One answer cures prejudice; two impose severe punishment. The stem says no intent. Which way should you lean?
drill_seeds.answer: Cure prejudice.

drill_seeds.prompt: The court may do nothing because ESI is not discoverable.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: fabricated categorical exclusion.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: reasonable appearance versus actual hidden rights
stem:
Ruth is volunteering in a privately run Christian bookstore’s Christmas-toy sorting warehouse. From the doorway, she sees Daniel yank Timothy backward by the collar and drive him into a stack of boxed nativity sets. Ruth does not know that Timothy had swung a metal tape dispenser at Daniel moments earlier and that Daniel is using reasonable force to stop Timothy from continuing. Ruth reasonably believes she is watching Daniel unlawfully attack Timothy, so she swats Daniel’s forearm hard enough to make him let go. In truth, Daniel had a valid self-defense claim against Timothy. The jurisdiction follows the majority rule on defense of others. Ruth is charged with battery.

Call: Under the majority rule, does Ruth have a valid defense-of-others claim?
call:
Call lock: defense of others under the majority rule.
Prediction: If majority rule means reasonable appearance, Ruth wins. If alter-ego actual-rights rule controls, Ruth loses. The call says majority rule, so reach for the Gold Key.
distilled_core_question: A defender reasonably but mistakenly protects the apparent victim; the apparent attacker was actually acting in self-defense. Under the majority defense-of-others rule, does the defender still have the defense?
review_truth: Majority defense of others protects a reasonable intervener from a reasonable mistake about who was legally entitled to use force.

choices.text: Yes, but only if Timothy asked Ruth to intervene.
choices.why_attractive: It sells the cognitive move that a bystander should wait for permission before using force. The breaker is that majority defense of others requires reasonable necessity, not a request.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Adds a request requirement not present in the majority defense-of-others rule.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the rule says request, relationship, or reasonable necessity.

choices.text: Yes, because Ruth reasonably believed Timothy was being unlawfully attacked and that using force was necessary.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. The call says majority rule. The stem says Ruth reasonably believed Timothy was being unlawfully attacked and that intervention was necessary. That is the operative defense-of-others frame.

Gold Key: Under the majority rule, defense of others turns on the intervener’s reasonable belief, not on whether the person defended actually had the right to self-defense. No special relationship, request, or full-view-of-the-fight requirement is needed.

Silver Key: Read this answer array as an actual-facts vs reasonable-appearance clash. The hidden truth points toward the alter-ego trap; the stated reasonable appearance points to the majority-rule answer.

choices.text: No, because Daniel actually had the right to use force, making Ruth’s intervention unjustified.
choices.why_attractive: It sells the hidden-truth move: Daniel really was justified, so Ruth should lose. The breaker is that the call selects the majority reasonable-appearance rule, not the alter-ego rule.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Uses the alter-ego actual-rights frame instead of the majority reasonable-appearance frame.
choices.future_cue: Name the axis: majority reasonable appearance versus actual-rights alter ego.

choices.text: No, because Ruth did not personally witness Timothy’s earlier attack on Daniel.
choices.why_attractive: It sells the idea that Ruth needed the whole history before acting. The breaker is that the majority rule allows action on a reasonable belief from the circumstances she saw.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Adds an eyewitness-origin requirement not present in the majority defense-of-others rule.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer adds a condition not in the Gold Key.

remediation_card.title: Defense of others: reasonable appearance beats hidden truth
remediation_card.signal: Intervener reasonably but mistakenly protects the apparent victim.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not ask who was actually entitled to self-defense until you know the rule frame.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Majority rule = reasonable belief; alter ego = actual rights.
remediation_card.trap: Hidden-truth answer feels precise but answers the wrong rule frame.

gold_keys.statement: Majority defense of others is judged by the intervener’s reasonable belief. A reasonable mistake about who was entitled to use force does not forfeit the defense.
gold_keys.trigger: Stem says majority rule and gives both hidden actual facts and reasonable apparent facts.
gold_keys.authority: Model Penal Code § 3.05(1)(b)-(c); representative reasonable-belief statutes; modern majority rule summaries.

silver_keys.statement: When a defense-of-others stem gives hidden actual facts and apparent reasonable facts, name the axis before choosing: actual-rights rule or reasonable-appearance rule.
silver_keys.trigger: Call says majority rule; one choice uses actual facts and one uses reasonable belief.

drill_seeds.prompt: A defender reasonably but mistakenly protects the apparent victim. Does the reasonable mistake defeat the defense under the majority rule?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Majority rule uses reasonable belief.

drill_seeds.target_skill: Actual hidden facts versus reasonable appearance
drill_seeds.prompt: One answer says the apparent attacker actually had self-defense. Another says the intervener reasonably believed force was needed. What is the axis?
drill_seeds.answer: Alter-ego actual rights versus majority reasonable appearance.

drill_seeds.prompt: Defense of others applies only if the person defended asked for help. What mold is this?
drill_seeds.answer: fabricated_rule; NOT_TRUE after the Gold Key.

drill_seeds.prompt: Defense of others fails because the defender did not witness the start of the fight. What mold is this?
drill_seeds.answer: fabricated_rule; NOT_TRUE after the Gold Key.

subject: EVIDENCE
tension_axis: testimonial route vs communications route
splitting_fact: divorced now; private statement during marriage
stem:
In a federal wire-fraud prosecution against Timothy over online sales from his small Christian-craft booth, the prosecutor plans to call Lydia. Timothy and Lydia finalized their divorce eighteen months ago. Years earlier, while they were married, the two were sitting alone in Timothy’s parked delivery van after a city winter fair when Timothy quietly told Lydia, “I forged the online invoices for those hymn-themed candle orders.” Timothy objects to Lydia’s testimony about that private statement on spousal-privilege grounds.

How should the court rule?

Source row: BARMATRIX Q# 19379, Evidence, Marital Communications Privilege.
call:
The call is a privilege ruling.

Prediction after Gold Key: divorce knocks out the adverse-testimonial route, but the private statement made during marriage points to the confidential-communications route. Expect a sustain answer using the communications route.
distilled_core_question: Former spouse is called in a federal criminal case to testify about a private statement made during the marriage. Does divorce defeat the privilege objection?
review_truth: Divorce ends the adverse-testimonial route, not the confidential-communications route for private statements made during marriage.

choices.text: Overrule the objection because incriminating statements between spouses are never privileged in a criminal case.
choices.why_attractive: A student may think incriminating criminal statements should always come in. The breaker is that incriminating content alone does not erase a valid confidential marital communication privilege.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word never overclaims; incriminating content does not itself erase communications privilege.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether any privilege route survives despite incriminating content.

choices.text: Sustain the objection if Timothy’s statement was a confidential marital communication made during the marriage; divorce ends the adverse spousal testimonial privilege, but it does not by itself eliminate the marital communications privilege for prior confidential communications.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. Gold Key: spousal testimonial privilege and confidential marital communications privilege are separate routes. The testimonial privilege depends on a current marriage; the communications privilege can protect confidential private communications made during the marriage even after divorce.

Silver Key: when the array splits “sustain/overrule” and “testimonial/communications,” match the privilege route to the timing facts. Timothy and Lydia are divorced now, but the statement was private and made while they were married. The communications route, not the testimonial route, is the responsive route.

choices.text: Overrule the objection because divorce ends every spousal privilege for statements made during the marriage.
choices.why_attractive: A student may know divorce matters and overapply that fact to every spousal privilege. The breaker is the Gold Key distinction between testimonial privilege and confidential communications privilege.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word every collapses two spousal privileges into one divorce rule.
choices.future_cue: Separate testimonial privilege from confidential marital communications privilege.

choices.text: Sustain the objection under the adverse spousal testimonial privilege because Lydia is being asked to testify adversely against Timothy.
choices.why_attractive: A student may stop at the correct surface result, sustain. The breaker is that the route is adverse testimonial privilege, and the divorce fact points away from that route.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It reaches sustain under the wrong privilege route.
choices.future_cue: Between two sustain answers, choose the privilege route that matches the timing facts.

remediation_card.title: Do not collapse the two spousal privileges
remediation_card.signal: Divorced spouse asked about a private statement from the marriage.
remediation_card.student_move: Separate testimonial privilege from communications privilege before choosing sustain or overrule.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Current marriage matters for testimonial privilege; private communication during marriage matters for communications privilege.
remediation_card.trap: Divorce ends everything.

gold_keys.statement: Spousal testimonial privilege and confidential marital communications privilege are separate. Testimonial privilege requires a current marriage; communications privilege can protect confidential private communications made during the marriage even after divorce.
gold_keys.trigger: Divorced former spouse + private statement made during marriage.
gold_keys.authority: FRE 501; Trammel v. United States; Pereira v. United States.

silver_keys.statement: When the answer set splits sustain/overrule and testimonial/communications, pick the route that matches the timing facts: divorced now, private communication then.
silver_keys.trigger: Two sustain answers with different privilege labels.

drill_seeds.prompt: A divorced former spouse is called to testify about a private statement from the marriage. Which privilege route is live?
drill_seeds.answer: Confidential marital communications privilege.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut the defect: 'Divorce ends every spousal privilege.'
drill_seeds.answer: Tiered absolute; divorce does not end every spousal privilege.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two answers say sustain. One says adverse testimonial privilege; one says confidential marital communications privilege. The parties are divorced, but the statement was private and made during marriage. Which route wins?
drill_seeds.answer: Confidential marital communications privilege.

subject: REAL_PROPERTY
topic: Conveyance by Deed — Requirements for Valid Deed
tension_axis: recording as validity condition vs recording as notice/priority protection
splitting_fact: No third party claims the parcel.
stem:
Naomi owned a small olive-press parcel behind her bakery. After Lydia completed a private hymn-calligraphy commission for Naomi, Naomi signed and handed Lydia a deed conveying the parcel to Lydia. The deed contained all required deed terms, and Lydia accepted it. Lydia tucked the deed inside a Psalms hymnal and never recorded it. No later buyer, lender, creditor, or other third party claims the parcel. Naomi later says the deed did not work because no recorder’s stamp was ever placed on it.

Who owns the olive-press parcel?
call: The call is ownership between the original grantor and grantee. The adjacent trap is recording priority. Prediction after Gold Key: Lydia owns.
distilled_core_question: Grantor signed, delivered, and grantee accepted a valid deed, but the grantee never recorded it. No third party claims the land. Who owns it?
review_truth: Recording protects against outsiders; it is not required for a valid deed to pass title between grantor and grantee.

choices.text: Naomi, because a deed that is not recorded is void.
choices.why_attractive: This sells the harsh memory that missing a public filing kills a property transfer. The breaker is the Gold Key: recording protects priority, not validity between the original parties.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice states the recording myth in its harshest form: unrecorded equals void.
choices.future_cue: Apply the Gold Key and ask whether a protected third party appears.

choices.text: Naomi, because the county recorder’s stamp is a deed-validity formality.
choices.why_attractive: This sells a formalities reflex by turning the recorder’s stamp into another deed requirement. The breaker is that the stem already gives the deed-validity facts and the stamp belongs to recording.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice invents a recorder-stamp deed-validity requirement.
choices.future_cue: Use the stem: all required deed terms were already supplied.

choices.text: Lydia, because recording is not required for a valid deed to pass title between grantor and grantee.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. The stem gives the title-transfer facts: Naomi signed the deed, delivered it, Lydia accepted it, and the deed contained the required deed terms. No outsider claims the parcel. That makes the question a validity-between-the-parties question, not a recording-priority question.

Gold Key: A valid deed passes title between grantor and grantee when delivered and accepted; recording protects notice and priority against outsiders, not validity between the original parties.

Silver Key: Read the answer array as a 3-vs-1 recording trap. Three choices give the property back to Naomi because of recording; one choice answers the actual call: title between the original parties.

choices.text: Naomi, until Lydia records the deed.
choices.why_attractive: This sells a timing compromise: Lydia will own later, after recording. The breaker is that title passed when the valid deed was delivered and accepted; no later recording step is needed between these parties.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice reverses the timing by treating recording as the event that passes title.
choices.future_cue: Delivery and acceptance do the title-passing work; recording is not the timing gate here.

remediation_card.title: Recording vs Validity
remediation_card.signal: Valid deed delivered and accepted, but not recorded.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask: original parties or outsider priority?
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No outsider: recording is not required for title to pass between grantor and grantee.
remediation_card.trap: Treating the recorder’s office as the title-transfer event.

gold_keys.statement: A valid deed delivered and accepted passes title between grantor and grantee even if unrecorded; recording protects notice and priority against outsiders.
gold_keys.trigger: Valid deed + delivery + acceptance + no recording + no third-party claimant.

silver_keys.statement: When three choices make missing recording decide ownership, first ask whether the stem has an outsider. No outsider means the array is testing validity between the original parties.
silver_keys.trigger: All distractors point to nonrecording.

drill_seeds.prompt: A valid deed is delivered and accepted but not recorded. No third party appears. Who owns?
drill_seeds.answer: The grantee owns; recording is not required between grantor and grantee.

drill_seeds.prompt: Three choices give the grantor title because the deed was not recorded. One gives the grantee title because delivery and acceptance occurred. What is the array testing?
drill_seeds.answer: Recording vs validity.

drill_seeds.prompt: What fact would change this into a recording-act priority question?
drill_seeds.answer: A later buyer, lender, creditor, or other protected third-party claimant.

subject: CONTRACTS
tension_axis: same-contract cap travels with intended-beneficiary right vs nonparty escape from the cap
splitting_fact: The beneficiary promise and liability cap are in the same written contract.
stem: Hannah spent $26,000 replacing unusable Scripture-memory audio tracks after Lydia, a freelance sound engineer, delivered corrupted masters. The work had been commissioned under Peter's written service contract with Lydia. That contract required Lydia to prepare the tracks for Hannah's private tutoring program and stated, "Lydia's total liability for any audio-work claim is capped at $12,000." Hannah sues Lydia as an intended beneficiary and seeks $26,000.
call: Which argument is Lydia's strongest response?
distilled_core_question: A written service contract directly benefits a named third party and caps liability. The third party sues as an intended beneficiary for more than the cap. Is the beneficiary limited by the cap?
review_truth: A third-party beneficiary can enforce the contract only as the contract gives it; the beneficiary does not get the benefit without the cap.

choices.text: Hannah may enforce the promise only up to the contract's $12,000 liability cap.
choices.c3_signal: This choice keeps the benefit and the cap inside the same contract.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It is true and responsive after C is cut for overclaim, B for wrong route, and D under the same-contract cap axis.

choices.text: Hannah may recover only if Peter first assigns her the audio-service contract.
choices.c3_signal: The stem says intended beneficiary; the answer demands assignment.
choices.why_attractive: Assignment sounds like a legitimate way for a nonparty to receive contract rights. The breaker is that the stem already supplies third-party-beneficiary status, so assignment answers the wrong route.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Assignment is a real contract-rights route, but it answers a different route from the one in the stem.
choices.future_cue: Say: 'TPB route is already in the stem; assignment is not required.'

choices.text: Hannah cannot recover anything because beneficiaries can never enforce audio-service contracts.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'never' makes a categorical claim the stem itself pressures.
choices.why_attractive: The privity reflex makes it feel safe to say an outsider gets nothing. The breaker is the categorical word 'never,' because intended beneficiaries are not categorically barred from enforcing service contracts.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word 'never' overstates the rule by denying all intended-beneficiary enforcement of audio-service contracts.
choices.future_cue: Circle 'never' and ask whether the stem directly names the beneficiary.

choices.text: Hannah may recover the full $26,000 because she did not sign the liability cap.
choices.c3_signal: It uses the contract for the right but rejects the same contract for the cap.
choices.why_attractive: Nonparty status makes the liability cap feel like a private bargain Hannah never accepted. The breaker is the package rule: Hannah's enforcement right and the cap come from the same contract.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer reverses the package rule by letting Hannah use the contract for the right while escaping the same contract's cap.
choices.future_cue: Ask: 'What document creates the right, and what document creates the limit?'

remediation_card.title: Third-party beneficiary package deal
remediation_card.signal: A nonparty enforces a contract that also limits the claim.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not split the contract into benefit-only and cap-free pieces.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: TPB right travels with the contract terms.
remediation_card.trap: Nonparty status feels like freedom from the cap.

gold_keys.statement: An intended beneficiary takes the contract as written. If the same contract creates the beneficiary's right and caps liability, the beneficiary's claim is capped.
gold_keys.trigger: A nonparty sues as an intended beneficiary and seeks more than a limit in the same contract.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 302, 309.

silver_keys.statement: In a no-recovery / capped-recovery / full-recovery / assignment answer set, compare the source of the right with the source of the limit. Same source means package answer.
silver_keys.trigger: A beneficiary claims more than a contract limit.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says intended beneficiaries can never enforce service contracts. What is the visible breaker?
drill_seeds.answer: The categorical word 'never' overclaims.

drill_seeds.prompt: A beneficiary sues under a contract that also caps the promisor's liability. What axis decides cap vs full recovery?
drill_seeds.answer: Whether the right and the cap come from the same contract.

drill_seeds.prompt: State the Gold Key for an intended beneficiary and a contract cap.
drill_seeds.answer: An intended beneficiary takes the contract as written; same-contract caps apply.

drill_seeds.prompt: The stem says the plaintiff sues as an intended beneficiary. A choice says recovery requires assignment. What is the mold?
drill_seeds.answer: Bait doctrine / wrong frame.

subject: REAL_PROPERTY
topic: Conveyance by Deed — Requirements for Valid Deed
tension_axis: role-holder grantee vs formalities/entity shortcuts
stem:
Lydia owned a fenced olive grove outside Capernaum. Before leaving for a psalm-singing festival, she signed and delivered a deed stating, “I convey the olive grove to the harp instructor of Capernaum Hymn School today.” At that moment, Daniel was the only harp instructor of Capernaum Hymn School. Daniel accepted the deed.

Who owns the olive grove?
call:
Call: ownership after deed delivery.

Prediction: Daniel owns, if the role description can identify him as grantee.

Adjacent-call traps: personal name, grantee signature, organization name.
distilled_core_question: A deed conveys land to a role-holder; one person held that role at delivery and accepted. Who owns?
review_truth: A role description can identify the grantee if the person holding the role is ascertainable at delivery.

choices.text: Daniel, because the role description identified a specific person when the deed was delivered.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
A is correct. The deed uses a role description, not Daniel’s personal name. Gold Key: A deed can identify a grantee by an office or role if one person fitting that description is reasonably ascertainable when the deed is delivered. Silver Key: Read the recipient phrase before reading the formalities traps: “to the harp instructor” points first to the person who holds that role, not automatically to the school and not back to the grantor.

Daniel was the only harp instructor at the moment of delivery, and he accepted the deed. That makes Daniel the ascertainable grantee.

choices.text: Lydia, because Daniel did not sign the deed.
choices.why_attractive: The student imports the contract habit that the recipient must sign. The breaker is the deed Gold Key: the grantee accepts, but generally need not sign.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Adds a required grantee signature that the Gold Key rejects.
choices.future_cue: Separate grantor execution from grantee acceptance.

choices.text: Lydia, because a deed must state the grantee’s personal name.
choices.why_attractive: The student over-formalizes the deed and thinks only a personal name can work. The breaker is the ascertainability Gold Key: the role description can identify Daniel.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Adds a personal-name requirement that the Gold Key rejects.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether exactly one person fit the role at delivery.

choices.text: Capernaum Hymn School, because the role title automatically makes the school the grantee.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees Capernaum Hymn School inside the phrase and jumps to the organization. The breaker is the recipient phrase: the deed says to the harp instructor, not to the school.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Changes the recipient from the role-holder to the school.
choices.future_cue: Read “to the harp instructor” as pointing to the role-holder.

remediation_card.title: Role Description as Grantee
remediation_card.signal: Deed conveys to “the [role holder] of [organization].”
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether one person fit that role at delivery.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Role description is enough if it identifies one person at delivery.
remediation_card.trap: Do not require the personal name or grantee signature.

gold_keys.statement: A deed does not fail merely because the grantee is described by role rather than personal name. If one person fits the description at delivery, that person is ascertainable and can take title.
gold_keys.trigger: Deed says to the role-holder and one person held that role at delivery.
gold_keys.authority: Vineyard v. O’Connor, 36 S.W. 424 (Tex. 1896), as cited in ConocoPhillips Co. v. Hahn.

gold_keys.statement: A grantee generally need not sign the deed to take title; delivery by the grantor and acceptance by the grantee do the work.
gold_keys.trigger: Answer says the recipient loses because the recipient did not sign.
gold_keys.authority: Tex. Prop. Code § 5.021.

silver_keys.statement: When a deed names a role, separate the role-holder from the organization named inside the role phrase before checking formalities.
silver_keys.trigger: Choice set includes the role-holder, the grantor, and the organization as possible owners.

drill_seeds.prompt: A deed says “to the choir director of a school today.” One person held that role at delivery. Who is the grantee?
drill_seeds.answer: The role-holder.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut the choice: “Grantor keeps title because the grantee did not sign the deed.”
drill_seeds.answer: NOT_TRUE; fabricated_rule; grantee signature generally not required.

drill_seeds.prompt: A deed says “to the treasurer of Mercy Hall.” Does that automatically make Mercy Hall the grantee?
drill_seeds.answer: No; first ask who the role-holder was.

subject: TORTS
stem:
Before Lydia played handbells at a community hymn festival, her physician, Stephen, prescribed a prescription-only wrist nerve stimulator to control hand tremors. The stimulator carried a rare risk of finger numbness that could make fine hand movement difficult. Before Stephen ordered it, Barnabas Biotech sent Stephen an updated professional safety notice that clearly described the risk, symptoms, and alternative treatments. Stephen read the notice, discussed the risk with Lydia, and ordered the stimulator because alternatives were unsuitable. Lydia later suffered finger numbness and sued Barnabas Biotech, arguing that Barnabas did not send the same warning directly to her. The jurisdiction follows the learned-intermediary rule.

Call:
call: Is Lydia likely to prevail on a strict products liability claim for failure to warn against Barnabas Biotech?
distilled_core_question: A prescription-only product had a clear risk warning sent to the prescribing physician, who read it and discussed it with the patient. The patient suffered the warned-of risk and sues because the manufacturer did not warn her directly. Does the failure-to-warn claim succeed?
review_truth: In a learned-intermediary jurisdiction, an adequate warning to the prescribing physician can defeat a direct-to-patient failure-to-warn theory for a prescription product.

choices.text: Yes, because Lydia was injured by the exact risk described in the warning.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: control/supply versus formal ownership
stem: At a rented civic auditorium, Lydia organized a private Christian music night. A vendor left a compressed-air T-shirt cannon for authorized staff to use between songs. Lydia was not the cannon's owner, but under the event agreement she had the key and authority to decide who could handle it during the event. During setup, Lydia handed the cannon to Barnabas, a visibly intoxicated friend who had never used one, so he could "make the praise-team singers laugh." Barnabas fired wildly, knocked over two music stands, and then struck Ruth, a visiting photographer, in the face. Ruth sues Lydia for negligence.
call: Is Ruth likely to establish a negligent entrustment duty against Lydia?
distilled_core_question: A person with authority to control a dangerous chattel gives it to a visibly intoxicated, inexperienced user, who injures a third party. Can the controller face negligent entrustment liability even though she is not the owner?
review_truth: For negligent entrustment, control/supply plus known unsafe user beats formal title.

choices.text: Yes, because negligent entrustment makes Lydia strictly liable for any injury caused by the T-shirt cannon.
choices.c3_signal: The call says negligence duty, but the choice says strict liability and any injury.
choices.why_attractive: The injury makes automatic liability feel satisfying because the chattel was dangerous. The breaker is that 'strictly liable' and 'any injury' overstate a negligence theory.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer converts a negligence-duty theory into strict liability for any injury.
choices.future_cue: Circle 'strictly' and 'any' and cut the overclaim.

choices.text: No, because only the legal owner of a chattel can be liable for negligent entrustment.
choices.c3_signal: This needs the Gold Key: control/supply, not title, is the gate.
choices.why_attractive: Formal title sounds like the clean legal gate for responsibility over property. The breaker is the Gold Key: negligent entrustment looks to control or supply, not just ownership.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer invents a legal-owner-only gate that the Gold Key defeats.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the defendant supplied or controlled access to the chattel.

choices.text: No, because Barnabas alone fired the cannon and third-party conduct always cuts off Lydia's duty.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'always' is the tell, and the call is Lydia's duty.
choices.why_attractive: Barnabas physically fired the cannon, so the student may stop at the operator. The breaker is the word 'always' and the call-focus move: Lydia's duty can arise from foreseeable misuse by the person she supplied.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer overclaims that third-party conduct always cuts off the target defendant's duty.
choices.future_cue: Reject 'always' and ask whether the third-party misuse was the foreseeable risk.

choices.text: Yes, because Lydia supplied the T-shirt cannon to a visibly intoxicated and inexperienced person.
choices.c3_signal: It matches the call and the trigger facts: control, handoff, intoxication, inexperience.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It is the only answer that is both true under the Gold Key and responsive to the duty call.

remediation_card.signal: Non-owner had authority over who could use the chattel.

remediation_card.tiny_rule: For negligent entrustment, supplier/control can be enough; title is not the gate.
remediation_card.trap: Owner-only answer.

silver_keys.statement: Lock the target defendant first: the call asks about Lydia's duty, so an answer focused only on Barnabas's operation is adjacent-call bait.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: minimum required participants vs extra participants
stem:
A state criminalizes an unlicensed paid chariot race between two racers. Peter and John agree to drive such a race at a private Bible-themed harvest fair. Lydia, Ruth, and Barnabas agree to rent a fairground track, sell admission wristbands, and handle the cashbox and livestream fees. Prosecutors charge all five with conspiracy to conduct the illegal chariot race. The defendants invoke Wharton’s Rule.

What is the best response?
call:
Call: best response to a Wharton’s Rule defense.
Prediction: count the needed participants and the actual agreement participants. If extra people joined, the charge survives.
distilled_core_question: A two-person target offense has two required participants, but three extra people join the plan. Does Wharton’s Rule bar conspiracy?
review_truth: Wharton’s Rule does not bar conspiracy when extra participants beyond the target offense’s minimum join the agreement.

choices.text: Wharton’s Rule always bars a conspiracy charge whenever the target offense involves any agreement.
choices.why_attractive: The student reaches for a clean universal rule because the answer sounds decisive. The breaker is that always/whenever language over-expands a narrow doctrine.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer expands a narrow rule with always/whenever language.
choices.future_cue: Mark always/whenever and ask whether a narrow exception exists.

choices.text: Wharton’s Rule bars the conspiracy charge only because the organizers hoped to make money from the event.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats profit as the reason the organizers matter. The breaker is that participant count, not payment, is the Wharton's Rule axis.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer focuses on money rather than participant count.
choices.future_cue: Rename the axis as participant count, not compensation.

choices.text: Wharton’s Rule does not bar the charge because the agreement includes extra participants beyond the two racers needed for the offense.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: C is correct. Gold Key: Wharton’s Rule is narrow; the extra-participant exception takes the case outside the merger idea when people beyond those necessary for the target offense join the agreement. Silver Key: count the people the target offense needs, then count the people who joined the plan. Here, the chariot-race offense needs two racers, but five people joined the plan. The three organizers are extra participants, so Wharton’s Rule does not bar the conspiracy charge.

choices.text: Wharton’s Rule bars the conspiracy charge because the illegal chariot race requires two racers.
choices.why_attractive: The student remembers the base Wharton's Rule idea that a two-party offense can absorb conspiracy. The breaker is the extra-party exception when unnecessary organizers join the agreement.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer states the base two-party idea but omits the extra-party exception.
choices.future_cue: Apply the extra-party exception after counting actual participants.

remediation_card.title: Wharton Count Check
remediation_card.signal: Wharton's Rule plus extra people in the agreement
remediation_card.student_move: Count required participants first; count actual agreement participants second.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Extra participants defeat Wharton's Rule.
remediation_card.trap: Stopping at the two-party offense and missing the extra-party exception.

gold_keys.statement: Wharton's Rule can bar conspiracy only when the target offense already requires the same minimum parties. If extra people beyond that minimum join the agreement, the conspiracy charge survives.
gold_keys.trigger: two-person target offense plus organizers or other extra participants
gold_keys.authority: Iannelli v. United States, 420 U.S. 770 (1975)

silver_keys.statement: When Wharton's Rule appears, count twice: how many people the target offense needs, then how many people joined the plan.
silver_keys.trigger: a two-party offense with extra planners, sellers, organizers, or facilitators

misconception_tags: all agreement crimes merge with conspiracy

drill_seeds.prompt: Two required participants plus one unnecessary helper join the plan. Does Wharton's Rule bar conspiracy?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Extra participants defeat the bar.

drill_seeds.answer: Minimum required participants vs actual agreement participants.

drill_seeds.answer: Cut as overclaim.

drill_seeds.answer: Wrong fact axis; payment is not the trigger.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
tension_axis: taxing-power revenue frame vs imported scrutiny/equality/economic-impact frames
stem:
After several costly nationwide flood-control projects, Congress enacted the Manna Festival Finals Revenue Act as part of a broader plan to retire federal disaster-recovery debt. For six years, the Act imposed a 40% excise tax on the price of paid admission wristbands to final-round artisan food competitions. Covered events included the Manna Bread Cup, the Loaves-and-Fishes Fish-Fry Crown, the Ruth Harvest Pie Finals, and similar paid championship food contests.

This federal tax is probably
call:
Call: Is this federal tax probably constitutional?
Prediction: Yes. This is framed as a revenue tax. No protected-right trigger appears.
distilled_core_question: Congress imposes a high temporary federal excise tax on paid admission to one category of final-round events to raise revenue. Is the tax likely constitutional despite possible economic harm to the taxed events?
review_truth: A facially revenue-raising federal excise tax is usually valid even if it hurts the taxed activity; do not jump to strict scrutiny or equal protection without a trigger.

choices.text: unconstitutional, because Congress violates the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment by taxing final-round artisan food competitions while failing to tax other large paid food festivals.
choices.why_attractive: This sells the fairness instinct that if Congress taxes one large paid event category, it should tax neighboring paid event categories too. The breaker is the fabricated all-or-nothing tax rule; no suspect class or fundamental-right trigger appears.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice invents an all-or-nothing tax classification rule.
choices.future_cue: Require a protected trigger or a truly irrational classification before using equal protection to defeat a tax.

choices.text: unconstitutional, because a 40% admission tax is likely to reduce attendance at these final-round competitions and, therefore, is not rationally related to Congress’s legitimate interest in retiring disaster-recovery debt.
choices.why_attractive: This sells the economic-impact worry that a high tax might shrink attendance and therefore look self-defeating. The breaker is the non sequitur; a paid-admission excise tax can still be rationally connected to revenue even if attendance drops.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The attendance-impact reason does not prove the tax lacks a revenue relationship.
choices.future_cue: Say: burdening the taxed activity is not the same as lacking a revenue relation.

choices.text: constitutional, because an act of Congress that appears to be a revenue-raising measure on its face is not rendered invalid because it may have adverse economic consequences for the activity taxed.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: C is correct. The Act is framed as a revenue measure: it imposes an excise tax on paid admissions and is tied to retiring federal debt. Gold Key: A federal tax that is facially revenue-raising is not invalid merely because it burdens, discourages, or economically harms the taxed activity. Silver Key: In this array, first lock the call as a federal taxing-power question; then distrust the answers that import strict scrutiny, equal protection, or attendance-impact framing without a trigger.

choices.text: constitutional, because the compelling national interest in retiring federal disaster-recovery debt justifies this tax as a temporary emergency measure.
choices.why_attractive: This sells the strongest-sounding constitutional vocabulary by pairing an emergency with a compelling national interest. The breaker is the wrong frame; the stem gives a revenue tax, not a strict-scrutiny trigger.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice imports strict-scrutiny language without a trigger.
choices.future_cue: Classify the claim home first: this is a tax-power item, not a heightened-scrutiny item.

remediation_card.title: Tax-power frame before scrutiny frame
remediation_card.signal: Federal excise tax + revenue purpose + answer choices invoking strict scrutiny or equal protection.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the stem gives a protected trigger. If not, stay in the revenue-tax frame.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Bad economic effects do not by themselves invalidate a facial revenue tax.
remediation_card.trap: Picking the dramatic constitutional standard instead of the tax-power answer.

gold_keys.statement: A federal excise tax that is facially revenue-raising is usually valid even if it burdens, discourages, or economically harms the taxed activity.
gold_keys.trigger: federal excise tax + revenue/debt purpose + argument that the tax hurts the taxed activity
gold_keys.authority: U.S. Const. art. I, §8; Sonzinsky v. United States; Fernandez v. Wiener

gold_keys.statement: Ordinary economic and tax classifications do not get strict scrutiny unless the stem gives a suspect class, fundamental right, or other protected trigger.
gold_keys.trigger: tax classification + compelling-interest or equal-protection answer with no protected trigger
gold_keys.authority: Regan v. Taxation With Representation; FCC v. Beach Communications

silver_keys.statement: When a Con Law tax array mixes compelling interest, rational relation, equal protection, and economic-impact language, first lock the question as taxing power before liking the strongest-sounding constitutional phrase.
silver_keys.trigger: revenue tax stem with multiple constitutional standards in the answer set

drill_seeds.answer: Cut the strict-scrutiny frame unless the stem gives a protected trigger.

drill_seeds.answer: No. Economic burden does not erase the revenue-tax frame.

drill_seeds.answer: A facial revenue tax is usually valid even if it burdens or discourages the taxed activity.

drill_seeds.answer: Taxing power.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
tension_axis: heightened-review trigger vs default rational basis
stem: The State of Galilee funds its public schools with a statewide foundation grant plus whatever each local district raises through local property taxes. In Cana Hills, a lakeside district with expensive homes and commercial property, the public schools spend about $22,400 per student each year. In Bethany Flats, an old cannery district with a small tax base, the public schools spend about $7,300 per student each year. Mary, Peter, and Lydia, parents of children in Bethany Flats, bring an Equal Protection challenge. They argue that the funding plan denies their children an equal public education. The state responds that the plan preserves local control of schools and rationally connects local tax revenue to local school spending.
call: Under Equal Protection analysis, which standard of review applies, and how should the court likely rule?
distilled_core_question: A state public-school funding plan creates large district spending gaps because local property-tax bases differ. Parents in the lower-funded district sue under Equal Protection. What review applies, and does the plan likely survive?
review_truth: School-funding disparities tied to local property-tax wealth get rational basis review under federal Equal Protection unless a real suspect-class, quasi-suspect-class, or fundamental-right trigger is present.

choices.text: Strict scrutiny applies because the funding gap falls most heavily on low-income students, and low-income students are a suspect class.
choices.student_label: False trigger: low-income status as suspect class.
choices.c3_signal: Strict scrutiny requires a valid heightened-review trigger; this choice names poverty/low income as the trigger.
choices.why_attractive: The choice makes the student’s inequality instinct do the work by treating low-income status as suspect. The breaker is that school-funding poverty or local wealth disparities do not trigger strict scrutiny under the Gold Key.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice treats low-income status as a suspect-class trigger for strict scrutiny.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the claimed class is a recognized suspect class for this federal Equal Protection claim.

choices.text: Strict scrutiny applies because the disparity effectively denies students in the lower-tax-base district equal access to public education, which is a fundamental right.
choices.student_label: False trigger: education as federal fundamental right.
choices.c3_signal: Strict scrutiny requires a valid fundamental-right trigger; this choice supplies education.
choices.why_attractive: The choice feels right because education sounds too important to be reviewed deferentially. The breaker is the Gold Key that public education is not a federal fundamental right in this school-funding Equal Protection setting.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice treats public education as a federal fundamental right in a school-funding case.
choices.future_cue: Recall that Rodriguez places local-property-tax school funding in rational basis review.

choices.text: Intermediate scrutiny applies because the facially neutral funding plan systematically disadvantages lower-income districts that substantially overlap with racial-minority communities.
choices.c3_signal: The choice names effect and racial overlap, but the heightened-review trigger is not supplied.
choices.why_attractive: The choice converts racial overlap and unequal effects into a heightened-scrutiny trigger. The breaker is that disparate impact alone is not enough without discriminatory purpose or a racial classification.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice gives impact and racial overlap, but not discriminatory purpose or a racial classification.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the stem gives discriminatory purpose or a facial racial classification.

choices.text: Rational basis review applies, and the plan likely survives because local control of public schools and tying local tax revenue to local school spending are conceivable legitimate government interests.
choices.c3_signal: Default tier plus state rationale matches the call.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: After the invalid heightened-review triggers are cut by Gold Keys, only the default-tier answer remains.

remediation_card.title: Tier trigger before tier label
remediation_card.signal: Answer names strict or intermediate scrutiny.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask what trigger the answer supplies.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No valid trigger means default rational basis.
remediation_card.trap: Picking the strongest-sounding tier because the facts feel unfair.

gold_keys.statement: Public education is not a federal fundamental right, and poverty/local district wealth is not a suspect class for school-funding disparities; rational basis applies.
gold_keys.trigger: public-school funding gap caused by local property-tax bases
gold_keys.authority: San Antonio Independent School District v. Rodriguez, 411 U.S. 1 (1973)

gold_keys.statement: A facially neutral policy’s racial disparate impact does not by itself trigger heightened Equal Protection scrutiny; look for discriminatory purpose or a racial classification.
gold_keys.trigger: neutral funding formula plus racial overlap language
gold_keys.authority: Washington v. Davis, 426 U.S. 229 (1976)

silver_keys.statement: In a scrutiny-tier array, read each heightened-review answer by its trigger, not by how morally serious the inequality feels.
silver_keys.trigger: Strict / intermediate / rational-basis answer spread

drill_seeds.prompt: A local-property-tax public-school funding plan creates richer and poorer districts. Is education a federal fundamental right for strict scrutiny?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Rational basis applies under the school-funding Gold Key.

drill_seeds.answer: Check the trigger each heightened-review choice names.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
stem:
Mary, a freelance scenic painter and citizen of State F, sued MannaJoy Props, Inc., a company incorporated in State G with its principal place of business in State H, in federal district court. Mary demanded $130,000 for false imprisonment. Her complaint stated that “Mary was shut inside the whale-belly compartment of a Jonah parade float from late cleanup until sunrise when a MannaJoy technician negligently latched the service hatch without realizing Mary was still painting inside.” Mary suffered no physical harm from being in the float.

MannaJoy filed a motion to dismiss. How should the court rule?
call:
Call: How should the court rule on the motion to dismiss?

Prediction:

* Do not start with damages probability.
* Check the complaint’s own facts.
* The complaint says “false imprisonment” but pleads negligent confinement.
* With the Gold Key, that means the complaint fails to state the chosen claim.

Predicted ruling: grant the motion.
distilled_core_question: A federal complaint claims false imprisonment but pleads negligent confinement. On a motion to dismiss, should the court dismiss for failure to state a claim?
review_truth: A motion-to-dismiss answer must match the defect in the complaint; negligent confinement does not state false imprisonment.

choices.text: Grant the motion, because a court would be unlikely to award more than $75,000 in damages on these facts.
choices.why_attractive: This choice gives the same grant result and makes the damages feel too speculative. The breaker is that likely recovery is not the amount-in-controversy standard and not the claim-sufficiency defect.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This invents a likely-recovery amount-in-controversy standard and does not resolve the claim-sufficiency defect.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the reason is the actual motion defect.

choices.text: Deny the motion, because there is no indication that it is impossible for recovery to exceed $75,000.
choices.why_attractive: This choice states the amount-in-controversy frame students remember from diversity jurisdiction. The breaker is that the motion is granted because the complaint fails to state false imprisonment, not because federal jurisdiction is missing.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This uses the amount-in-controversy frame when the operative defect is failure to state false imprisonment.
choices.future_cue: Separate jurisdiction survival from claim survival.

choices.text: Grant the motion, because the complaint fails to state a claim.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. The motion should be granted because the complaint’s own facts defeat the claim it chose. The complaint says the technician negligently latched the hatch without realizing Mary was inside. That pleaded fact does not support false imprisonment as an intentional confinement claim.

Gold Key: False imprisonment is an intentional-confinement claim. If the complaint pleads only negligent confinement, the complaint itself knocks out the claim.

Silver Key: Do not pick by outcome alone. A “grant” answer with the wrong jurisdictional reason is still a trap; the credited answer must match the ground that defeats the complaint.

choices.text: Deny the motion, because the complaint gives MannaJoy notice of the claim being asserted.
choices.why_attractive: This choice leans on the familiar notice-pleading idea. The breaker is that notice does not cure a complaint that pleads facts defeating the selected claim.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This supplies notice but does not answer the complaint-negates-element problem.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether notice also shows entitlement to relief.

remediation_card.title: Complaint label vs complaint facts
remediation_card.signal: The complaint labels an intentional tort but describes negligence.
remediation_card.student_move: Check whether the pleaded facts support the claim label.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: A complaint can defeat itself by pleading facts inconsistent with an element of the selected claim.
remediation_card.trap: Notice pleading and amount-in-controversy side paths.

gold_keys.statement: False imprisonment requires intentional confinement. A complaint that pleads only negligent confinement defeats that claim at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
gold_keys.trigger: Complaint labels false imprisonment but says the confinement happened negligently.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §35; Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6); Ashcroft v. Iqbal.

gold_keys.statement: Amount in controversy is not a likely-verdict test. The pleaded amount controls unless it is legally certain the claim is below the jurisdictional threshold.
gold_keys.trigger: Answer choice talks about unlikely recovery above $75,000.
gold_keys.authority: 28 U.S.C. §1332; St. Paul Mercury Indem. Co. v. Red Cab Co.

silver_keys.statement: On a motion-to-dismiss array, match the reason to the motion. Same outcome plus wrong procedural reason is a trap.
silver_keys.trigger: Two choices talk about amount in controversy while one choice talks about failure to state a claim.

drill_seeds.prompt: A motion should be granted. One answer grants on the wrong jurisdictional reason; another grants on failure to state a claim. Which survives?
drill_seeds.answer: The answer with the correct motion ground survives.

drill_seeds.prompt: Complaint says false imprisonment but pleads accidental or negligent confinement. Does it state false imprisonment?
drill_seeds.answer: No. False imprisonment requires intentional confinement.

drill_seeds.prompt: Complaint gives notice but pleads facts defeating one element. Is notice enough?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Notice does not cure facts that defeat the claim.

drill_seeds.prompt: Is federal amount in controversy defeated merely because recovery over $75,000 is unlikely?
drill_seeds.answer: No. The likely recovery is not the standard.

Peter says paying workers to locate, box, and scan the papers will be expensive, so he seeks an immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine.
call: Is the court of appeals likely to hear the appeal now?
distilled_core_question: A party is ordered to produce ordinary nonprivileged documents in discovery and says compliance is expensive. Is that discovery order immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine?
review_truth: Ordinary discovery orders generally wait for final-judgment review; cost does not make them collateral orders.

choices.text: Yes, because any discovery order that deals with a side issue instead of the merits is immediately appealable.
choices.c3_signal: The answer gives only side-issue separateness and treats it as enough.
choices.why_attractive: The student recognizes that collateral-order doctrine deals with issues separate from the merits. The breaker is that one prong is not the whole appealability gate.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It treats separateness from the merits as enough and omits the narrowness/effective-unreviewability gate.
choices.future_cue: Say: one prong is not the test.

choices.text: No, because an ordinary document-production order usually must wait for final-judgment review.
choices.c3_signal: The answer matches the procedural gate and the ordinary-discovery trigger.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is the best answer. The order is an ordinary document-production order. The fact that retrieving and scanning the documents will cost money does not make the order immediately appealable.

Gold Key: Collateral-order review is narrow. A discovery order must fit the small class of orders that are effectively unreviewable after final judgment; ordinary discovery-cost complaints do not.

Silver Key: In an appealability array, read the fight as review now vs review later. Cut the extreme “any/every/never/automatically” answers first, then ask whether final-judgment review is enough.

choices.text: No, because a discovery order can never be challenged by any route.
choices.c3_signal: The word never overclaims. Later or extraordinary review is not the same as immediate appeal.
choices.why_attractive: The student knows ordinary discovery orders usually are not appealable now and overcorrects. The breaker is that no immediate appeal does not mean no challenge by any route.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It says discovery orders can never be challenged, turning no immediate appeal into no review by any route.
choices.future_cue: Say: not now is not never.

choices.text: Yes, because an expensive production order automatically qualifies as a collateral order.
choices.c3_signal: Automatically turns litigation cost into immediate appeal.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats expense as a fairness reason for immediate appellate protection. The breaker is that cost does not automatically satisfy collateral-order narrowness.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It says expense automatically creates a collateral order.
choices.future_cue: Say: cost is bait; gate first.

remediation_card.title: Finality Gate: Ordinary Discovery Waits
remediation_card.signal: Immediate appeal from a discovery order.
remediation_card.student_move: Treat cost as bait; check whether later review is enough.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Collateral order is narrow; ordinary discovery orders usually wait.
remediation_card.trap: Turning expense or separateness into immediate appeal.

gold_keys.statement: Collateral-order review is narrow. Ordinary discovery orders generally wait for final judgment; expense alone is not effective unreviewability.
gold_keys.trigger: Immediate appeal from a discovery order under the collateral order doctrine.
gold_keys.authority: 28 U.S.C. §1291; Cohen; Mohawk; Cunningham.

silver_keys.statement: In an appealability array, sort answers as review-now or review-later. Cut the extreme words first, then ask whether final judgment review is enough.
silver_keys.trigger: Immediate appeal + discovery order + collateral order doctrine.

drill_seeds.prompt: Classify: 'An expensive discovery order automatically qualifies as a collateral order.'
drill_seeds.answer: NOT_TRUE; tiered_absolute; cost is not automatic appealability.

drill_seeds.prompt: A party must produce ordinary nonprivileged records and wants immediate appeal because production is costly. Appeal now?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Ordinary discovery waits for final judgment.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two choices say yes-now, two choices say no-now. What axis should you name?
drill_seeds.answer: Review now vs review after final judgment.

drill_seeds.prompt: Why is 'separate from the merits' not enough?
drill_seeds.answer: It is only one collateral-order requirement.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
tension_axis: fact itself vs communication about the fact
stem: At Lydia's privately owned Christian bookstore, Ruth was injured when a portable wooden "Red Sea crossing" bridge used for a paid Bible-story craft night shifted under her. Ruth sues Lydia in federal court for negligence. In an interrogatory, Ruth asks Lydia to identify who tightened the bridge's bolts earlier that day. Lydia refuses, saying the answer is privileged because she gave that name to her lawyer during a confidential meeting seeking legal advice.
call: Is the identity of the person who tightened the bolts protected from discovery on that ground?
distilled_core_question: Can a party refuse to identify a relevant fact in an interrogatory just because the party told that fact to a lawyer while seeking legal advice?
review_truth: Privilege can protect the lawyer conversation, but it does not hide the underlying fact.

choices.text: Yes, unless Lydia's lawyer later states the name in open court.
choices.c3_signal: The choice introduces later courtroom repetition, a fact not in the stem and not the ground asserted.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells a waiver story because lawyers repeating facts in court sounds like the moment a privilege would be lost. The breaker is that the asked-for item is an underlying fact, so waiver timing is not the question.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice answers a later waiver problem, not whether the underlying name was privileged when requested.
choices.future_cue: Circle the asserted ground in the stem and reject events not in the stem.

choices.text: No, because attorney-client privilege never applies in civil cases.
choices.c3_signal: The word never tries to erase the whole civil attorney-client privilege category.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells an easy no by using a broad civil-case shortcut. The breaker is the absolute never, which contradicts the privilege frame rather than answering the fact-versus-communication split.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word never overclaims by erasing civil attorney-client privilege.
choices.future_cue: Test both halves: the outcome may be right while the reason is overbroad.

choices.text: Yes, because every fact a client discusses with a lawyer while seeking legal advice becomes privileged.
choices.c3_signal: The word every overextends privilege from communications to all facts discussed.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells privacy because the fact was discussed with a lawyer during a legal-advice meeting. The breaker is the word every, which tries to convert all discussed facts into protected material.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The phrase every fact overextends privilege from communications to underlying facts.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the request seeks the fact itself or the lawyer conversation.

choices.text: No, because an opposing party may discover relevant underlying facts even if those facts were communicated to counsel.
choices.c3_signal: This directly answers the call and separates the fact from the lawyer conversation.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It is the only choice that says no for the fact-versus-communication reason.

remediation_card.title: Fact, not chat
remediation_card.signal: Discovery asks for a fact; privilege objection points to a lawyer conversation.
remediation_card.student_move: Separate the underlying fact from the communication that reported it.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Facts do not become privileged by being told to counsel.
remediation_card.trap: Every fact discussed with a lawyer becomes privileged.

gold_keys.statement: Attorney-client privilege protects confidential legal-advice communications, not the underlying facts. A fact does not become privileged just because the client told it to a lawyer.
gold_keys.trigger: The discovery request asks for a fact, but the refusal says the fact was told to counsel.
gold_keys.authority: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383 (1981); Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1); Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(a)(2).

silver_keys.statement: Before reading privilege choices, name the object of discovery. If the other side asks for the fact itself, do not let an answer switch you to the lawyer conversation.
silver_keys.trigger: Interrogatory asks for an identity or event fact; objection says the fact was told to counsel.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says every fact discussed with counsel becomes privileged. Name the mold.
drill_seeds.answer: tiered_absolute

drill_seeds.prompt: A privilege choice turns on whether the lawyer later repeated the fact in court, but the stem asks whether the fact was privileged in the first place. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut as NOT_RESPONSIVE / bait_doctrine.

drill_seeds.prompt: A client tells a lawyer the name of a witness. Can the client refuse to disclose the witness's name solely for that reason?
drill_seeds.answer: No. The fact is not privileged merely because it was communicated to counsel.

drill_seeds.prompt: You cut every-fact, never-civil, and wrong-frame waiver. What confidence band?
drill_seeds.answer: ANCHOR_ASSISTED high; commit after read-check.

subject: REAL_PROPERTY
tension_axis: process threshold versus sale-scope merits
stem:
Ruth owned a private orchard cottage where she made Scripture memory cards for sale at weekend markets. To buy a new printing press, Ruth borrowed $74,000 from Barnabas and gave Barnabas a promissory note and a mortgage on the orchard parcel. Barnabas immediately and properly recorded the mortgage.

Six weeks later, Ruth borrowed $41,000 from Lydia and gave Lydia a promissory note and a mortgage on the same parcel. Lydia immediately and properly recorded the mortgage.

Ruth died soon afterward. Her will left the orchard parcel to Stephen for life, then to Mary. Stephen moved into the cottage. Neither Barnabas nor Lydia received the payments due on their notes. Without notifying or serving Stephen or Mary, Barnabas asks a court to order a foreclosure sale of the orchard parcel.

The court should:
call:
Call: What should the court do?

Prediction: Deny the request. The lender is asking for a foreclosure sale without notifying or serving the people who hold the present and future interests in the property.

Adjacent-call trap: What estate could be sold after proper notice and joinder?
distilled_core_question: A senior mortgagee seeks judicial foreclosure without notifying or serving the life tenant or remainderman. Should the court order a sale or deny the request?
review_truth: Foreclosure sale waits for process: present and future interest holders must receive notice before their interests can be cut off.

choices.text: order the sale of a remainder only.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees Mary’s future interest and treats the remainder as the legally precise target. The breaker is that the court cannot choose a sale target before the affected interest holders are served.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice isolates the remainder but does not answer whether a sale may be ordered without notice/service to the interest holders.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the remainderman was notified or served before any sale answer can be chosen.

choices.text: order the sale of a life estate only.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees Stephen in possession and follows the visible life estate. The breaker is that possession does not answer the missing service on both interest holders.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice isolates the life estate but does not answer the missing-service threshold.
choices.future_cue: List the holders: life tenant and remainderman. Then check service.

choices.text: deny Barnabas’s request.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Barnabas has a senior recorded mortgage, and the later devisees took their property interests subject to that mortgage. But that does not let Barnabas jump straight to a foreclosure sale without bringing the current property-interest holders into the case.

Gold Key: In a judicial foreclosure, all holders of present or future property interests that may be cut off by the sale must receive notice and be made parties before the court orders the sale.

Silver Key: The phrase “without notifying or serving Stephen or Mary” turns the question into a process-first item. Do not choose what estate can be sold until the people who hold those estates are in court.

Stephen holds the life estate. Mary holds the remainder. Both interests would be affected by a foreclosure sale. Since neither Stephen nor Mary was notified or served, the court should deny Barnabas’s request.

choices.text: order the sale of a fee interest.
choices.why_attractive: The student knows a senior recorded mortgage can support foreclosure of the mortgaged fee and reaches the substantive result. The breaker is the Gold Key: sale scope comes only after the necessary parties receive notice.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice may describe the sale scope after proper procedure, but it skips the current notice/service defect.
choices.future_cue: Say: fee sale may be later; denial is now.

remediation_card.title: Foreclosure: bring interest holders into court
remediation_card.signal: Foreclosure request + life estate/remainder + no notice/service
remediation_card.student_move: Cut every sale-scope answer until the service threshold is satisfied.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No notice to affected estate holders, no sale order.
remediation_card.trap: Choosing the estate that can be sold instead of the process answer.

gold_keys.statement: In judicial foreclosure, holders of present or future property interests that may be cut off by the sale must receive notice and be made parties before the court orders the sale.
gold_keys.trigger: Foreclosure requested without notice or service on a life tenant or remainderman.
gold_keys.authority: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co.; Mennonite Board of Missions v. Adams.

silver_keys.statement: When a foreclosure stem says the lender did not notify or serve the estate holders, lock the call as process first and sale scope second.
silver_keys.trigger: without notifying or serving

drill_seeds.prompt: A foreclosure stem says the lender did not notify the life tenant or remainderman. Three choices order a sale. What is the first cut?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut the sale-scope choices as premature; choose the process answer.

drill_seeds.prompt: Which comes first in foreclosure: identifying the estate to sell or serving the holders of affected estates?
drill_seeds.answer: Serving the affected estate holders.

drill_seeds.prompt: Who must receive notice when a judicial foreclosure may cut off a life estate and remainder?
drill_seeds.answer: Both the life tenant and the remainderman.
