subject: EVIDENCE
tension_axis: compliance advice versus furthering fraud
splitting_fact: If that would be fraudulent, I will not use that description.
stem: Lydia runs a small Bible-study gift cart at weekend retreats. Before selling a shipment of wooden crosses, she privately told her lawyer, Paul, “I am thinking about advertising these as carved from Bethlehem olivewood. Would that be legal? If that would be fraudulent, I will not use that description.” Paul researched the law and advised Lydia not to use the description.
call: Are Lydia’s communications protected by attorney-client privilege?
distilled_core_question: Client asks lawyer whether planned conduct would be fraudulent and says she will not do it if unlawful. Lawyer advises against it. Are the communications privileged?
review_truth: Suspicious subject matter does not defeat attorney-client privilege unless the client seeks legal advice to carry out or cover up wrongdoing.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the customers later fail to prove substantial need for the communications.
choices.c3_signal: The answer imports substantial need, a neighboring discovery-protection idea, into an attorney-client privilege call.
choices.why_attractive: The student recognizes substantial need as a real discovery phrase and assumes it can defeat privilege. The breaker is that substantial need answers work-product, not attorney-client privilege.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Substantial need is a work-product idea, not the attorney-client privilege test.
choices.future_cue: Ask which protection the call names before applying any exception phrase.

choices.text: No, because any discussion of a potentially fraudulent advertisement triggers the crime-fraud exception.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'any' makes suspicious subject matter an automatic exception.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees fraud-related subject matter and treats the exception as automatic. The breaker is that crime-fraud turns on purpose, not mere topic.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word 'any' overreads crime-fraud by making suspicious subject matter automatic.
choices.future_cue: Find the client-purpose sentence in the stem.

choices.text: Yes, because she sought confidential legal advice to determine and avoid unlawful conduct, not to further a fraud.
choices.c3_signal: This choice answers the exact privilege call and tracks the compliance-advice fact.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Only C is true and responsive after the wrong-frame and overclaim traps are removed.

choices.text: No, because Paul ultimately advised against the advertisement.
choices.c3_signal: The answer treats advice against the act as privilege-destroying, but that fact points toward compliance advice.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats the lawyer's negative advice as a reason privilege should fail. The breaker is that advice against the act supports the compliance-advice route.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Advice against the act points toward compliance advice, not loss of privilege.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the fact points toward compliance or wrongdoing.

remediation_card.title: Purpose beats suspicious topic
remediation_card.signal: Client asks whether a proposed act would be fraudulent.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the client is seeking compliance advice or help carrying out wrongdoing.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Crime-fraud needs furtherance; compliance advice remains privileged.
remediation_card.trap: Fraud word = automatic exception.

gold_keys.statement: Crime-fraud is purpose-based, not topic-based: privilege fails only when legal advice is sought to commit, continue, or cover up crime or fraud.
gold_keys.trigger: Client asks whether planned conduct would be fraudulent and says she will not do it if unlawful.
gold_keys.authority: FRE 501 common law; United States v. Zolin; Clark v. United States.

gold_keys.statement: Substantial need is a work-product concept; it is not the test for overriding attorney-client communications.
gold_keys.trigger: A privilege answer says 'substantial need.'
gold_keys.authority: Federal privilege and work-product doctrine distinction.

silver_keys.statement: When a privilege answer says 'fraud,' do not stop at the topic. Name the axis: compliance advice versus using the lawyer to further fraud.
silver_keys.trigger: Client says she will not proceed if the conduct is fraudulent.

drill_seeds.prompt: Client asks lawyer whether a planned act would be fraudulent and says she will not do it if unlawful. Does crime-fraud automatically apply?
drill_seeds.answer: No. The purpose is compliance advice, not furtherance.

drill_seeds.prompt: A privilege answer says disclosure depends on substantial need. What is the C3 label?
drill_seeds.answer: bait_doctrine / wrong_frame.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two answers fight: fraud topic kills privilege versus legal advice to avoid fraud. What fact decides?
drill_seeds.answer: Client says she will not proceed if the conduct is fraudulent.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: precise defect proof required vs res ipsa inference without direct defect proof
stem: Lydia owns a for-profit Bible-story dinner theater that sells tickets to a Nativity show. During a performance, an overhead Bethlehem star prop that was supposed to glide slowly above the stage suddenly dropped from its track and struck Martha, a ticketed guest standing in the marked viewing area. Lydia had hired Timothy's rigging company to inspect and service the overhead track, but Lydia kept responsibility for deciding whether the star prop would be used during each show and received all inspection reports. Martha did not touch the rigging, controls, or stage equipment. Martha sues Lydia for negligence but cannot prove the exact clamp, cable, or motor failure that caused the star to drop.
call: Will res ipsa loquitur likely be available in Martha's negligence claim against Lydia?
distilled_core_question: A maintained overhead prop suddenly drops during normal use; the defendant kept operational responsibility, the plaintiff did not cause it, and the plaintiff lacks direct defect proof. Is res ipsa likely available?
review_truth: Res ipsa can supply a negligence inference from an abnormal event without direct defect proof, but it does not force judgment.

choices.text: No, because hiring a rigging contractor always defeats Lydia's responsibility for res ipsa.
choices.c3_signal: The word always makes a full wipeout claim.
choices.why_attractive: A student sees Timothy's contractor role and assumes Lydia is out. The breaker is the absolute word always, plus Lydia's retained operational responsibility.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word always makes the contractor point an overclaim.
choices.future_cue: Circle always and look for retained responsibility facts.

choices.text: No, because Martha cannot identify the precise rigging defect.
choices.c3_signal: This is the live residual fight against D; it needs the Gold Key.
choices.why_attractive: A student thinks a negligence plaintiff must identify the precise mechanical failure. The breaker is the Gold Key that res ipsa can supply a circumstantial inference without direct defect proof.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It invents a precise-defect-proof requirement that the Gold Key defeats.
choices.future_cue: Say: res ipsa is the bridge when exact direct proof is missing.

choices.text: Yes, because res ipsa requires judgment for Martha once the overhead prop falls.
choices.c3_signal: The answer converts may infer into must win.
choices.why_attractive: A student recognizes res ipsa and overcorrects into a plaintiff win. The breaker is that res ipsa permits an inference rather than requiring judgment.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It pushes a permissible inference into required judgment.
choices.future_cue: Replace requires judgment with permits inference.

choices.text: Yes, because the prop's sudden drop during normal show use can support a negligence inference without direct defect proof.
choices.c3_signal: Matches the call and the Gold Key.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A and C overclaim; B loses the Gold-Key fight on direct proof.

remediation_card.title: Res ipsa: inference, not proof shortcut to judgment
remediation_card.signal: Abnormal malfunction, defendant responsibility, plaintiff non-contribution, no direct proof.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not punish the plaintiff for lacking the exact defect; ask whether the event itself can speak.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No exact defect needed; no automatic judgment.
remediation_card.trap: Missing direct proof feels fatal.

gold_keys.statement: Res ipsa is an inference bridge. It can apply when the plaintiff lacks direct proof of the exact defect, and it permits but does not compel a negligence finding.
gold_keys.trigger: The call asks whether res ipsa is available and the stem says the plaintiff lacks direct defect proof.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 328D

gold_keys.statement: Contractor involvement does not automatically erase res ipsa responsibility when the defendant retained operational responsibility for the instrumentality.
gold_keys.trigger: The stem says a contractor serviced the mechanism but the defendant retained operational responsibility and received reports.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 328D responsibility/control formulation

silver_keys.statement: Cut the absolute contractor and automatic-judgment answers first. Then resolve the residual pair by asking whether the missing exact defect is fatal or is the reason res ipsa matters.
silver_keys.trigger: One answer says no exact defect, one says inference without exact defect.

drill_seeds.prompt: Plaintiff lacks proof of the exact defect but the instrumentality fails abnormally under defendant responsibility. Fatal to res ipsa?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Missing exact defect proof is compatible with res ipsa.

drill_seeds.prompt: Hiring a contractor always defeats res ipsa responsibility.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut. Always overclaims.

drill_seeds.prompt: Res ipsa requires judgment for the plaintiff once an accident happens.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut. It permits an inference; it does not require judgment.

drill_seeds.prompt: No exact defect proof vs inference without exact defect proof. Name the axis.
drill_seeds.answer: Whether res ipsa requires direct proof of the precise defect.

subject: CONTRACTS
tension_axis: mutual-mistake fact vs contractual risk allocation
stem: Barnabas owns a privately run Bible-story mini-golf course called The Exodus Course. He sells it to Ruth. The sale contract says that Ruth buys the course "as is, including all hidden subsurface drainage defects, whether known or unknown." Both Barnabas and Ruth believe the underground drainage tunnels beneath the "Red Sea Crossing" hole are intact. Before signing, however, those tunnels had already collapsed from storm erosion. Ruth later discovers the collapse and seeks rescission for mutual mistake. How should the court rule?
call: How should the court rule?
distilled_core_question: Buyer signs an as-is clause covering hidden unknown defects. Both parties are wrong about a hidden preexisting defect. Buyer seeks mutual-mistake rescission. Who wins?
review_truth: A mutual mistake does not support rescission when the contract assigned that mistake-risk to the party seeking rescission.

choices.text: Grant rescission because hidden subsurface drainage defects are always outside an as-is clause.
choices.c3_signal: The word always claims hidden defects can never be allocated by an as-is clause, even when the clause expressly names them.
choices.why_attractive: It sells the thought that hidden defects are too serious for an as-is clause to cover. The breaker is the word always, because the clause expressly names hidden defects.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word always overclaims the effect of hidden-defect status.
choices.future_cue: Circle always and test whether the stem's exact clause names the risk.

choices.text: Deny rescission only if Barnabas proves that Ruth personally inspected every drainage tunnel.
choices.c3_signal: Only if plus every drainage tunnel creates a proof condition the stem and answer array do not support.
choices.why_attractive: It sells the idea that assumption of risk must be backed by personal inspection. The breaker is that the inspection requirement is invented.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer invents a personal-inspection prerequisite.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer's proof condition appears in the stem or a taught anchor.

choices.text: Grant rescission because both parties were mistaken about the drainage tunnels.
choices.c3_signal: This answers whether both parties were mistaken; it does not answer the risk-allocation fact in the call.
choices.why_attractive: It sells the true mutual-mistake fact and feels like the classic rule. The breaker is that it skips the as-is risk-allocation term.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer proves mutual mistake but omits risk allocation.
choices.future_cue: After confirming both parties were mistaken, ask who bore the mistake-risk.

choices.text: Deny rescission because Ruth expressly assumed the risk of hidden subsurface drainage defects.
choices.c3_signal: This choice matches the explicit as-is hidden-defect term and answers why rescission is denied.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Only D is true and responsive after the Gold Key risk-allocation check.

remediation_card.title: Risk before rescission
remediation_card.signal: Mutual mistake plus as-is / unknown-defect clause.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not stop at both mistaken. Ask who took the risk.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: If the claimant accepted the mistake-risk, rescission is denied.
remediation_card.trap: Picking the mutual-mistake-only grant answer.

gold_keys.statement: A mutual mistake does not support rescission if the party seeking rescission bore the risk. An as-is clause can allocate unknown hidden-defect risk to that party.
gold_keys.trigger: A mutual mistake stem plus an express as-is or unknown-defect risk-allocation term.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 152, 154.

silver_keys.statement: In a grant/deny rescission matrix, separate the mistake fact from the risk-allocation fact. The answer that engages the explicit risk term beats the answer that only says both parties were mistaken.
silver_keys.trigger: Two choices grant rescission, two deny; one denial tracks the as-is clause.

drill_seeds.prompt: Hidden defects are always outside an as-is clause.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: tiered_absolute.

drill_seeds.prompt: Deny rescission only if the buyer inspected every hidden component personally.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: fabricated_rule.

drill_seeds.prompt: Both parties were mistaken, but the buyer agreed to take unknown hidden-defect risk. Rescission?
drill_seeds.answer: No rescission.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two choices grant because of mistake; two deny because of risk or a proof condition. Which axis decides?
drill_seeds.answer: Risk allocation.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
stem:
Final variation — “The Baptism-Tank Burst at the Handbell Expo”

In a federal diversity action, Lydia, a citizen of State A, sues Barnabas, a citizen of State B, for $120,000 after Barnabas’s privately owned portable baptism-tank display burst at a Christian handbell expo and ruined Lydia’s sound equipment. Barnabas counterclaims against Lydia for $18,000 for damage to the tank display from the same burst. The counterclaim has no independent amount in controversy.

May the federal court hear the counterclaim?
call:
Call: court power to hear the counterclaim.
Adjacent traps: amount in controversy for every claim; federal-question jurisdiction; overreading §1367(b).
Prediction: yes, because the counterclaim is defendant-side and same-event.
distilled_core_question: In a diversity case with a proper $120,000 anchor claim, may the court hear a defendant's $18,000 counterclaim against the plaintiff when it arises from the same incident?
review_truth: A same-event defendant counterclaim can use supplemental jurisdiction even if it does not independently exceed $75,000.

choices.text: No, because Section 1367(b) bars all low-value or nondiverse counterclaims by defendants in diversity cases.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees Section 1367(b) and assumes the specific statute must be the sophisticated answer. The breaker is that the answer expands plaintiff-side limits into an all-defendant-claim bar.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Over-expands Section 1367(b) into an all-defendant-counterclaim bar.
choices.future_cue: Say the Gold Key: defendant same-event counterclaims may ride supplemental jurisdiction.

choices.text: Yes, but only because the counterclaim presents a federal question.
choices.why_attractive: The student senses the court can hear the counterclaim and accepts the first yes answer. The breaker is that no federal-law fact appears, so the yes reason is the wrong jurisdictional hook.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Uses a federal-question reason when the stem supplies a same-event supplemental-jurisdiction hook.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the stem gives federal law; if not, use the same-event hook.

choices.text: No, because each claim in a diversity case must independently exceed $75,000.
choices.why_attractive: The student remembers the $75,000 diversity threshold and applies it to every claim. The breaker is the word each, because supplemental jurisdiction can carry a related defendant counterclaim below the threshold.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Turns the diversity amount threshold into an every-claim independent-amount rule.
choices.future_cue: Separate the anchor diversity claim from a related counterclaim riding supplemental jurisdiction.

choices.text: Yes, because the counterclaim arises from the same burst and forms part of the same Article III case.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: D is correct. The counterclaim is by the defendant against the existing plaintiff, and it comes from the same burst that supports the anchor diversity claim. Gold Key: a same-transaction defendant counterclaim can ride supplemental jurisdiction even if it is below $75,000, unless a specific §1367(b) plaintiff-side bar applies. Silver Key: match the “yes” answer to the correct jurisdictional hook; here, the hook is same-event supplemental jurisdiction, not federal-question jurisdiction.

remediation_card.title: Defendant counterclaim under supplemental jurisdiction
remediation_card.signal: Diversity anchor claim plus low-value defendant counterclaim from the same incident.
remediation_card.student_move: Check whether the low-value claim is defendant-side and same occurrence before applying §1367(b).
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Same-event defendant counterclaims may ride §1367(a); §1367(b) is plaintiff-side.
remediation_card.trap: Treating every low-value diversity claim as independently barred.

gold_keys.statement: In a diversity case, a defendant's same-transaction counterclaim can use supplemental jurisdiction even below $75,000 unless a specific plaintiff-side §1367(b) bar applies.
gold_keys.trigger: Defendant counterclaim + same incident + no independent amount in controversy.

silver_keys.statement: Read the array as result plus jurisdictional reason. A 'yes' answer is not enough; the reason must be same-event supplemental jurisdiction, not federal question.
silver_keys.trigger: A counterclaim in a diversity case with no independent amount.

drill_seeds.prompt: A diversity anchor claim is for $110,000. The defendant asserts a $12,000 same-incident counterclaim. Cut: 'No, each claim must independently exceed $75,000.'
drill_seeds.answer: CUT as tiered_absolute after Gold Key.

drill_seeds.prompt: A counterclaim arises from the same incident but no federal statute appears. Cut: 'Yes, because the counterclaim presents a federal question.'
drill_seeds.answer: CUT as misfit / wrong_frame.

drill_seeds.prompt: State the Gold Key for a same-event defendant counterclaim below $75,000 in a diversity case.
drill_seeds.answer: It can use supplemental jurisdiction unless a specific plaintiff-side §1367(b) bar applies.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two answers say yes; one says federal question, one says same Article III case. The stem gives only same-incident facts. Which yes survives?
drill_seeds.answer: The same Article III case answer.

subject: CONTRACTS
subtopic: Acceptance, rejection, notice of breach, and seller action for price
tension_axis: notice-after-acceptance vs defect-alone defense
stem: Paul, a devotional-merchandise wholesaler, sued Lydia on August 9 for the price of 360 ceramic “Faith, Hope, Love” mugs. The sale began on March 7, when Lydia, who operates a Christian gift shop, ordered mugs finished with a gold dove decal, for delivery by March 18. On March 18, the mugs reached Lydia’s shop. Timothy, Lydia’s stockroom manager, opened the cartons and told Lydia both that the order had arrived and that the mugs were missing the gold dove decals. Lydia meant to text Paul that afternoon, but while preparing a children’s choir sale she forgot. On April 27, Lydia received Paul’s invoice but neither paid nor contacted him. In defense to Paul’s action, Lydia asserted that the mugs did not conform to the contract of sale.
call: The court should rule for
distilled_core_question: A buyer learns on delivery that goods are nonconforming, says nothing for months, and raises the defect only after the seller sues for the price. Who wins?
review_truth: In a goods sale, a buyer who accepts goods and sits on a known defect without timely notice loses the defect remedy.

choices.text: Paul, because a merchant buyer that accepts delivery of nonconforming goods is bound to pay for them at the contract price.
choices.c3_signal: The choice says acceptance alone binds the buyer, but the Gold Key adds the missing notice-remedy condition.
choices.why_attractive: This choice reaches the seller-wins side and uses the real accepted-goods idea. The breaker is that acceptance alone is incomplete because timely notice can preserve defect remedies.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Same seller outcome, but acceptance alone is an incomplete reason because timely notice can preserve nonconformity remedies.
choices.future_cue: Force the same-outcome wrong-reason check: winner side is not enough; reason must match the trigger fact.

choices.text: Lydia, because a merchant seller is not entitled to the price of nonconforming goods if a reasonable inspection before shipment would have disclosed the nonconformity.
choices.c3_signal: The choice points to seller inspection, but the stem's loaded axis is buyer notice after delivery.
choices.why_attractive: This choice makes seller inspection sound like a fair commercial responsibility. The breaker is that it invents a price-action defense not supplied by the UCC notice path.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The seller-inspection condition is an invented bar to the price action.
choices.future_cue: Cut invented commercial-sounding requirements unless the rule or stem makes them controlling.

choices.text: Paul, because Lydia failed to notify him that the mugs were missing the gold dove decals.
choices.c3_signal: This choice matches the call and the loaded fact: Lydia knew the defect and did not notify Paul.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Lydia knew the mugs were missing the gold dove decals when Timothy reported the defect on delivery day. She did not notify Paul then. She also did not notify him when the invoice arrived more than a month later. She raised the defect only after Paul sued for the price.

Gold Key: When a buyer accepts goods and discovers a defect, the buyer must notify the seller of the breach within a reasonable time or lose the defect remedy. Silver Key: Do not pick the seller-wins choice just because it reaches the right side; in this array, the winning seller choice must use the notice fact, not acceptance alone.

choices.text: Lydia, because the mugs did not conform to the contract of sale.
choices.c3_signal: The mugs were defective, but the live question is whether Lydia preserved that defense after silence.
choices.why_attractive: This choice uses the most visible fact: the mugs did not match the order. The breaker is that the call asks whether Lydia preserved that defect defense after months of silence.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The defect is real, but the price-action call turns on whether Lydia preserved the remedy after discovering it.
choices.future_cue: Name the call: seller price action after buyer silence, not abstract nonconformity.

remediation_card.title: Accepted goods: notice keeps the remedy alive
remediation_card.signal: Buyer knows goods are defective, keeps silent, then raises defect after being sued.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the buyer notified the seller within a reasonable time.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Known defect plus no seasonable notice means no defect remedy after acceptance.
remediation_card.trap: Picking the nonconformity answer because the goods were genuinely defective.

gold_keys.statement: After accepting goods, a buyer who discovers a defect must notify the seller within a reasonable time or lose the defect remedy.
gold_keys.trigger: Known nonconformity on delivery plus months of silence before a price suit.

silver_keys.statement: Read the 2x2 by reason, not outcome: the seller-wins choice with the notice fact beats the seller-wins choice with acceptance alone.
silver_keys.trigger: Two choices name the seller and two name the buyer.

drill_seeds.prompt: Seller sues for price after buyer accepted defective goods. Choice says seller wins because acceptance alone always binds buyer to contract price. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut; acceptance alone is incomplete because timely notice can preserve defect remedies.

drill_seeds.prompt: Buyer knew goods were defective on delivery and stayed silent for months. Choice says buyer wins because goods were defective. What is the skipped element?
drill_seeds.answer: Notice after discovery; defect alone is not responsive.

drill_seeds.prompt: After accepting goods, what must a buyer do after discovering a defect to preserve remedies?
drill_seeds.answer: Notify the seller within a reasonable time.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says seller loses the price if a reasonable pre-shipment inspection would have found the defect. What mold is this?
drill_seeds.answer: fabricated_rule.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: violation versus remedy
stem: Detectives investigating the theft of Stephen’s personal olivewood chess set from a Christian bookstore already had the shop’s security video and written statements from two shoppers identifying Peter. Three weeks later, officers saw Peter outside the store after a Psalms-and-coffee night and arrested him without a warrant or probable cause. The arrest produced no physical evidence and no statement. Prosecutors later indicted Peter for the theft using the video and shopper statements. Peter moves to dismiss the indictment solely because the arrest was unlawful.
call: How should the court rule?
distilled_core_question: Police make an unlawful arrest, get no evidence or statement from it, and indict using evidence already in the file. The defendant moves to dismiss solely because of the arrest. Should dismissal be granted?
review_truth: A bad arrest can suppress tainted evidence, but it does not automatically erase a prosecution supported by independent evidence.

choices.text: Grant the motion unless the prosecutor proves that the arresting officers acted in good faith.
choices.student_label: good-faith exception in the wrong remedy lane
choices.c3_signal: The call asks for dismissal. This choice talks like an evidence-admissibility exception.
choices.why_attractive: The choice recognizes a familiar good-faith rescue from Fourth Amendment suppression doctrine. The breaker is that the call asks for dismissal and no arrest-derived evidence is being offered.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Good faith belongs to the suppression/admissibility lane; the call asks dismissal and no arrest-derived evidence is being offered.
choices.future_cue: Ask what the motion requests and whether any arrest-derived evidence is being offered.

choices.text: Deny the motion only if Peter was released and rearrested with a valid warrant.
choices.c3_signal: The 'only if' condition is a made-up procedural repair rule.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells procedural cleanup by making a new valid arrest sound like a cure. The breaker is that independent evidence lets the prosecution proceed without rerunning the arrest.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer invents a release-and-rearrest prerequisite for prosecution on independent evidence.
choices.future_cue: Reject invented 'only if' prerequisites unless the anchor supplies them.

choices.text: Grant the motion, because an unlawful arrest nullifies any later indictment.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'any' turns one unlawful arrest into a prosecution-ending rule.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells the moral shortcut that an illegal arrest poisons the whole case. The breaker is that the remedy targets tainted evidence, not the indictment itself.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer overclaims by making an unlawful arrest nullify any later indictment.
choices.future_cue: Name the remedy: suppression of tainted evidence, not automatic dismissal.

choices.text: Deny the motion, because an unlawful arrest does not require dismissal when the prosecution rests on evidence independent of the arrest.
choices.c3_signal: This choice matches the remedy call and the independent-evidence facts.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
D is correct. The motion asks for dismissal of the indictment, not suppression of evidence. The arrest produced no statement and no physical evidence, and the prosecution is relying on video and shopper statements already in the file before the arrest.

Silver Key: Lock the remedy first. This is a dismissal question, not an evidence-admissibility question.

Gold Key: An unlawful arrest does not automatically erase a later prosecution. The criminal-case remedy targets evidence obtained through the illegality; a prosecution supported by independent evidence may proceed.

remediation_card.title: Bad arrest is not automatic dismissal
remediation_card.signal: Unlawful arrest + motion to dismiss + independent evidence
remediation_card.student_move: Separate the violation from the requested remedy.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Suppress tainted evidence when applicable; do not dismiss charges supported by independent evidence.
remediation_card.trap: Treating illegality as automatic case erasure.

gold_keys.statement: An unlawful arrest is not itself a prosecution-ending defect. The remedy targets evidence obtained through the illegality; charges supported by untainted evidence are not dismissed merely because the arrest was bad.
gold_keys.trigger: unlawful arrest + no arrest-derived evidence + motion to dismiss
gold_keys.authority: United States v. Crews, Gerstein v. Pugh, Frisbie v. Collins.

silver_keys.statement: Lock the remedy before applying Fourth Amendment exceptions. If the call asks for dismissal and the stem gives no arrest-produced evidence, suppression exceptions are side streets.
silver_keys.trigger: motion to dismiss solely because arrest was unlawful

drill_seeds.prompt: Unlawful arrest; no evidence or statement obtained; independent evidence supports indictment. Motion to dismiss?
drill_seeds.answer: Deny; dismissal is not required.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says dismissal depends on officer good faith. What is the C3 signal?
drill_seeds.answer: Good faith is an evidence-admissibility lane; lock the dismissal call.

drill_seeds.prompt: What is the remedy for an unlawful arrest when no evidence was obtained from it?
drill_seeds.answer: No automatic dismissal; suppress tainted evidence only when applicable.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says an unlawful arrest voids any later indictment. Name the mold.
drill_seeds.answer: tiered_absolute.

subject: EVIDENCE
stem: Mary operates a private “Acts & Axes” booth that sells scripture-engraved toy arks at summer fairs. She sues Stephen, her weekend cash-box clerk, for taking booth receipts. Before the records evidence is offered, Stephen testifies that Mary paid him $3,200 for the season and that he never took any receipts. Mary calls a prepaid-card records custodian, who will testify that during that same season Stephen made $18,600 in cash loads onto his personal prepaid card. Stephen objects that the cash loads could have come from birthday gifts or family loans.
call: The custodian’s testimony is:
distilled_core_question: A civil-theft defendant denies taking receipts and claims low seasonal pay; the plaintiff offers records showing much larger same-season cash deposits. Is that admissible even though the deposits have possible innocent explanations?
review_truth: A clue can be admissible even when it is not a confession; weakness usually goes to weight, not admissibility.

choices.text: inadmissible, because financial records are always unfairly prejudicial in a civil theft case.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'always' turns a balancing idea into automatic exclusion.
choices.why_attractive: This choice sells the fear that money evidence will make the jury punish Stephen for being suspiciously flush with cash. The breaker is the absolute word always, which tries to turn a balancing question into an automatic exclusion.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word always makes unfair prejudice automatic.
choices.future_cue: Replace automatic exclusion with a balancing frame.

choices.text: admissible as circumstantial evidence that Stephen received funds from a source beyond his stated pay.
choices.c3_signal: This answer matches the call and the fact gap: stated pay versus larger cash loads.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is correct. The cash-load records are admissible because they make Mary’s claim more probable: Stephen said he received only $3,200 for the season, while the records show $18,600 in same-season cash loads. Gold Key: relevance is an “any tendency” threshold, not a conclusive-proof requirement. Silver Key: in a relevance array, cut answers that demand “conclusive,” “always,” or “only”; the surviving answer states what the evidence tends to show. Stephen may argue gifts or family loans, but that attacks weight, not admissibility.

choices.text: inadmissible, because the cash loads do not conclusively prove Stephen took Mary’s receipts.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'conclusively' invents a higher admissibility threshold.
choices.why_attractive: This choice sells a certainty instinct: if the cash could be gifts or loans, it feels too weak to admit. The breaker is that relevance asks for tendency, not conclusive proof.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice invents a conclusive-proof threshold.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the evidence makes a consequential fact more probable.

choices.text: admissible only to impeach Stephen, but not as circumstantial proof that he took the receipts.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'only' underclaims the evidence's purpose.
choices.why_attractive: This choice offers a safe compromise by letting the evidence in only to contradict Stephen. The breaker is that the same cash-gap fact can also be substantive circumstantial proof.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice uses only to understate the evidence's substantive purpose.
choices.future_cue: Check whether the same fact also supports the claim substantively.

remediation_card.title: Relevance is a clue threshold
remediation_card.signal: Opponent says the evidence has innocent explanations or is not conclusive.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask what fact the evidence tends to make more likely.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: A clue need not be a confession.
remediation_card.trap: demanding certainty before admissibility

gold_keys.statement: Relevant evidence does not need to prove the whole case by itself. If it has any tendency to make a consequential fact more probable, it clears the relevance threshold.
gold_keys.trigger: The opponent says the evidence could have another explanation.
gold_keys.authority: Fed. R. Evid. 401, 402, 403; see pass-1 legal verification.

silver_keys.statement: In a relevance array, cut 'conclusive,' 'always,' and 'only' before weighing the story. The survivor usually states what the evidence tends to show.
silver_keys.trigger: Three choices narrow admissibility; one states the fact relation.

drill_seeds.prompt: Classify: inadmissible because financial records are always unfairly prejudicial.
drill_seeds.answer: tiered_absolute; NOT_TRUE.

drill_seeds.prompt: Does circumstantial evidence need to conclusively prove the fact before it is admissible?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Any tendency is enough if the fact matters.

drill_seeds.prompt: Records contradict a witness and also support the claim. Is an only-impeachment answer safe?
drill_seeds.answer: No. It underclaims the substantive use.

subject: EVIDENCE
tension_axis: belief-as-truthfulness versus affiliation-for-bias
stem:
At a federal civil trial over a broken Christmas-pageant stage wagon, Peter sues Galilee Props, Inc., a private prop-rental company. Ruth testifies for Galilee. On cross-examination, Peter’s lawyer asks Ruth whether she is the paid treasurer of New Covenant Fellowship, the religious organization that owns Galilee’s voting shares and appoints its managers. Galilee objects under the rule barring religious-belief credibility evidence. Peter says he offers the question to show Ruth’s possible bias toward Galilee, not to suggest that her religious views make her truthful or untruthful.

How should the court rule?

The source row for QID 20423 supplies the Evidence topic, original Rule 610 bias-purpose stem, original answer choices, official key C, and official explanation.
call:
Call: rule on the objection.

Prediction: overrule. The offered purpose is bias from a paid organizational tie, not religious belief as a truthfulness trait.
distilled_core_question: A witness has a paid role in a religious organization that controls a party. The question is offered to show bias, not religious truthfulness. Should the objection be sustained?
review_truth: Religion evidence is barred for truthfulness character, not for bias from affiliation or interest.

choices.text: Overrule the objection because the question targets possible bias from Ruth’s paid tie to the organization that owns Galilee, not her religious beliefs as a truthfulness trait.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A is correct. The objection should be overruled because the question is aimed at Ruth’s possible bias: she is a paid treasurer of the religious organization that owns and controls Galilee. Gold Key: Rule 610 blocks religion-as-truthfulness use; it does not block affiliation or interest evidence offered to show bias. Silver Key: Purpose first. The same religious-affiliation fact is barred for one credibility purpose but allowed for a different credibility purpose.

choices.text: Sustain the objection because any reference to a witness’s religious affiliation is inadmissible.
choices.why_attractive: It turns the Rule 610 objection into a blanket ban, which feels safe because religious references sound prejudicial. The breaker is the offered-purpose split: the question is about a paid organizational tie and bias, not belief-as-truthfulness.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer overclaims by treating any religious affiliation reference as inadmissible.
choices.future_cue: Circle any and ask whether the purpose is truthfulness or bias.

choices.text: Overrule the objection only if Ruth’s character for truthfulness has first been attacked.
choices.why_attractive: It borrows the familiar Rule 608(a) sequence, so a student sees truthfulness attacked first and thinks foundation. The breaker is that the offered purpose is bias, not truthful-character rehabilitation.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer imports a truthfulness-character precondition into a bias-purpose question.
choices.future_cue: Match the answer to the stem’s stated purpose: bias.

choices.text: Sustain the objection because bias may be shown only by reputation evidence.
choices.why_attractive: It confuses bias impeachment with opinion/reputation character proof, which sounds plausible because the bank topic is opinion/reputation. The breaker is that bias is its own credibility purpose and is not limited to reputation evidence.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer invents a rule that bias may be shown only by reputation evidence.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer created a proof-method limit not in the stem or the Gold Key.

remediation_card.title: Religion Evidence: Purpose Split
remediation_card.signal: Religious affiliation appears, but the proponent says bias.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not stop at the religious-evidence objection. Ask the offered purpose.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Belief-as-truthfulness is barred; affiliation-for-bias is not.
remediation_card.trap: Blanket religious-affiliation ban.

gold_keys.statement: Rule 610 blocks religion-as-truthfulness evidence. It does not block religious affiliation or organizational ties when offered to show bias, interest, or relationship to a party.
gold_keys.trigger: religion objection plus paid role or organizational tie to a party
gold_keys.authority: Federal Rule of Evidence 610 Advisory Committee Note

silver_keys.statement: When an Evidence answer turns on the same fact being used for different credibility purposes, name the offered purpose first and grade only that lane.
silver_keys.trigger: The stem says offered to show bias and not to show truthfulness.

drill_seeds.prompt: A witness belongs to a religious organization connected to a party. The question is offered to show bias. Is Rule 610 a blanket bar?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Bias purpose is outside the belief-as-truthfulness ban.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut the flaw: any reference to religious affiliation is inadmissible.
drill_seeds.answer: Overclaim. Any erases the bias-purpose lane.

drill_seeds.prompt: Truthful character may be supported only after attack. Does that govern a bias question?
drill_seeds.answer: No. That is Rule 608(a) truthfulness-character doctrine, not bias.

drill_seeds.prompt: Bias may be shown only by reputation evidence.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut. The only limit is invented.

subject: TORTS
subtopic: Standard of Due Care / Best Argument
stem:
Christian variation — QID `20439_floating_star_driveway`

Timothy was walking on the public sidewalk past Lydia’s house on Saturday morning. Lydia, a professional director of children’s Christmas pageants, was rehearsing a “floating star” scene for a neighborhood Advent program. She tested a rented battery-powered cable rig in her open driveway beside the sidewalk. A defect in the rig caused a plywood star to swing outside the driveway and strike Timothy.

If Timothy asserts a claim against Lydia, Timothy’s most effective argument in support of his claim would be that
call:
Call lock: best argument for the injured walker.

Prediction: look for a liability basis. The answer should say what Lydia did wrong, not merely that she is a professional, used a defective product, or helped cause the harm.
distilled_core_question: A professional pageant director uses a defective stage rig in an exposed driveway and a passerby is hurt. Which argument best supports the passerby’s tort claim?
review_truth: A tort claim needs an operative liability basis; unreasonable conduct can supply negligence, while product defect, causation, or professional status alone does not.

choices.text: Lydia was a professional Christmas-pageant director.
choices.why_attractive: The professional title sounds like it carries a higher legal duty. The breaker is that the answer never says Lydia breached any professional or ordinary standard.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Professional status does not supply breach.
choices.future_cue: Ask what the professional did unreasonably.

choices.text: Lydia’s conduct was a concurring cause of Timothy’s harm.
choices.why_attractive: Causation sounds like the missing link in a tort case. The breaker is that causation without negligence, intent, or strict liability is only a fragment.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Causation alone does not supply a liability basis.
choices.future_cue: Add the question: cause plus what fault or strict-liability category?

choices.text: It was unreasonable for Lydia to test the cable rig in her open driveway beside a public sidewalk.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: C is correct. Timothy’s strongest listed argument is that Lydia acted unreasonably by testing the cable rig in an open driveway beside a public sidewalk. Gold Key: negligence needs an unreasonable-risk theory; here, the argument supplies a fault basis instead of merely pointing to a product, a cause, or Lydia’s professional title. Silver Key: on a “most effective argument” call, do not demand a guaranteed win. Choose the only answer that gives the plaintiff a legally operative route to liability.

choices.text: Lydia is strictly liable for harm resulting from her use of a defective product.
choices.why_attractive: Strict liability and defective-product language sound powerful because they reduce the need to prove fault. The breaker is that Lydia is a user of the rig, not the commercial supplier or distributor.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Strict products liability is aimed at commercial sellers or distributors, not a mere user.
choices.future_cue: Use GK-TORTS-USER-SUPPLIER-01.

remediation_card.title: Cause/status/product are not the claim
remediation_card.signal: A Torts answer names only cause, status, or product defect.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the answer supplies a liability basis.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: For negligence, look for unreasonable conduct.
remediation_card.trap: Choosing a legally flavored fragment instead of the operative ground.

gold_keys.statement: Strict products liability for a defective product is aimed at commercial sellers or distributors, not a person who merely uses the product.
gold_keys.trigger: Defendant is using/testing/operating a product rather than selling or distributing it.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability § 1

gold_keys.statement: Cause and status are not enough; the plaintiff’s argument must supply negligence, intent, or a strict-liability category. Unreasonable conduct supplies the negligence route.
gold_keys.trigger: Best-argument tort call with status/cause/product fragments
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 3

silver_keys.statement: On a best-argument call, pick the answer that gives the plaintiff a legal route to liability; do not require the answer to prove the whole case.
silver_keys.trigger: The call asks for the claimant’s most effective argument.

drill_seeds.prompt: A Torts answer says only that the defendant’s act was a concurring cause. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut unless another part of the answer supplies negligence, intent, or strict liability.

drill_seeds.prompt: A passerby is injured by a defective device used by a pageant director. The answer says the director is strictly liable for using a defective product. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut; strict products liability targets commercial sellers or distributors, not mere users.

drill_seeds.prompt: The call asks for the plaintiff’s most effective argument. One answer gives possible unreasonable conduct; another gives only causation. Which wins?
drill_seeds.answer: The unreasonable-conduct answer.

drill_seeds.prompt: Which phrase best supplies negligence: professional status, concurring cause, unreasonable conduct, or product defect?
drill_seeds.answer: Unreasonable conduct.

subject: CONTRACTS
stem:
Barnabas Wax Co. promptly accepted a signed email from Lydia, who runs a Bible-verse candle studio. The email said: “I offer to buy all the beeswax my studio requires for the next nine months at $18 per slab, shipment every other Friday.” Lydia later asserted that no contract had formed because the email did not list a fixed number of slabs.

Which statement is most accurate?
call:
Call lock: most accurate formation statement.
Adjacent-call trap: price quote, price fairness, and illusory-promise anxiety.
Prediction: the fight is the missing fixed number. The answer should say whether “all I require” can supply quantity.
distilled_core_question: Buyer offers to buy all goods her business requires at a set unit price and delivery schedule; seller accepts; buyer says no fixed number means no contract. Is the quantity too indefinite?
review_truth: A requirements term is a quantity term when it measures the buyer's actual good-faith needs.

choices.text: No contract formed unless the court finds $18 per slab was an adequate price.
choices.why_attractive: A student may think courts must check whether the price was fair before enforcing the deal. The breaker is that price adequacy is not the formation gate.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice invents a court price-adequacy gate.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the call is price fairness or quantity sufficiency.

choices.text: A contract can form because the quantity is measured by Lydia’s good-faith requirements.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is correct. Gold Key: a requirements quantity is not an empty quantity; it is measured by the buyer’s actual good-faith requirements. Silver Key: in a 3-vs-1 no-contract array, do not let “no fixed number” erase a quantity phrase that the stem already gives you. Lydia’s email gives a price, a delivery schedule, goods, duration, and the quantity formula: all beeswax the studio requires. That can support contract formation.

choices.text: No contract formed because the email was only a price quote.
choices.why_attractive: A student may see a unit price and reach for the price-quote doctrine. The breaker is that the stem gives a buyer's offer and acceptance, not a seller's quote.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice answers a price-quote frame instead of the buyer's offer and missing-number objection.
choices.future_cue: Read the speaker and verb: Lydia says 'I offer to buy,' and Barnabas accepted.

choices.text: No contract formed because a requirements quantity is always too indefinite and illusory.
choices.why_attractive: A student may treat no fixed number as no quantity and call the promise illusory. The breaker is the Gold Key that requirements quantity is measured by good-faith needs.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice says requirements quantity is always too indefinite, which overclaims against the requirements-quantity Gold Key.
choices.future_cue: Mark 'always,' then apply the requirements-quantity Gold Key.

remediation_card.title: Flexible quantity is not empty quantity
remediation_card.signal: all goods the buyer requires
remediation_card.student_move: Do not equate no fixed number with no quantity.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Requirements quantity is measured by good-faith needs.
remediation_card.trap: Illusory-promise overread.

gold_keys.statement: A requirements term is a quantity term: it measures the buyer's quantity by actual good-faith needs, not by a fixed number.
gold_keys.trigger: all goods the buyer requires

silver_keys.statement: When three choices say no contract and the stem gives a requirements phrase, cut the no-contract reasons one at a time before assuming the missing number is fatal.
silver_keys.trigger: No fixed number objection after an 'all I require' phrase.

misconception_tags: no fixed quantity means no quantity

drill_seeds.prompt: A buyer offers to purchase all widgets her shop requires for six months. No fixed number is stated. Is the quantity automatically too indefinite?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Requirements quantity can be measured by good-faith needs.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut or keep: 'Requirements quantities are always illusory.'
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: tiered_absolute.

drill_seeds.answer: NOT_RESPONSIVE / bait_doctrine / wrong_frame.

drill_seeds.answer: Fabricated adequacy gate; anchor-assisted cut.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: extra manipulation/immediate apparentness vs no-warrant-after-pocket-entry
splitting_fact: The officer rolled and rubbed the tablet before deciding it was contraband.
stem: After a city Christmas pageant called Road to Bethlehem, Officer Hannah lawfully stopped Peter on a public plaza near vendor tents where officers had recently seen illegal pill sales. Peter was still wearing his shepherd costume, including a robe with a small sash pocket. During a pat-down of Peter’s outer clothing for weapons, Hannah felt a pea-sized hard tablet in the sash pocket. She knew it was not a weapon. Curious, Hannah rolled and rubbed the tablet through the fabric for a few moments until she decided it felt like an illegal opioid pill. She then reached into the pocket and seized it. Peter moves to suppress.
call: Was the officer’s warrantless seizure of the pill valid under the plain-feel doctrine?
distilled_core_question: During a lawful weapons frisk, an officer feels a nonweapon object, manipulates it to identify contraband, then seizes it. Is the seizure valid under plain feel?
review_truth: Plain feel allows seizure only when contraband is immediately apparent during the lawful frisk; extra manipulation of a nonweapon item breaks the search.

choices.text: No, because the officer’s continued rolling and rubbing of the tablet through the robe fabric to identify it as contraband exceeded the lawful scope of the frisk; its incriminating character was not immediately apparent.
choices.c3_signal: This answer names the same fact the stem makes decisive: extra manipulation before contraband identity became apparent.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
A is correct. The frisk began lawfully, but the plain-feel path works only if the contraband character is apparent during the lawful weapons pat-down itself. Here, Hannah knew the object was not a weapon and then rolled and rubbed it through the fabric to figure out what it was. That extra tactile exploration is the defect.

Gold Key: Plain feel requires immediate apparentness. If the officer must manipulate a nonweapon item to identify it as contraband, the frisk has become an additional search.

Silver Key: In the two “No” answers, do not stop at the shared result. Compare the defect each answer names. The winning defect is the extra manipulation before identification, not the mere absence of a warrant after pocket entry.

choices.text: Yes, because the officer had reasonable suspicion that Peter was involved in illegal-pill activity, justifying a search for drugs.
choices.c3_signal: It answers whether drug suspicion justified a search for drugs, not whether this seizure fit plain feel.
choices.why_attractive: The illegal-pill setting makes drug suspicion feel like the central fact. The breaker is that reasonable suspicion answers the wrong question; the call is plain-feel seizure validity.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer uses drug reasonable suspicion to answer the wrong frame. The call is plain-feel seizure validity.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the choice answers plain-feel seizure validity.

choices.text: No, because the officer needed a warrant before reaching into the sash pocket once she realized the object was not a weapon.
choices.c3_signal: It picks the correct side but points to the wrong moment. The stem’s decisive moment is manipulation before identification.
choices.why_attractive: The answer gets the suppression outcome and therefore feels safer than the technical answer. The breaker is that it names the wrong defect; the first unlawful move was the manipulation before identification.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer reaches the right result but names the wrong defect. The defect is manipulation before identification, not simply lack of a warrant before pocket entry.
choices.future_cue: Compare the two No answers by the first unlawful move.

choices.text: Yes, because the officer was conducting a lawful Terry frisk and any item discovered during the frisk may be seized.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'any' is the tell. A limited weapons frisk is being inflated into a permission to seize everything found.
choices.why_attractive: The lawful Terry frisk makes the broad permission sound legitimate. The breaker is the absolute 'any item,' which inflates a limited weapons frisk into a general search.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The phrase 'any item' overstates a lawful Terry frisk. Plain feel does not authorize seizing everything discovered.
choices.future_cue: Mark 'any item' and apply the plain-feel Gold Key.

remediation_card.title: Plain feel: immediate apparentness, not tactile investigation
remediation_card.signal: Lawful frisk; nonweapon object; officer keeps feeling it to identify it.
remediation_card.student_move: Stop the frisk at the moment the officer knows the item is not a weapon unless contraband is already immediately apparent.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Manipulation to identify contraband breaks plain feel.
remediation_card.trap: Treating Terry frisk as permission to search for drugs.

gold_keys.statement: Plain feel works only when the contraband identity is immediately apparent during the lawful weapons frisk. If the officer must squeeze, roll, rub, or otherwise manipulate a nonweapon item to identify it, the frisk has become a new search.
gold_keys.trigger: Lawful frisk + nonweapon object + extra manipulation before identification
gold_keys.authority: Minnesota v. Dickerson, 508 U.S. 366 (1993); Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)

silver_keys.statement: When two choices both say the seizure is invalid, ask which one names the first unlawful move. Here, the first unlawful move is the extra manipulation, not the later hand-in-pocket act.
silver_keys.trigger: Two 'No' answers with different defect rationales

drill_seeds.prompt: During a lawful frisk, the answer says any item found may be seized. Name the mold.
drill_seeds.answer: tiered_absolute

drill_seeds.prompt: Two answers both say suppression. One names manipulation before identification; one names lack of warrant before pocket entry. Which fact resolves it?
drill_seeds.answer: The officer manipulated the nonweapon object before identifying contraband.

drill_seeds.prompt: What must be true before an officer may seize contraband felt during a lawful frisk?
drill_seeds.answer: Its contraband character must be immediately apparent by touch.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice justifies a drug search because the area was known for drug sales. Why is it off-call?
drill_seeds.answer: The call asks about plain-feel seizure validity, not drug-investigation suspicion.

subject: REAL_PROPERTY
topic: Conveyance by Deed — Requirements for Valid Deed
stem: Esther owned a small vacant lot that she used for neighborhood Bible-memory picnics. After one picnic, she pulled a clean paper lunch wrapper from the basket and wrote, “I convey my vacant lot at 48 Galilee Court to Timothy.” Because Esther’s hands were too stiff to write her name, she drew a small fish symbol at the bottom intending it as her signature. She gave the wrapper to Timothy and said, “This little lot belongs to you today.” Timothy accepted. Timothy paid nothing, and nobody notarized or recorded the wrapper.
call: Who owns the lot?
distilled_core_question: A landowner writes present transfer words identifying herself, the grantee, and the land, signs by an intended mark, delivers the writing, and the grantee accepts. No money is paid, and the writing is not notarized or recorded. Who owns the land?
review_truth: A deed can be valid between grantor and grantee without a printed form, consideration, notarization, or recording if the minimal transfer formalities are present.

choices.text: Esther, unless the wrapper is later notarized and recorded.
choices.c3_signal: After the Gold Key, this adds a later formal gate not required for baseline validity between the parties.
choices.why_attractive: The student trusts courthouse ceremony because notarization and recording sound like the official ownership moment. The breaker is that those steps are not the baseline validity condition between the immediate parties.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: Who paid?
stem:
At Esther’s backyard “Loaves and Fishes” game night, Lydia was standing beside a table of Bible-verse prize cards when Daniel negligently lost control of a wheeled prop cart stacked with foam bread baskets. The cart struck Lydia and caused injuries that required emergency treatment. Lydia’s medical bills were substantial, but they were paid in full under a health-insurance policy that Lydia had purchased before the game night.

Lydia sued Daniel for negligence. The jury found for Lydia and awarded her $64,000. Before judgment was entered, Daniel’s lawyer made a proper motion asking the court to reduce the award by the amount Lydia had already received from her health insurer.

The motion to reduce Lydia’s damage award should be:
call:
The call asks whether the court should reduce the damage award. Predict the axis before reading the choices: the motion turns on the source of payment, not on the amount of the bills, the existence of negligence, or whether “double recovery” sounds unfair.

Prediction: deny the motion if the payment came from Lydia’s own insurer.
distilled_core_question: The plaintiff's own insurer paid her medical bills before she won a negligence verdict. May the negligent defendant reduce the verdict by that insurance payment?
review_truth: Plaintiff-side insurance is collateral; it does not reduce the negligent defendant's damages judgment.

choices.text: Denied, because the payment from Lydia’s insurer was not made after any court decided that Daniel was liable.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees the right result, denial, and accepts the first plausible reason attached to it. The breaker is that judicial determination is not the source-identity switch.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice gives the right outcome but rests on judicial determination, not payment source.
choices.future_cue: Ask: court determination or payment source?

choices.text: Granted, because Daniel is entitled to partial indemnity.
choices.why_attractive: The student recognizes partial indemnity as a serious tort-allocation phrase. The breaker is that indemnity belongs to common-liability actors, not plaintiff-side insurance.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice imports partial indemnity from the joint-tortfeasor allocation frame.
choices.future_cue: Reserve indemnity/contribution for common-liability actors.

choices.text: Denied, because Lydia’s insurer was not acting for anyone who was liable to Lydia for negligence.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. The motion should be denied. The answer locks onto the source of the payment: Lydia’s own health insurer, not Daniel, not someone acting for Daniel, and not another person liable to Lydia for the same injury.

Gold Key: A negligent defendant does not get a credit for payments the injured plaintiff received from the plaintiff’s own insurance or another source independent of the defendant. The defendant gets credit only for payments made by the defendant, someone acting for the defendant, or another person subject to the same tort liability.

Silver Key: Do not start with “double recovery.” Start with “who paid, and whose liability was the payer connected to?” That source check points to C.

choices.text: Granted, because Lydia should not be allowed to recover twice for the same medical expenses.
choices.why_attractive: The student wants to prevent a double recovery and follows common-sense fairness. The breaker is the collateral-source Gold Key: plaintiff-side insurance does not reduce the tortfeasor's judgment.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice uses double-recovery fairness language that the collateral-source rule defeats.
choices.future_cue: Plaintiff-side insurance is collateral.

remediation_card.title: Who paid?
remediation_card.signal: Insurance payment before or after tort verdict.
remediation_card.student_move: Sort the payer: defendant-side, joint-tortfeasor-side, or plaintiff-side.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Plaintiff-side insurance does not reduce the judgment.
remediation_card.trap: Double recovery feels fair but points the wrong way.

gold_keys.statement: Plaintiff-side insurance is collateral. A negligence defendant gets no credit for benefits paid by the plaintiff's own insurer; credit is for payments by the defendant, someone acting for the defendant, or another actor subject to the same tort liability.
gold_keys.trigger: Defendant asks to reduce a tort award because plaintiff's own insurer already paid.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 920A

silver_keys.statement: For setoff questions, ask who paid and whose liability the payer was tied to before reacting to double-recovery language.
silver_keys.trigger: Motion to reduce damages after insurance or settlement payment.

drill_seeds.prompt: A plaintiff's own insurer paid medical bills before a tort verdict. Can the defendant reduce the verdict by that amount?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Plaintiff-side insurance is collateral.

drill_seeds.prompt: Classify the payer: defendant, joint tortfeasor, plaintiff's own insurer.
drill_seeds.answer: Only plaintiff's own insurer is collateral.

drill_seeds.answer: Who paid, and whose liability was the payer tied to?

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: imminence threshold vs real-but-incomplete fear/family facts
stem:
Timothy works the evening shift in the shipping room at Manna Games, a private company that sells Bible-themed board games and collector study-Bible sets. On Monday night, Barnabas, a collector with a reputation for using hired muscle, sends Timothy a video message from a retreat center three states away:

> “Before the warehouse closes on Friday, take the locked case of gold-edition study Bibles worth $18,000 and leave it behind the Noah’s Ark mini-golf sign, or after next Sunday’s hymn-sing I will have your sister Hannah badly hurt.”

Timothy believes Barnabas is serious and is terrified for Hannah. On Thursday, Timothy takes the case. Charged with theft, Timothy asserts duress.

Should the court accept Timothy’s duress defense?
call:
The call asks whether the duress defense succeeds.

Prediction: No. The threat is future and remote. The missing piece is imminence.
distilled_core_question: A worker commits theft after a remote person threatens to hurt his sister at a future time. Does duress succeed?
review_truth: Duress is not fear alone; it requires an imminent human threat and no reasonable legal alternative.

choices.text: Yes, because the threat was directed at Timothy’s sister, a close family member, which is sufficient.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees a close-family threat and recognizes a real duress element. The breaker is that one real element does not answer the threshold failure: no imminent threat.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice names the close-family fact but does not answer the missing imminence threshold.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer also proves imminence and no reasonable legal alternative.

choices.text: No, because the threat was not imminent — the threatened harm was scheduled for a future time and Barnabas was physically absent.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct.

Gold Key: Common-law duress is not a “real fear” defense. It needs an imminent human threat of death or serious bodily harm, directed at the defendant or a close family member, with no reasonable legal alternative. Here, the threat was for a future time, and Barnabas was physically absent. Timothy had time to seek help or protect Hannah without stealing.

Silver Key: Read the answer array as an element-completion test. Two “Yes” answers name sympathetic facts. The credited “No” answer names the missing threshold.

choices.text: No, because duress is available only as a defense to violent crimes.
choices.why_attractive: The student reaches a no-defense result and remembers that duress has crime-scope limits. The breaker is that the limit is not a violent-crime-only rule; theft is not excluded if the other elements are met.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice uses an absolute violent-crime-only rule that is not the duress scope rule.
choices.future_cue: Treat 'only' as a red flag and recall that theft is not excluded from duress.

choices.text: Yes, because Timothy had a genuine and reasonable fear that Barnabas would hurt Hannah.
choices.why_attractive: The student credits Timothy's fear because the stem makes it believable and reasonable. The breaker is that genuine fear still does not supply immediacy or eliminate legal alternatives.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice proves fear but not imminence or lack of reasonable legal alternative.
choices.future_cue: Separate believable fear from immediate compulsion.

remediation_card.title: Duress requires now-pressure.
remediation_card.signal: Future threat, remote threatener, time to seek help.
remediation_card.student_move: Cut fear-only and family-only answers; keep the answer that checks imminence.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Duress is immediate-threat plus no reasonable escape, not fear alone.
remediation_card.trap: Sympathy for a believable family threat.

gold_keys.statement: Common-law duress needs an imminent human threat of death or serious bodily harm, directed at the defendant or a close family member, with no reasonable legal alternative.
gold_keys.trigger: Threat scheduled for later, threatener absent, time to seek help.
gold_keys.authority: Common-law duress; United States v. Bailey and federal duress formulations.

gold_keys.statement: Duress is not a violent-crime-only defense; theft is not excluded if the duress elements are met.
gold_keys.trigger: Answer says duress is only for violent crimes.
gold_keys.authority: Common-law duress scope; homicide limitation.

silver_keys.statement: When two Yes answers each name one sympathetic fact and a No answer names a missing threshold, treat the array as an element-completion test.
silver_keys.trigger: Defense-success call with multiple partial-element answers.

misconception_tags: duress is only for violent crimes

drill_seeds.prompt: A defendant steals after a threatener far away promises to hurt a sibling next week. Does duress succeed?
drill_seeds.answer: No. The threat is future and remote, so imminence is missing.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says: 'Yes, because the threat was to a close family member.' Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut as NOT_RESPONSIVE / wrong_element unless imminence and no escape are also satisfied.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says: 'No, because duress is only for violent crimes.' Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut as NOT_TRUE / tiered_absolute.

subject: CONTRACTS
tension_axis: extra formalities versus party-to-be-charged memorandum
stem: After Peter failed to pay a private event-supply company for the portable stage and speakers used at a ticketed Easter concert at his bookstore café, the company sued Ruth. Before the rental, Ruth had orally told the company that she would pay Peter’s $18,400 rental bill if Peter did not. That evening, Ruth signed a note to Lydia, Peter’s concert scheduler, stating: “I told Galilee Gear Rentals I would cover Peter’s $18,400 stage-and-speaker rental if Peter does not pay it.” Ruth argues that the signed note cannot satisfy the Statute of Frauds because it was sent to Lydia, not to Galilee Gear Rentals.
call: Can Ruth’s signed note potentially satisfy the suretyship writing requirement?
distilled_core_question: A surety signs a note to someone other than the creditor admitting she promised to pay another person’s debt if that person defaults. Can that note potentially satisfy the Statute of Frauds?
review_truth: The Statute of Frauds memorandum test looks to the signer and content, not whether the writing was addressed to the enforcing party.

choices.text: No, because a guaranty memorandum must always be signed by both Peter and Ruth.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'always' plus 'both Peter and Ruth' adds a formality beyond the call’s party-to-be-charged fact.
choices.why_attractive: It feels safer because a guaranty involves both the debtor and the guarantor. The breaker is that the suit charges Ruth, so Peter’s signature is an added formality.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice adds an always-both-sign requirement. The Gold Key cuts the extra signature condition.
choices.future_cue: Ask whose promise the supplier is enforcing.

choices.text: Yes, because a signed memorandum by Ruth, the party to be charged, can satisfy the writing requirement even when sent to someone other than the supplier, if it sufficiently identifies the promise and parties.
choices.c3_signal: This choice answers the exact call: Ruth signed a memorandum that identifies the promise and parties; it does not add an addressee or debtor-signature requirement.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is correct. Ruth is the person being sued on the suretyship promise. The note is signed by Ruth, identifies the supplier, identifies Peter’s debt, states the amount, and states Ruth’s promise to cover the debt if Peter fails to pay. Gold Key: for a common-law Statute of Frauds memorandum, the key question is whether the writing is signed by the party to be charged and sufficiently identifies the promise and parties; it need not be addressed to the enforcing creditor. Silver Key: three choices add extra formalities; the answer array is asking whether the addressee and extra signatures are required.

choices.text: No, because a suretyship memorandum must be sent or addressed to the creditor seeking to enforce it.
choices.c3_signal: This is the stem’s bait objection: it treats the recipient of the note as a required formality.
choices.why_attractive: It mirrors Ruth’s stated objection that the note went to Lydia instead of the supplier. The breaker is that addressee identity is not the memorandum-sufficiency test.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice makes addressee identity decisive. The Gold Key cuts the creditor-addressee requirement.
choices.future_cue: Apply the Gold Key: signer and content, not addressee.

choices.text: Yes, but only if Peter also signed Ruth’s note.
choices.c3_signal: This choice keeps the yes outcome but adds Peter’s signature as a condition.
choices.why_attractive: It sounds like a careful yes answer because it adds Peter’s signature as a safeguard. The breaker is that Peter is not the party being charged on Ruth’s promise.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice adds Peter’s signature as a condition. The Gold Key cuts the debtor-signature requirement.
choices.future_cue: Peter’s signature is not required to charge Ruth.

remediation_card.title: SOF memorandum: signer beats addressee
remediation_card.signal: A signed writing admits a guaranty but was sent to someone other than the enforcing creditor.
remediation_card.student_move: Map who is being sued; then ask whether that person signed a writing identifying the promise.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: The memorandum need not be addressed to the enforcing party.
remediation_card.trap: extra formality

gold_keys.statement: For a common-law Statute of Frauds memorandum, the writing need not be addressed or delivered to the enforcing party. Ask whether it is signed by the party to be charged and whether it identifies the promise, parties, and essential terms.
gold_keys.trigger: signed note admits a guaranty but was sent to someone other than the creditor
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 131, 133; lawyer-confirmation only

silver_keys.statement: When three answers add formalities and one answer tracks the signer-plus-content path, group the formalities first. Then cut the addressee and extra-signature conditions as the same trap family.
silver_keys.trigger: choices say must be addressed, must always be signed by both, or only if debtor signed

drill_seeds.prompt: A guarantor signs a note to the debtor admitting the guaranty. The creditor sues. Does the note fail solely because it was addressed to the debtor?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Addressee is not the test; signer and content are.

drill_seeds.answer: CUT as tiered_absolute after the Gold Key; the party being charged must sign.

drill_seeds.answer: Extra formalities beyond the party-to-be-charged signed memorandum.
