subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: same-offense substance versus different label
splitting_fact: The question concerned the same booth, same cash box, and same festival incident.
stem:
Final variant — QID `20542_praise_festival_cashbox`

Peter is indicted for armed robbery of Lydia’s traveling Scripture-calligraphy booth at a private praise-music festival, and counsel is appointed. Later, while counsel is absent, detectives visit Peter at his apartment. They say they only want to ask whether he committed “the unarmed theft of the cash box from that same booth during the closing-night festival rush.” They obtain no waiver. Peter admits that he took Lydia’s cash box during that incident.

Call: Should Peter’s statement be suppressed under the Sixth Amendment?

Source row: the original BarMatrix item is QID 20542, with original key A and a Sixth Amendment post-indictment deliberate-elicitation issue.
call:
Call lock: suppression under the Sixth Amendment.

Prediction: suppress if this is the same charged offense in substance. Do not answer a Miranda custody question. Do not answer a global unrelated-crime question.
distilled_core_question: After indictment and counsel, police ask without waiver about a relabeled lesser version of the same charged incident. Suppress?
review_truth: After indictment, the Sixth Amendment follows the charged offense in substance, not the police's new label.

choices.text: No, because Peter was not in custody when the detectives spoke with him.
choices.why_attractive: A student sees a police-questioning problem and reaches for custody because custody is a real Miranda trigger. The breaker is that the call is Sixth Amendment deliberate elicitation after attachment, not Fifth Amendment custodial interrogation.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice uses a Fifth Amendment custody frame when the call asks for Sixth Amendment suppression after attachment.
choices.future_cue: Mark custody as wrong-frame unless the call asks Fifth Amendment or Miranda.

choices.text: Yes, because the questioning concerned the same charged criminal episode and a same-offense variant after attachment.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is correct. Peter had been indicted and counsel had been appointed. The detectives then deliberately sought an admission about the same festival-booth incident, merely recast as an unarmed theft rather than armed robbery. They did this without counsel and without a waiver. Gold Key: after attachment, the Sixth Amendment bars deliberate elicitation about the charged offense, and a lesser-included or same-offense relabeling does not create a clean new offense. Silver Key: do not let the answer turn on the noun-label; lock the call to “Sixth Amendment after indictment” and ask whether the new question is really about the charged event.

choices.text: Yes, because police may not question an indicted defendant about any unrelated offense.
choices.why_attractive: A student remembers that indictment gives the defendant a strong counsel right and inflates it into a universal shield. The breaker is that the Sixth Amendment right is offense-specific, so unrelated-crime questioning is not categorically barred by this rule.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice overclaims by treating indictment as a bar to questioning about any unrelated offense.
choices.future_cue: Strike any answer that bars any unrelated offense unless a Gold Key says the right is global.

choices.text: No, because unarmed theft and armed robbery use different labels.
choices.why_attractive: A student remembers the true phrase offense-specific and treats different crime names as enough. The breaker is that the stem points to the same charged event in a lesser-offense costume, so label-only reasoning is not responsive.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice borrows offense-specificity but answers by formal labels rather than same-offense substance.
choices.future_cue: Compare the event and lesser-included relation before trusting labels.

remediation_card.title: Same offense, new label
remediation_card.signal: Police say they only want to ask about a smaller version of the charged incident.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not stop at the label. Compare the factual event and offense substance.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Post-charge Sixth Amendment protection follows the same offense in substance.
remediation_card.trap: The label-only answer sounds precise but is too shallow.

gold_keys.statement: After formal charge, the Sixth Amendment bars deliberate elicitation about the charged offense without counsel or waiver; a lesser-included or same-Blockburger relabeling stays inside the charged offense.
gold_keys.trigger: indictment/counsel appointed + police ask about a renamed version of the same incident
gold_keys.authority: Massiah; Fellers; McNeil; Texas v. Cobb; Brown v. Ohio

gold_keys.statement: Sixth Amendment post-charge deliberate elicitation is not the same test as Fifth Amendment custodial interrogation.
gold_keys.trigger: Sixth Amendment call + post-indictment questioning
gold_keys.authority: Fellers; Massiah

silver_keys.statement: When the choices fight over crime labels, go back to the stem and ask whether the officers are really asking about the same charged event in a smaller costume.
silver_keys.trigger: charged armed robbery followed by police asking about unarmed theft from the same event

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: named-defendant premises breach vs adjacent product/contractor/status facts
stem:
Lydia owned Selah Studio, a private Bible-verse calligraphy studio open to the public for paid lettering workshops and sales of framed Scripture cards. After closing, Lydia hired Barnabas to install a motorized “Jericho Wall” display in the front room. When a participant stepped on a pressure mat, wooden panels were supposed to slide apart to reveal the day’s featured verse.

Barnabas read the manufacturer’s instructions but disregarded the warnings. When he finished, he did not test the display by stepping on the pressure mat, but told Ruth, Lydia’s night manager, that the installation was complete. The next morning, when Selah Studio opened, Mary entered and was struck by one of the moving panels. Mary asserted a claim for her injuries against Lydia.

Which one of the following additional facts or inferences, if it was the only one true, would be most likely to result in a judgment for Mary?
call:
Call: judgment for Mary against Lydia.
Prediction: look for the fact that ties Lydia to a dangerous condition she knew or should have discovered.
Adjacent-call traps: product defect, contractor fault, and payment/status.
distilled_core_question: A public business visitor is injured by a newly installed moving device. Which added fact most supports judgment against the owner: defect, contractor non-negligence, reasonable owner inspection, or completed payment?
review_truth: The winning premises-liability fact links the owner to a danger discoverable by reasonable inspection.

choices.text: Mary had paid the workshop fee before the panel struck her.
choices.why_attractive: The payment fact feels useful because business transactions often mark who counts as a protected customer. The breaker is that the claim needs owner-linked inspection or repair, not a completed payment.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The payment fact addresses entrant/status flavor but does not supply Lydia's inspection breach.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the choice proves Lydia knew, should have known, inspected, or failed to fix.

choices.text: A reasonable inspection by Lydia would have disclosed that the panel swung into the aisle improperly.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is the best answer. It connects the injury to Lydia’s own premises duty. The claim is against Lydia, not Barnabas and not the manufacturer. The added fact says a reasonable inspection by Lydia would have revealed the improper swing before Mary was injured. That supplies the owner-side breach path the call is asking for.

Gold Key: For a business invitee, the owner’s live duty is reasonable inspection and protection against dangerous conditions the owner knows about or would discover by reasonable care. Silver Key: Lock the named defendant first. The answer must create liability for Lydia, not merely explain how the device failed, whether Barnabas was careful, or whether Mary paid.

choices.text: Mary’s injury resulted from a defect in the pressure mat.
choices.why_attractive: The defect fact feels powerful because a broken device sounds like the cause of the injury. The breaker is that it points to product or manufacturer responsibility, not Lydia's discoverable premises breach.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The product-defect fact points to the product chain unless tied to Lydia's discoverable premises condition.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the defendant sold the product or whether the defect was discoverable by owner inspection.

choices.text: Barnabas was not negligent in installing the Jericho Wall display.
choices.why_attractive: The no-negligence fact feels helpful because it removes blame from Barnabas. The breaker is that removing another actor's fault does not supply Lydia's inspection breach.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Barnabas's lack of negligence does not prove Lydia's negligence.
choices.future_cue: Cross out third-party fault facts unless they supply owner breach.

remediation_card.title: Owner-inspection fact beats product/contractor/status bait
remediation_card.signal: Premises owner is sued after a third party installed a dangerous device.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask which choice supplies breach by the named owner.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: For invitees, reasonable inspection can be the breach path.
remediation_card.trap: Product defect and contractor conduct feel causal but do not answer owner breach.

gold_keys.statement: For a business invitee, owner liability turns on dangerous conditions the owner knew about or would discover by reasonable care, plus failure to protect.
gold_keys.trigger: public-facing business premises plus customer injury from a condition on the premises

gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A

silver_keys.statement: Lock the named defendant before reading the added facts: the winning fact must create liability for Lydia, not for Barnabas or the product chain.

subject: CONTRACTS
subtopic: Prospective inability to perform; reliance before cure
tension_axis: reliance before cure
splitting_fact: Martha hired Barnabas on December 5; Stephen was released on December 12.
stem:
Martha owns and operates Mustard Seed Puppet Caravan, a private for-profit company that tours Bible-story puppet shows for families. The caravan hires only one full-time performer-driver for each tour season because that person travels with the caravan, sleeps in its bunk compartment, receives meals, drives between towns, and maintains the puppets and sound equipment.

On September 3, Stephen entered into a valid written contract with Martha. Under the contract, Stephen was to begin traveling with the caravan on January 10 and continue until July 10. Martha was to pay Stephen $18,500 at the end of the season, and Stephen was to receive meals and bunk space during the tour.

On September 18, Stephen signed a three-year contract to join an overseas gospel recording tour. That tour was scheduled to begin on December 20. A notice of Stephen’s new tour contract appeared in the “Praise Notes” column of a local arts newsletter and was read by Martha’s managers. Martha immediately began looking for another performer-driver. On December 5, Martha entered into a valid written contract with Barnabas on terms identical to Stephen’s contract.

On December 12, Stephen failed the overseas tour’s health-clearance requirement and was released from that contract. On January 10, Stephen arrived at Martha’s garage ready to travel with the caravan, but Martha told him that his services were not needed.

If Stephen asserts a claim against Martha for damages resulting from breach of contract, the court should find for whom?
call:
Call: Stephen sues Martha for breach. Who should the court find for?

Prediction: Find the date of Martha’s reliance. If Martha hired a replacement before Stephen became available again, Stephen loses.
distilled_core_question: A service contractor made himself apparently unable to perform, the other party reasonably hired a replacement before the obstacle disappeared, and the contractor later appeared ready. Who wins the breach claim?
review_truth: Later readiness does not save the claimant when the other party reasonably relied on apparent future inability before the obstacle disappeared.

choices.text: Stephen, since he never personally notified Martha that he would not report for the caravan job.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees that Stephen never personally said he would miss the job and treats direct notice as decisive. The breaker is that Martha already had reasonable knowledge and changed position before Stephen became available again.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice answers personal notice, but the call turns on reasonable knowledge and reliance before cure.
choices.future_cue: Ask what Martha knew and whether she changed position before Stephen's release.

choices.text: Martha, since Stephen’s contract with the overseas tour was an anticipatory repudiation of his contract with Martha.
choices.why_attractive: The student recognizes future nonperformance vocabulary and grabs the most familiar label. The breaker is that the credited answer must state the reliance-before-cure fact, not merely a label.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice gives a nearby legal label but omits the reliance-before-cure fact that resolves the item.
choices.future_cue: Use the Silver Key: label-only loses to reliance/timing.

choices.text: Martha, since Martha hired Barnabas in reliance on the reasonable belief that Stephen would be unable to perform as agreed.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Martha reasonably treated Stephen’s overseas-tour contract as creating a prospective inability to perform the puppet-caravan contract. The fact that matters is not Stephen’s later readiness on January 10. The fact that matters is that Martha changed position first by hiring Barnabas on identical terms while Stephen still appeared unavailable.

Gold Key: A future-performance problem is locked when one side reasonably relies before the apparent inability disappears. Later readiness does not undo a completed, reasonable replacement step.

Silver Key: When one defendant answer gives the reliance/timing fact and another gives only a legal label, keep the fact-loaded answer. The answer that uses the reliance fact is doing the work.

choices.text: Stephen, since he was ready, willing, and able to perform as agreed on January 10.
choices.why_attractive: The student focuses on the clean plaintiff fact that Stephen appeared ready on the day performance was due. The breaker is that Martha's replacement contract came before Stephen's release from the outside tour.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice uses the later performance-date fact, but the trigger fact is earlier reliance.
choices.future_cue: Mark reliance before cure.

remediation_card.title: Prospective inability: reliance before cure
remediation_card.signal: Future performance appears impossible, then later becomes possible.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the other party changed position before the cure.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Reliance before cure locks the defendant-side discharge.
remediation_card.trap: Later readiness feels decisive, but it is late.

gold_keys.statement: If a party's own conduct makes future performance reasonably appear impossible, the other side can be discharged when it materially changes position in reliance before the obstacle disappears.
gold_keys.trigger: Outside commitment begins before contract performance; replacement hired before later release.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 250, 253, 256.

silver_keys.statement: In a future-performance clash, prefer the answer that states the reliance/timing fact over the answer that gives only a legal label.
silver_keys.trigger: Two defendant answers remain; one says only a label and the other says reliance.

drill_seeds.prompt: Replacement hired December 5; outside commitment released December 12. Which date controls?
drill_seeds.answer: December 5 controls because reliance came before cure.

drill_seeds.prompt: One answer says 'repudiation'; another says 'hired replacement in reliance.' Which is stronger?
drill_seeds.answer: The reliance answer.

drill_seeds.prompt: A performer is ready on the start date after the company already hired a replacement. What is the trap?
drill_seeds.answer: Later readiness.

drill_seeds.prompt: The performer never personally warned the company, but the company learned from a reliable notice. What is the trap?
drill_seeds.answer: Direct-notice wrong element.

subject: EVIDENCE
tension_axis: foundation gate vs jury weight
stem: In a federal products-liability action over a battery-powered fog machine used in a private Christmas pageant, Lydia offers a cracked purple plastic gear that Stephen found three weeks later inside a hymnbook tote at Martha’s rented banquet hall. Stephen did not see it come from the fog machine; no witness recognizes it; no logo, serial number, or marking ties it to the fog machine; and no evidence shows how it got into the tote. Lydia says the jury can decide what to make of it. The manufacturer objects. How should the court rule?
call:
Call: rule on the objection.
Adjacent-call trap: how much weight the jury should give the gear.
Prediction: exclude. The stem gives no link between the gear and the product or accident.
distilled_core_question: Plaintiff offers an unidentified object with no witness, marking, or circumstance connecting it to the product or accident. Should the court admit it for the jury to weigh, or exclude it for lack of foundation?
review_truth: A jury cannot weigh a physical object until the proponent supplies a threshold link connecting it to the case.

choices.text: Admit the gear because the manufacturer can argue about its weight.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells the common instinct that flaws go only to weight once the item is in the courtroom. The breaker is the missing foundation gate; without a threshold link, the jury never reaches weight.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A answers the later weight question before the foundation gate is crossed.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether there is any foundation link before discussing weight.

choices.text: Exclude the gear because there is no evidence sufficient to support a finding that it is connected to the fog machine or the accident.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is correct. The gear is offered as if it is connected to the fog machine or the pageant accident, but the stem gives no identifying witness, no recognizable marking, and no circumstance tying the gear to that product or event. Gold Key: A physical object needs a threshold link before the jury can consider it as case evidence. Silver Key: Gate before weight; the jury does not weigh an object that has not crossed the foundation gate.

choices.text: Exclude the gear only if the manufacturer proves it came from some other device.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells a burden-shift story: exclude only after the opponent proves a different source. The breaker is the proponent's first move; the offering party must supply the link.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: C reverses the first-showing burden by requiring the opponent to prove another source.
choices.future_cue: Ask who is offering the item and who must supply the first link.

choices.text: Admit the gear because any physical object may be considered by the jury.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells trust-the-jury breadth and makes all physical things sound eligible. The breaker is the word any; the rule still requires a case connection.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: D overclaims by saying any physical object may be considered by the jury.
choices.future_cue: Mark 'any' and check whether the rule really has no gate.

remediation_card.title: Gate Before Weight
remediation_card.signal: Unidentified object; no witness; no marking; no chain/source fact.
remediation_card.student_move: Cut weight arguments until a threshold link exists.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: A jury weighs weak evidence; it does not supply the first connection.
remediation_card.trap: Let the jury decide.

gold_keys.statement: A physical object does not reach the jury on 'maybe.' The proponent must first supply some link supporting a finding that the object is what it claims or is connected to the case.
gold_keys.trigger: An object is offered, but the stem gives no identifying witness, no marks, and no source facts.
gold_keys.authority: FRE 901(a); FRE 104(b).

silver_keys.statement: When a choice says the jury can weigh it, first ask whether the item crossed the foundation gate. No gate, no weight.
silver_keys.trigger: The proponent says the jury can decide what to make of an unidentified object.

drill_seeds.prompt: An unidentified object is offered with no witness, marking, or source fact. One answer says admit because the opponent can argue weight. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut. Weight comes after foundation.

drill_seeds.prompt: An answer says exclude only if the opponent proves the object came from somewhere else. What is the problem?
drill_seeds.answer: Backwards. The proponent must first show a connection.

drill_seeds.prompt: An answer says any physical object may be considered by the jury. What is the mold?
drill_seeds.answer: tiered_absolute; it erases the foundation requirement.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two choices survive: one says weight, one says no foundation. Which layer controls?
drill_seeds.answer: No foundation controls before weight.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
topic: Erie Doctrine and Choice of Law
tension_axis: federal statute on point vs Erie policy/state-law-claim bait
stem:
Mary, a citizen of State Jordan, runs a private business that rents hand-painted “Psalms & Parables” stage panels for paid community programs. She sued Barnabas, a citizen of State Carmel, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of State Carmel for breach of a paid restoration contract involving those panels.

A State Carmel statute provides that a civil action may be filed only in the county where the defendant resides. Barnabas resides in a county located in the Southern District of State Carmel. Federal venue statute § 1391 provides that venue is proper in a federal district where a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claim occurred. The design meetings, payment, restoration work, and disputed delivery all occurred in the Northern District.

Which venue rule should the federal court apply?
call:
Call: Which venue rule should the federal court apply?
Prediction: Apply § 1391.
Adjacent-call trap: Do not ask which rule produces dismissal. Do not ask which law governs the underlying state-law claim. The call is source-of-rule for federal venue.
distilled_core_question: Diversity case in federal court. State venue rule points to defendant’s county. § 1391 points to the federal district where the events occurred. The events occurred there. Which venue rule controls?
review_truth: When a valid federal statute directly governs federal venue, apply that statute before Erie forum-shopping analysis.

choices.text: Whichever rule would require dismissal, because Erie discourages forum shopping.
choices.why_attractive: The student remembers that Erie worries about forum shopping and treats that worry as the whole test. The breaker is that Erie policy does not override a valid federal statute directly on point.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Forum-shopping concerns are real Erie bait, but the answer skips the federal-statute-on-point step.
choices.future_cue: Run the Gold Key before Erie balancing.

choices.text: Neither rule, because a diversity case in federal court has no venue requirement.
choices.why_attractive: The student may confuse diversity jurisdiction with a free pass from procedural venue analysis. The breaker is that the stem itself gives venue statutes, so the no-venue answer fights the setup.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer denies venue requirements even though the stem names venue statutes.
choices.future_cue: Cut answers that contradict the setup.

choices.text: Section 1391, because a valid federal statute directly controls federal venue.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. The call asks which venue rule the federal court should apply. The stem supplies a federal venue statute that directly governs venue in a federal district where a substantial part of the events occurred. The events occurred in the chosen federal district.

Gold Key: When a valid federal statute directly controls a federal-court procedural issue, apply the federal statute before doing Erie twin-aims balancing.

Silver Key: Lock the call as a rule-source question, not a dismissal-outcome question. The answer is the rule that controls federal venue, not the rule that makes one party win fastest.

choices.text: The state county venue statute, because Mary’s claim arises under state law.
choices.why_attractive: The student hears state-law claim and jumps to state law controls. The breaker is that venue in federal court is directly governed by the federal statute named in the stem.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer uses state-law-claim language to answer the wrong layer.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the procedural issue is directly governed by a federal statute.

remediation_card.title: Federal statute on point beats Erie balancing
remediation_card.signal: Diversity + state procedural rule + federal statute directly addressing procedure.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the federal statute directly controls before discussing forum shopping.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Federal statute on point first; Erie twin aims only after no controlling federal law.
remediation_card.trap: State-law claim language makes the state procedural rule feel controlling.

gold_keys.statement: When a valid federal statute directly controls a federal-court procedural issue, apply the federal statute before Erie twin-aims balancing.
gold_keys.trigger: Diversity case + state procedural rule + federal statute on point.
gold_keys.authority: 28 U.S.C. § 1391; Hanna v. Plumer; Stewart Organization v. Ricoh.

silver_keys.statement: On a 'which rule controls' call, do not pick the rule that creates the preferred outcome. First identify whether a federal statute directly answers the procedural question.
silver_keys.trigger: Answer choices compare state rule, federal statute, and forum-shopping policy.

misconception_tags: diversity cases lack federal venue rules

drill_seeds.prompt: Diversity case; state service rule conflicts with valid Federal Rule. Which source controls?
drill_seeds.answer: Federal rule/statute on point controls if valid.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says state procedure controls because the claim arises under state law. Name the trap.
drill_seeds.answer: Bait doctrine / wrong frame.

drill_seeds.prompt: Call asks which rule controls. One answer picks the rule that would dismiss. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut if it answers outcome instead of source-of-rule.

drill_seeds.prompt: What federal district is proper under § 1391(b)(2)?
drill_seeds.answer: A district where a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claim occurred.

subject: CONTRACTS
tension_axis: exact stated terminating event vs neighboring contract doctrines
stem:
Lydia rented her hand-painted Noah’s Ark parade float to Ruth for a private neighborhood Bible-verse parade. The rental agreement stated, “The float rental remains effective unless the city engineer limits the float’s permitted load below 1,200 pounds before parade day.” The day before the parade, the city engineer issued an order limiting the float’s permitted load to 700 pounds. Lydia refused to provide the float.

Which statement is most accurate?
call:
Call: Which statement is most accurate about Lydia’s refusal?

Prediction: Lydia likely did not breach because the contract’s “unless” event happened before parade day.
distilled_core_question: A contract says an existing rental ends if a specified official order lowers a safety limit below a set threshold before the event. The order happens. Did the owner breach by refusing to provide the item?
review_truth: An existing contract duty can be discharged by a later 'unless' event stated in the contract.

choices.text: Lydia breached unless the city engineer’s order made use of the float impossible.
choices.why_attractive: The student reaches for impossibility because it sounds like a familiar excuse doctrine. The breaker is that the contract already named a different terminating event.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice replaces the contract's below-threshold order trigger with impossibility.
choices.future_cue: Ask: what event did the contract itself say would end the rental?

choices.text: Lydia’s duty to provide the float was discharged by the condition subsequent stated in the rental agreement.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. The rental agreement was already effective, but it contained an “unless” event that would end Lydia’s duty if it occurred before parade day. That event occurred: the city engineer lowered the permitted load below the contract’s threshold before the parade.

Gold Key: A condition subsequent is a later event that cuts off an existing duty.

Silver Key: Do not replace the contract’s stated “unless” trigger with a different doctrine. If the trigger happened, the contract clause does the work.

choices.text: Ruth may compel delivery of the float because substantial performance of the parade plan is enough.
choices.why_attractive: The student reaches for substantial performance because it sounds like a forgiving contracts rule. The breaker is that Ruth's performance plan does not decide Lydia's duty after the stated condition occurred.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice replaces the duty-discharge question with substantial performance of the parade plan.
choices.future_cue: Return to Lydia's duty to provide the float after the order.

choices.text: Lydia breached because the float rental was already effective when signed.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees that the rental was effective at signing and treats that as enough. The breaker is that the later 'unless' event is the dispositive fact.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice answers whether the rental was initially effective, not what happened after the later trigger.
choices.future_cue: Continue from signing to the later city-engineer order.

remediation_card.title: Unless-trigger cuts off duty
remediation_card.signal: Contract says 'remains effective unless' or similar.
remediation_card.student_move: Track the exact trigger and timing before defaulting to breach, impossibility, or substantial performance.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: If the terminating event happened, the duty is cut off.
remediation_card.trap: Treating initial effectiveness as permanent.

gold_keys.statement: A condition subsequent is a later event that cuts off an existing contractual duty when the contract says that event will end the duty.
gold_keys.trigger: remains effective unless

silver_keys.statement: When a contract gives an exact 'unless' trigger, do not let choices swap in a broader doctrine like impossibility or substantial performance.
silver_keys.trigger: answer uses a different doctrine than the clause's stated event

drill_seeds.prompt: A contract says a duty remains effective unless Event X happens. Event X happens. A choice says breach unless performance was impossible. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut. It swaps Event X for impossibility.

drill_seeds.prompt: What does a later 'unless' event do to an existing duty when the contract says it ends the duty?
drill_seeds.answer: It discharges the duty.

drill_seeds.prompt: The contract was effective when signed, but the stated later terminating event occurred before performance. Which fact is dispositive?
drill_seeds.answer: The later terminating event.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
stem: At a private 'Psalms-and-Paintbrushes' youth retreat, Hannah brings her 16-year-old son Timothy to Dr. Luke after Timothy's endocrinologist recommends a particular hormone medication for a diagnosis listed in the state medical code. A state statute prohibits physicians from prescribing that hormone medication to minors for that listed diagnosis, but it permits physicians to prescribe the same medication to minors for other diagnoses. The prohibition applies to every minor seeking the barred use. The text of the statute does not divide patients into male and female categories. Timothy challenges the statute under the Equal Protection Clause.
call: What is the key Equal Protection threshold question?
distilled_core_question: A state bars one hormone medication for minors for one medical use, allows the same medication for other uses, and does not classify male/female on its face. What classification does the Equal Protection analysis start with?
review_truth: On an Equal Protection threshold question, classify the line the law actually draws before arguing about scrutiny.

choices.text: Whether the statute is medically unwise, because bad medical policy automatically triggers strict scrutiny.
choices.c3_signal: The answer says bad policy automatically changes scrutiny. The automatic trigger is the visible defect.
choices.why_attractive: A student may think a medically disputed rule must be constitutionally suspicious. The breaker is that bad policy does not automatically trigger strict scrutiny.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer says bad medical policy automatically triggers strict scrutiny. The automatic trigger is the visible overclaim.
choices.future_cue: Circle automatically and ask whether policy wisdom is a suspect classification.

choices.text: Whether minors must be treated the same as adults in every medical setting.
choices.c3_signal: The word every makes the answer too broad, and it answers a generalized minors-rights question instead of the classification threshold.
choices.why_attractive: A student may see the adult/minor contrast and jump to minors' rights. The breaker is that the answer says every medical setting and misses the classification threshold.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer says minors must be treated like adults in every medical setting. The every-setting language is visibly overbroad.
choices.future_cue: Return to the question: the threshold is the classification drawn, not every adult/minor medical right.

choices.text: Whether the statute classifies by medical use and age, rather than by sex as such.
choices.c3_signal: This answer matches the call. It asks what line the statute draws before jumping to scrutiny.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Silver Key: On an Equal Protection threshold call, do not start with whether the policy is good or bad. Start with the line the law actually draws. Gold Key: A medical-use-and-age line does not become a sex classification merely because the same medication is allowed for other diagnoses; the threshold question is what classification the statute itself draws.

The answer tracks the threshold task: classify the statute before choosing a scrutiny tier.

choices.text: Whether the hormone medication is prescribed for other diagnoses, because that fact alone automatically proves sex discrimination.
choices.c3_signal: The answer says one fact alone automatically proves sex discrimination. Fact-alone automatic proof is the visible overclaim.
choices.why_attractive: A student may treat same medication for other diagnoses as enough to prove discrimination. The breaker is that fact alone does not automatically prove sex classification.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer says same medication elsewhere fact alone automatically proves sex discrimination. The Gold Key confirms why that automatic inference fails.
choices.future_cue: Separate medical use from sex-as-such classification.

remediation_card.title: Classification First, Scrutiny Second
remediation_card.signal: Answer choices jump to strict scrutiny, rights in every context, or automatic discrimination.
remediation_card.student_move: Name the line the law draws before choosing a tier.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Equal Protection starts with classification.
remediation_card.trap: Policy-disagreement and same-medication facts are not automatic scrutiny triggers.

gold_keys.statement: A statute that bars the same medication only for a specified medical use and age group is not automatically a sex classification. Start with the classification the law actually draws.
gold_keys.trigger: same medication allowed for some diagnoses but barred for minors for one diagnosis
gold_keys.authority: United States v. Skrmetti, 605 U.S. 495 (2025); Massachusetts Board of Retirement v. Murgia; Vacco v. Quill

silver_keys.statement: On an Equal Protection threshold call, cut answers that jump straight to automatic scrutiny. The answer that names the classification actually drawn is the responsive lane.
silver_keys.trigger: call asks key Equal Protection threshold question

drill_seeds.prompt: Which phrase makes this answer structurally suspect: 'bad medical policy automatically triggers strict scrutiny'?
drill_seeds.answer: automatically triggers

drill_seeds.prompt: Before choosing scrutiny, what must you identify in an Equal Protection question?
drill_seeds.answer: The classification the law actually draws.

drill_seeds.prompt: Same medication, different permitted uses. Does that fact alone automatically prove sex discrimination?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Start with the classification drawn by the law.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: foreseeable rescue versus actual awareness
stem: For a private Bible-story block party in his driveway, Daniel built a wheeled “Jonah’s whale” float. The night before the party, Daniel climbed inside the float to test the hatch on his sloped driveway, even though he had not set the brake or chocked the wheels. The float began rolling downhill toward a retention pond with Daniel trapped inside. Lydia saw the float rolling, ran to pull open the hatch before it reached the water, and the hatch spring snapped back and broke her wrist. Daniel did not see Lydia approach before she was hurt.
call: If Lydia asserts a negligence claim against Daniel for the injury she sustained, the court should find for:
distilled_core_question: A defendant carelessly creates danger to himself; a rescuer is injured while trying to save him. Can the rescuer recover from the defendant?
review_truth: Danger invites rescue: negligent danger to human life can make the rescuer a foreseeable plaintiff.

choices.text: Lydia, because a rescuer is entitled to indemnity from the person whom the rescuer was attempting to rescue.
choices.c3_signal: The choice gives every rescuer a categorical indemnity right instead of tying recovery to Daniel's unreasonable danger.
choices.why_attractive: The choice rewards the instinct that rescuers deserve reimbursement. The breaker is that rescue doctrine is not automatic indemnity; it requires negligent danger and foreseeable rescue.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Automatic rescuer indemnity overclaims the legal basis for recovery.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer states negligence-based recovery or a blanket remedy.

choices.text: Daniel, because Daniel did not know that Lydia would try to rescue him.
choices.c3_signal: The choice treats Daniel's subjective knowledge as the deciding element.
choices.why_attractive: The choice makes Daniel's lack of actual knowledge feel decisive. The breaker is that the rescue rule uses foreseeability of rescue, not actual awareness of this rescuer.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Actual awareness is not the dispositive element; foreseeable rescue is.
choices.future_cue: Use the Gold Key: rescue is foreseeable when danger invites it.

choices.text: Lydia, because her injury resulted from Daniel’s failure to act reasonably.
choices.c3_signal: This choice ties Lydia's injury to Daniel's unreasonable conduct, which is the operative rescue-duty lane.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Gold Key: Danger invites rescue. When Daniel unreasonably created a danger to human life, including his own, a rescue attempt was a foreseeable response. Lydia’s injury came from trying to respond to that danger, so the negligence answer that ties her injury to Daniel’s unreasonable conduct is the credited answer.

Silver Key: On a “because” answer set, do not pick the party first. Test the because-clause. C wins because it gives the legally operative ground: unreasonable danger causing a foreseeable rescue injury.

choices.text: Daniel, because Lydia was an officious intermeddler.
choices.c3_signal: The stem shows an apparent human rescue, not purposeless interference.
choices.why_attractive: The choice uses a formal-sounding label that makes Lydia look like a meddler. The breaker is that apparent human peril gives her a legitimate rescue reason.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The officious-intermeddler frame does not fit an apparent human rescue.
choices.future_cue: Check whether the plaintiff had a legitimate rescue reason.

remediation_card.title: Danger invites rescue, not automatic indemnity
remediation_card.signal: Rescuer injured while responding to apparent human peril.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the defendant's unreasonable conduct created the danger; then reject actual-awareness and automatic-payment traps.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Rescue is foreseeable when negligent danger creates apparent human peril.
remediation_card.trap: Treating rescue as either meddling or automatic reimbursement.

gold_keys.statement: Danger invites rescue: when a person negligently creates apparent human peril, even to himself, a reasonable rescue attempt is foreseeable and the rescuer may recover for rescue injuries caused by that negligence.
gold_keys.trigger: rescuer injured while trying to save someone from danger the defendant negligently created
gold_keys.authority: Wagner v. International Railway Co., 232 N.Y. 176 (1921); self-peril applications recognized in later rescue-doctrine cases.

silver_keys.statement: In a party-result answer set, test the because-clause before choosing the winner. A correct party with a wrong reason is still out.
silver_keys.trigger: choices split between plaintiff/defendant and each uses 'because'

drill_seeds.prompt: A negligent defendant creates apparent danger to himself, and a rescuer is injured. State the rescue rule.
drill_seeds.answer: Danger invites rescue; reasonable rescue is foreseeable, and the rescuer may recover for injury caused by the negligent peril.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two answers choose the same party but give different reasons. What do you test first?
drill_seeds.answer: The because-clause.

drill_seeds.prompt: The defendant did not know a rescuer would appear. Is that the rescue-doctrine element?
drill_seeds.answer: No. The key is whether rescue was foreseeable from the danger.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: fact mistake versus law mistake
stem:
At a community Advent craft swap, Stephen sees a hand-carved olivewood nativity figurine on a table beside small giveaway cards printed with Bible verses. A sign on the table says, “Free verse cards—take one.” Stephen honestly believes the figurine itself has been left as part of the giveaway and takes it home intending to keep it. The figurine actually belongs to Ruth, who had set it down briefly while stacking programs. Stephen is charged with larceny, a specific intent crime requiring intent to permanently deprive another of property.

Later, at the same event, Mary sees Paul set down a similar olivewood figurine while he helps lead the closing song. Mary knows the figurine belongs to someone at the event, but she mistakenly believes state law permits a person to keep any item left unattended on a public craft-swap table after the closing song. Mary takes it intending to keep it. Mary is also charged with larceny; her belief about the law was wrong.
call: Which of the following correctly analyzes both prosecutions?
distilled_core_question: One larceny defendant honestly mistakes property as abandoned/giveaway; another knows it belongs to someone but misunderstands the law. Which one has a defense?
review_truth: For specific-intent larceny, an honest fact mistake can negate intent; a law mistake usually cannot.

choices.text: Both Stephen and Mary are not guilty because both acted from genuine beliefs that excused the taking.
choices.c3_signal: This treats both genuine beliefs the same even though the stem separates factual belief from legal belief.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because both actors are described as genuine or sincere. The breaker is that sincerity does not erase the fact/law distinction.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This extends the excuse from fact mistake to law mistake.
choices.future_cue: Ask what each defendant was mistaken about before judging guilt.

choices.text: Both Stephen and Mary are guilty because only reasonable mistakes can provide a defense.
choices.c3_signal: The stem says larceny is specific intent; this answer imports the wrong frame by requiring reasonableness for Stephen's fact mistake.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because reasonableness sounds like a familiar mistake-defense requirement. The breaker is that the stem says specific intent, so Stephen's honest fact mistake need not be reasonable.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This imports a reasonableness requirement from the wrong mistake-defense frame.
choices.future_cue: When the stem says specific intent, test whether the fact mistake negates that intent.

choices.text: Stephen is not guilty because his honest mistake of fact negates the specific intent for larceny; Mary is guilty because mistake of law is generally no defense.
choices.c3_signal: This splits the two scenarios on the fact/law axis and matches both stem facts.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It is true and responsive to both scenarios.

choices.text: Stephen is guilty; Mary is not guilty—his mistake was unreasonable, and her mistake concerned the law and is a valid defense.
choices.c3_signal: This points the two mistake rules in the wrong direction.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because Stephen's assumption feels careless and Mary's legal belief sounds principled. The breaker is direction: fact mistake can help Stephen, while law mistake generally does not help Mary.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This reverses both outcomes.
choices.future_cue: State the direction aloud: fact mistake helps; law mistake usually does not.

remediation_card.title: Fact mistake / law mistake split
remediation_card.signal: One actor misunderstands ownership facts; another understands facts but misunderstands legality.
remediation_card.student_move: First label each mistake as fact or law, then apply the specific-intent Gold Key.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Specific-intent fact mistake can negate intent; law mistake generally cannot.
remediation_card.trap: Treating all sincere mistakes the same or requiring reasonableness for every mistake.

gold_keys.statement: For a specific intent crime, an honest mistake of fact can negate the required specific intent even if the mistake is unreasonable.
gold_keys.trigger: The stem says specific intent and the defendant honestly thinks the property is abandoned or free.
gold_keys.authority: Morissette v. United States; DOJ Justice Manual larceny formulation; Cornell Wex mistake-of-fact summary.

gold_keys.statement: Mistake of law generally does not excuse criminal conduct; sincerity alone is not enough.
gold_keys.trigger: The defendant knows the object belongs to someone but misunderstands whether taking it is legal.
gold_keys.authority: Cheek v. United States; Justia mistake-of-law summary.

silver_keys.statement: Read the answer array as two switches: Stephen's mistake is about a fact; Mary's mistake is about the law. The credited answer must split them, not treat both defendants the same.
silver_keys.trigger: Two scenarios plus choices that say both guilty, both not guilty, and two split answers.

drill_seeds.prompt: One defendant mistakenly thinks property is free; another knows it belongs to someone but misunderstands the law. Which outcome pair should you expect?
drill_seeds.answer: Fact-mistake defendant not guilty if intent is negated; law-mistake defendant guilty.

drill_seeds.prompt: For a specific-intent crime, must an honest fact mistake be reasonable?
drill_seeds.answer: No. It must honestly negate the specific intent.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut: 'Both are guilty because only reasonable mistakes count.'
drill_seeds.answer: Wrong frame. Specific-intent fact mistake does not require reasonableness.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: identity-use/commercial-consent answer vs extra-condition traps
stem:
Final Christian variation — `20598_write_it_on_your_heart`

Ruth is a nationally known Christian calligraphy teacher whose short devotional videos are instantly recognized by her turquoise headscarf, sand-timer necklace, whispery cadence, spiral hand-lettering flourish, and catchphrase, “write it on your heart.” Peter’s private Bible-memory app company hired Lydia, an actress and animator, to recreate those traits in a paid social-media ad for the app. The ad never used Ruth’s legal name or photograph, and Ruth did not consent. Commenters overwhelmingly understood the ad’s guide character to be Ruth. Ruth sues Peter’s company for appropriation.

Call:
call: Should a court rule for Ruth?
distilled_core_question: A company uses a clearly recognizable imitation of a person’s identity in a product ad without consent and without using the person’s name or photograph. Does appropriation lie?
review_truth: Appropriation can rest on unauthorized commercial use of recognizable identity; exact name/photo, insult, and false statement are not required.

choices.text: No, because the ad portrayed the guide character in a respectful and admiring way.
choices.c3_signal: The answer rests on respectful tone instead of the identity-use facts.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because flattering use feels harmless. The breaker is that the call turns on unauthorized commercial identity use, not insult.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Respectful tone feels harmless, but the call asks commercial identity use.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer uses a legal trigger or only a tone judgment.

choices.text: Yes, because the company used Ruth’s distinctive identity for commercial advantage without consent.
choices.c3_signal: This choice matches the trigger facts: distinctive identity, commercial advantage, and no consent.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Only B is both true and responsive to the appropriation call.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the ad stated a false fact about Ruth.
choices.c3_signal: False fact language points to a different tort frame from the identity-use call.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because false statements feel like the familiar reputation-tort path. The breaker is that this is an identity-use call, and the Gold Key makes false-fact language a neighbor-frame trap.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: False fact is a neighbor-frame answer, not the appropriation call.
choices.future_cue: Name the call: appropriation. Then remove false-statement conditions unless the call asks for a reputation tort.

choices.text: No, because the ad did not use Ruth’s exact name or photograph.
choices.c3_signal: The answer adds an exact-name-or-photo requirement.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because exact name or photo feels like the safest proof of identity use. The breaker is that the Gold Key says recognizable commercial evocation can be enough.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Exact name/photo is an added requirement defeated by the Gold Key.
choices.future_cue: Use the identity-evocation Gold Key: recognizable commercial imitation can be enough.

remediation_card.title: Name/photo trap in appropriation
remediation_card.signal: The stem says no exact name or photograph, but many identity cues are copied.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not require exact name/photo. Ask whether the ad clearly uses the plaintiff’s identity for commercial advantage without consent.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Recognizable commercial evocation can be enough.
remediation_card.trap: Exact-name/photo-only answer.

gold_keys.statement: Appropriation is not limited to exact name or photograph. A clearly recognizable, unauthorized commercial evocation of the plaintiff’s identity can be enough.
gold_keys.trigger: Ad uses a lookalike, soundalike, persona, or identity cues to sell a product.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 652C; Midler v. Ford Motor Co., 849 F.2d 460 (9th Cir. 1988).

silver_keys.statement: For appropriation calls, sort the array by the three trigger facts: identity use, commercial advantage, and no consent. Extra requirements like exact name/photo, insult, or false fact are trap add-ons.
silver_keys.trigger: One answer mirrors identity-use facts while others add conditions.

drill_seeds.prompt: A commercial uses a distinctive soundalike and costume to evoke a celebrity but avoids the celebrity’s name and photo. Cut the answer: 'No, because no exact name or photograph was used.'
drill_seeds.answer: CUT as fabricated_rule once the Gold Key is applied.

drill_seeds.prompt: A commercial respectfully imitates a performer’s identity to sell a product. Cut the answer: 'No, because the imitation was flattering.'
drill_seeds.answer: CUT as colloquialism; tone is not the appropriation trigger.

drill_seeds.prompt: A product ad uses a person’s recognizable identity without consent. Cut the answer: 'Yes, but only if the ad stated a false fact.'
drill_seeds.answer: CUT as bait_doctrine / wrong_frame; false fact belongs to neighboring reputation torts.

drill_seeds.prompt: Pick the survivor: exact name/photo requirement, flattering-use answer, false-fact answer, or identity-use/commercial/no-consent answer.
drill_seeds.answer: Identity-use/commercial/no-consent answer.

subject: CONTRACTS
subtopic: Complete integration / merger clause / consistent additional term barred
tension_axis: complete-and-exclusive integration vs mere non-contradiction
splitting_fact: The writing says it is the complete and exclusive statement.
stem: Stephen agreed to write and rehearse a Scripture-themed puppet play for Martha’s family Advent party. Before anyone signed, Stephen allegedly said he would also prepare a handbell cue sheet at no extra charge. The signed agreement that followed listed the fee, scenes to be written, rehearsal dates, delivery deadline, and payment schedule. It also provided, “This writing is the complete and exclusive statement of the parties’ agreement.” When a dispute arose, Martha offered evidence of the earlier handbell promise. The agreement says nothing about handbells. How should the court rule?
call: How should the court rule?
distilled_core_question: A signed service contract says it is the complete and exclusive agreement. One party offers a prior oral extra term that does not conflict with the writing. Admit or exclude the oral term?
review_truth: Complete-and-exclusive beats merely consistent: a prior oral add-on inside the same deal is excluded.

choices.text: Exclude the oral promise because the writing was intended as a complete and exclusive statement of the parties’ agreement.
choices.c3_signal: Matches the complete-and-exclusive trigger and answers the evidence offered.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The complete-and-exclusive phrase defeats the prior oral consistent add-on.

choices.text: Admit the oral promise because it does not conflict with any term in the signed writing.
choices.c3_signal: It answers the partial-integration question, not the complete-and-exclusive question.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees no direct conflict and treats consistency as enough. The breaker is the complete-and-exclusive signal, which moves the question from contradiction to integration level.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It uses the partial-integration consistency frame when the stem gives a complete-and-exclusive writing.
choices.future_cue: Circle complete and exclusive before evaluating consistency.

choices.text: Exclude the signed writing because it left out the handbell cue sheet.
choices.c3_signal: The offered evidence is the oral promise; the answer excludes the signed writing.
choices.why_attractive: The student thinks an omitted promised feature damages the signed document. The breaker is that the offered evidence is the oral promise, not the signed writing.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It excludes the signed writing even though the offered evidence is the oral promise.
choices.future_cue: Ask what evidence the proponent is offering.

choices.text: Admit the oral promise because merger clauses affect only sales of goods.
choices.c3_signal: The word only is a danger signal, but the falsehood needs the Gold Key.
choices.why_attractive: The student recognizes UCC parol-evidence language and assumes merger clauses live only there. The breaker is the Gold Key: complete integration is also a common-law services-contract concept.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It falsely limits merger clauses to sales of goods.
choices.future_cue: Use the Gold Key: complete integration is not goods-only.

remediation_card.title: Complete beats consistent
remediation_card.signal: Signed writing says complete and exclusive; offered term came before signing.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not ask only whether the oral term conflicts; ask whether the writing is complete.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Complete integration excludes prior consistent add-ons.
remediation_card.trap: Consistency trap

gold_keys.statement: A complete-and-exclusive writing is a complete integration. Prior or contemporaneous oral additions inside the same deal are excluded even if they do not contradict the writing.
gold_keys.trigger: complete and exclusive statement + prior oral extra term
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 210, 213, 216

silver_keys.statement: When one choice says the oral term does not contradict and another points to complete/exclusive language, clash them on integration level before judging consistency.
silver_keys.trigger: not conflict vs complete and exclusive

drill_seeds.prompt: A party offers an oral side promise, but an answer excludes the signed contract. What filter breaks?
drill_seeds.answer: NOT_RESPONSIVE / misfit.

drill_seeds.prompt: One answer says the oral term is consistent; another says the writing is complete and exclusive. What is the axis?
drill_seeds.answer: Complete integration versus mere non-contradiction.

drill_seeds.prompt: A complete-and-exclusive writing is silent about a prior oral add-on. Does consistency alone admit it?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Complete integration excludes prior consistent add-ons.

subject: EVIDENCE
subtopic: Rule 407 product defect, design defect, and need for warning or instruction
tension_axis: Barred defect/warning purpose versus general relevance/feasibility/negligence-only drift.
stem: Naomi bought a portable “David’s Harp” hymn-projector kit for a neighborhood praise-night in her garage. As she unfolded the aluminum tripod, the hinge bracket snapped shut and crushed her hand. In a federal products-liability action governed by the Federal Rules of Evidence, Naomi offers evidence that, after her injury, the manufacturer replaced the hinge with a spring-loaded locking hinge and added a bold “keep hands clear / load limit” warning tag. Naomi offers the evidence to prove that the original hinge design was defective and that the original warning was inadequate.
call: How should the court rule under Rule 407?
distilled_core_question: After a product injury, the plaintiff offers a later product redesign and stronger warning to prove the original design defect and warning defect. Under Rule 407, admissible?
review_truth: Rule 407 blocks later fixes offered to prove defect or warning need; feasibility only matters when that is the actual disputed purpose.
dominant_trap: No measured pick rates supplied; likely diagnostic trap is negligence-only Rule 407 scope.

choices.text: Admit the evidence because the hinge change is relevant and relevant evidence is generally admissible.
choices.student_label: General relevance answer to a Rule 407 purpose question.
choices.c3_signal: The call asks Rule 407; this answer gives a general relevance rule and never handles the public-policy exclusion.
choices.why_attractive: The student remembers that relevant evidence usually comes in. The breaker is that Rule 407 is a specific public-policy exclusion and the answer never handles the offered purpose.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: General relevance is true as a background idea but does not answer the specific Rule 407 public-policy exclusion.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer addresses the named exclusion, not just relevance.

choices.text: Exclude the evidence for this purpose because Rule 407 bars subsequent remedial measures offered to prove a product defect, design defect, or need for a warning or instruction.
choices.c3_signal: It answers the exact call and uses the purpose phrase: exclude for this purpose.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is correct. Gold Key: Rule 407 is not negligence-only. It also bars later remedial measures when offered to prove product defect, design defect, or the need for a warning or instruction. Silver Key: lock the stated purpose first. Naomi is not offering the later hinge and warning to prove a disputed alternative purpose; she is offering them to prove original defect and warning inadequacy. That is the barred purpose lane.

choices.text: Admit the evidence because Rule 407 applies only to negligence claims, not products-liability claims.
choices.c3_signal: This requires the Gold Key; the problem is not visible from grammar alone.
choices.why_attractive: The student remembers the negligence language in Rule 407 and stops there. The breaker is the Gold Key that Rule 407 also covers product defect, design defect, and warning-need uses.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The negligence-only version of Rule 407 is too narrow.
choices.future_cue: Recall that Rule 407 includes product defect, design defect, and warning/instruction need.

choices.text: Admit the evidence automatically because a later redesign always proves feasibility.
choices.c3_signal: The words automatically and always overclaim; the stated purpose is defect and warning inadequacy.
choices.why_attractive: Feasibility is a real permitted-purpose word, so the choice feels like it found the exception. The breaker is that feasibility is not automatic and is not the purpose Naomi stated.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Feasibility is not automatic; the stem states a barred defect/warning purpose.
choices.future_cue: Match the exception word to the actual purpose stated in the stem.

remediation_card.title: Rule 407 Purpose Lock
remediation_card.signal: Post-injury fix plus answer choices about relevance, feasibility, or negligence-only scope.
remediation_card.student_move: Name the offered purpose before reading exceptions.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Defect/warning purpose is barred; feasibility is not automatic.
remediation_card.trap: Treating feasibility or relevance as a universal admission route.

gold_keys.statement: Rule 407 is not negligence-only: it bars later fixes offered to prove product defect, design defect, or a need for warning or instruction. Feasibility is only a separate permitted purpose when it is genuinely disputed and actually offered for that purpose.
gold_keys.trigger: Post-injury redesign or stronger warning offered in a product case.
gold_keys.authority: Federal Rule of Evidence 407; 1997 Advisory Committee note.

silver_keys.statement: When the stem tells you why evidence is offered, hold that purpose fixed. Relevance and exception words do not matter until they match the stated purpose.
silver_keys.trigger: The stem says the later measure is offered to prove defect or inadequate warning.

drill_seeds.prompt: A plaintiff offers a later product redesign to prove the original product was defective. Name the offered purpose.
drill_seeds.answer: Product/design defect; barred under Rule 407.

drill_seeds.prompt: True or false: Rule 407 applies only to negligence and culpable conduct.
drill_seeds.answer: False; it also covers product defect, design defect, and warning/instruction need.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut the phrase: 'A later redesign always proves feasibility.'
drill_seeds.answer: Always is the overclaim; feasibility is only a permitted purpose when disputed and actually offered.

drill_seeds.prompt: Why is 'relevant evidence is generally admissible' a bad answer to a Rule 407 call?
drill_seeds.answer: It answers the wrong layer; relevance does not override a specific exclusion.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: Daniel's negligent creation of peril vs Ruth-centered rescue facts
stem: During a private, for-profit Bible-themed escape-room contest called 'The Road to Emmaus,' Daniel, although acting with reasonable care, crawled into a narrow prop tunnel as part of the puzzle and became wedged, unconscious, and critically injured in a compartment that was difficult to reach. Ruth, an experienced stagehand who was attending the event, was seriously injured while trying to free Daniel. Ruth's attempt failed, and Daniel died before he could be reached. Ruth brought an action against Daniel's estate for compensation for her injuries. In this jurisdiction, traditional common-law rules relating to contributory negligence and assumption of risk remain in effect.
call: Is Ruth likely to prevail against Daniel's estate?
distilled_core_question: A careful person gets trapped and needs rescue. The rescuer is injured in a failed rescue. Can the rescuer recover from the careful person's estate?
review_truth: A rescuer's claim needs a negligent peril-maker; noble rescue alone does not create liability against a careful person.

choices.text: Yes, because the law should encourage rescue of helpless people.
choices.c3_signal: The choice says what the law should encourage, but it never states what Daniel did wrong.
choices.why_attractive: The student wants to reward rescue as a social good. The breaker is that policy language does not state Daniel's negligent creation of the peril.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer gives a policy reason, not the legal test against Daniel's estate.
choices.future_cue: Cut 'should encourage' language unless it is tied to the defendant's legal fault.

choices.text: No, because Daniel's peril did not arise from his own failure to exercise reasonable care.
choices.c3_signal: This choice locks onto the defendant-side fact: Daniel did not fail to exercise reasonable care.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. Daniel is the person Ruth sued. The answer must explain why Daniel’s estate is or is not responsible for Ruth’s injury. The stem says Daniel was acting with reasonable care. That fact blocks the rescue-doctrine route against Daniel’s estate.

Gold Key: Rescue doctrine needs a negligent peril-maker. A rescuer’s injury is charged to the person whose negligence created the peril, not merely to the person who needed help.

Silver Key: Lock the target actor. When the rescuer sues the imperiled person’s estate, ask what the imperiled person did wrong. Do not start with how noble, reasonable, or unsuccessful the rescue was.

choices.text: Yes, because Ruth's rescue attempt was reasonable.
choices.c3_signal: The call is against Daniel's estate; this choice talks only about Ruth's rescue attempt.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats Ruth's reasonable rescue as enough. The breaker is that the claim is against Daniel's estate and needs Daniel-side fault.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer addresses Ruth's rescue conduct rather than Daniel's fault.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the defendant, Daniel, failed to exercise reasonable care.

choices.text: No, because Ruth's attempt failed and therefore did not benefit Daniel.
choices.c3_signal: The answer focuses on whether Daniel was saved or benefited, but the call asks whether Ruth can recover for her own injury.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats the failed rescue as defeating the claim. The breaker is that rescue success is not the defendant-fault element.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer addresses failed benefit rather than Daniel's negligence.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether failed rescue is the legal axis or only a decoy fact.

remediation_card.title: Rescue Doctrine: Actor-Fault Gate
remediation_card.signal: Rescuer is hurt and sues the person rescued or that person's estate.
remediation_card.student_move: Target the defendant's negligence before praising the rescue.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No negligent peril-maker, no rescuer recovery from that defendant.
remediation_card.trap: Noble rescue facts feel dispositive.

gold_keys.statement: Rescue doctrine needs a negligent peril-maker. A rescuer's injury is charged to the person whose negligence created the peril, not merely to the person who needed help.
gold_keys.trigger: rescuer sues the imperiled person's estate
gold_keys.authority: Wagner v. International Railway, 232 N.Y. 176, 133 N.E. 437 (N.Y. 1921); Cornell Wex rescue doctrine

silver_keys.statement: Lock the target actor before judging the rescue. If the rescuer sues the imperiled person's estate, ask what that imperiled person did wrong.
silver_keys.trigger: choices discuss the rescuer's reasonableness, public policy, or failed benefit

drill_seeds.prompt: An answer says, 'Yes, because the law should encourage rescue.' Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut. It is policy language, not the operative legal test.

drill_seeds.prompt: A rescuer sues the rescued person's estate. One answer says the rescuer acted reasonably. What is missing?
drill_seeds.answer: The rescued person's negligent creation of the peril.

drill_seeds.prompt: When can a rescuer recover from the person rescued?
drill_seeds.answer: Only when that person negligently created the peril that led to the rescue injury.

drill_seeds.prompt: The choices discuss the rescuer, policy, and failed rescue. The suit is against the estate. What is the first move?
drill_seeds.answer: Lock the target actor and ask what the estate's decedent did wrong.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: false-light publicity vs neighboring privacy/defamation frames
stem:
Daniel first learned of Martha’s accusation when Martha later apologized to him. At a privately run Bible-character board-game tournament, Martha had pulled Lydia behind the prize table and falsely whispered, “Daniel is secretly swapping the Scripture-quiz answer cards.” Lydia kept the accusation to herself. Daniel sued Martha for false light.

Is Daniel likely to prevail on false light?
call:
Call: Will the plaintiff win false light?

Prediction after Gold Key: No. The accusation was false, but it was not publicized to a broad audience.

Adjacent-call traps:

* Defamation.
* Appropriation / commercial use.
* General “false impression” intuition.
distilled_core_question: A defendant falsely accused the plaintiff to one person in private; that person did not repeat it. Can the plaintiff win false light?
review_truth: False light needs public-style publicity; a private one-listener accusation does not create false-light liability.

choices.text: No, because false light requires commercial use of Daniel’s identity.
choices.why_attractive: The choice is attractive because it says No and uses a real privacy-sounding commercial-use concept. The breaker is that commercial identity use belongs to appropriation, not the false-light publicity call.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice imports the commercial-use element from appropriation rather than answering the false-light publicity call.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the reason belongs to false light or to a neighboring privacy tort.

choices.text: No, because the accusation was not publicized to a broad enough audience.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. Martha made the accusation only to Lydia, in a private aside, and Lydia kept it to herself. Daniel has a false-light theory only if the false light was publicized to the public or to a broad enough audience. That publicity threshold is missing.

Gold Key: False light needs public-style publicity. A private one-listener accusation is not enough, even if the statement is false and offensive.

Silver Key: In a No/No pair, keep the No reason that tracks the decisive fact in the stem. Here the repeated fact is the private one-person communication, not commercial use.

choices.text: Yes, because the accusation cast Daniel in a false light.
choices.why_attractive: The choice is attractive because the accusation really did make Daniel look dishonest. The breaker is that false impression alone skips the broad-publicity threshold.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice proves only the false-impression element and skips the publicity gate.
choices.future_cue: Run the Gold Key: false light needs broad publicity.

choices.text: Yes, because false light and defamation are the same tort.
choices.why_attractive: The choice is attractive because false light and defamation both involve false statements and often appear together. The breaker is that they are not identical, and false light has its own publicity gate.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice collapses false light and defamation into the same tort.
choices.future_cue: Treat 'same' and 'identical' as danger words when two neighboring torts are being collapsed.

remediation_card.title: False light publicity gate
remediation_card.signal: False-light claim after a private accusation.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the matter reached the public or a broad audience.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: One private listener is not false-light publicity.
remediation_card.trap: Treating falsity or defamation overlap as enough.

gold_keys.statement: False light needs publicity to the public or a broad audience. A private one-listener accusation is not enough, even if it is false.
Commercial use of a person's identity is appropriation, not false light. Do not borrow the neighboring privacy tort's element.

silver_keys.statement: When two answers say No, keep the No reason that matches the stem's decisive fact. Here, private audience beats commercial-use vocabulary.

drill_seeds.prompt: A false accusation is made privately to one person and not repeated. False light?
drill_seeds.answer: No; no public-style publicity.

drill_seeds.prompt: Commercial use of name or likeness belongs to which privacy tort home?
drill_seeds.answer: Appropriation, not false light.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says yes because the statement created a false impression. What element is missing?
drill_seeds.answer: Publicity to the public or a broad audience.
