subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
tension_axis: complete venue buckets vs incomplete/poisoned venue list
stem:
Final Christian variation

Lydia, a worship harpist domiciled in the Northern District of State G, was injured when a propane coffee cart exploded during a privately run Christian music festival in the Central District of State H. Lydia filed a federal action based on diversity against two individuals involved in setting up the cart. Peter, a stage electrician, is domiciled in the Eastern District of State J. Ruth, a carpenter who built the cart platform, is domiciled in the Western District of State J.

In which judicial districts would venue be proper for Lydia’s action?
call:
Call: identify all proper venue districts.
Prediction after Gold Key: event district plus both defendant-residence districts. No plaintiff-home district.
distilled_core_question: A federal diversity tort suit has one event district and two individual defendants domiciled in different districts of the same state. Which districts are proper venue?
review_truth: Venue list questions are bucket checks: include the event district and defendant-residence districts when all defendants reside in one state; do not add the plaintiff's home district.

choices.text: The Eastern District of State J and the Western District of State J.
choices.why_attractive: This choice sees that both defendants live in State J, so it grabs the residence bucket. It drops the event bucket, which the venue checklist also requires for a complete all-proper-districts answer.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It gives the defendant-residence bucket but omits the event bucket.
choices.future_cue: Add the event bucket before selecting a list answer.

choices.text: The Central District of State H.
choices.why_attractive: This choice sees the accident district and stops at the most concrete fact. It skips the defendant-residence bucket that also works because both defendants reside in the same state.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It gives the event bucket but omits the defendant-residence bucket.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether all defendants live in one state and then add each defendant-residence district.

choices.text: The Central District of State H, the Eastern District of State J, and the Western District of State J.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Gold Key: For ordinary federal civil actions, venue can be proper in a district where a substantial part of the events occurred, and also in a district where any defendant resides if all defendants reside in that same state. Silver Key: Treat the answer choices as bucket checklists: event bucket, defendant-residence bucket, and plaintiff-home lure.

The explosion occurred in the Central District of State H, so that district is a proper event venue. Peter and Ruth both reside in State J, though in different districts, so each district where one of them resides is also a proper defendant-residence venue. The complete list is therefore the Central District of State H, the Eastern District of State J, and the Western District of State J.

choices.text: The Northern District of State G and the Central District of State H.
choices.why_attractive: This choice rewards the impulse to include the plaintiff's home because she chose the lawsuit. The ordinary venue checklist does not use the plaintiff's home, so the added district poisons the list.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It adds the plaintiff-home district, which is not a venue bucket here.
choices.future_cue: Use the Gold Key: plaintiff home is not a venue bucket in this ordinary private-defendant action.

remediation_card.title: Venue bucket checklist
remediation_card.signal: The call asks which judicial districts are proper.
remediation_card.student_move: Build the complete venue bucket list before reading combinations.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Event district plus qualifying defendant-residence districts; plaintiff home is a lure.
remediation_card.trap: Stopping after the loudest fact or adding the plaintiff's home.

gold_keys.statement: For ordinary federal civil actions, venue can sit in the event district or in a defendant-residence district when all defendants reside in that same state; the plaintiff's home is not a venue bucket.
gold_keys.trigger: The call asks which judicial districts are proper and gives accident location plus defendants from different districts of one state.

silver_keys.statement: Read list answers as bucket checklists: keep every valid bucket and reject any answer that adds a false bucket or omits a true one.
silver_keys.trigger: Choices mix event district, defendant districts, and plaintiff home district.

drill_seeds.answer: X, Y, and Z; not P.

drill_seeds.answer: Plaintiff residence is not a venue bucket here.

drill_seeds.answer: The complete event-plus-defendants list.

stem:
Daniel was packing his private Scripture-verse printing booth for a Colorado craft fair when Ruth sued him in federal district court. The lawsuit, filed on April 4, was a state-law contract action seeking $144,000 for allegedly ruined illuminated hymn posters Ruth had commissioned for her private Easter pageant. When the complaint was filed, Ruth was domiciled in Arizona, and Daniel was also domiciled in Arizona. On April 25, before filing any answer, Daniel permanently moved to Colorado and changed his domicile.

Call: Did Daniel’s Colorado move create diversity jurisdiction?
call:
Call: Did the later move create diversity jurisdiction?

Prediction with Gold Key: No. Check citizenship at filing. Ruth and Daniel were both Arizona citizens then.

distilled_core_question: P and D were citizens of the same state when P filed a $144,000 state-law case in federal court. D later moved to another state before answering. Does the move create diversity jurisdiction?
review_truth: Diversity is a filing-day snapshot; a later domicile change does not create diversity that was missing when the complaint was filed.

choices.text: No, because state-law contract claims can never be heard under diversity.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees a state-law contract claim and overcorrects into thinking federal court is unavailable. The breaker is the categorical word never; diversity jurisdiction can hear qualifying state-law civil actions.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word never makes an overbroad category claim. State-law contract claims are not categorically excluded from diversity jurisdiction.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer is making a categorical claim broader than diversity doctrine allows.

choices.text: Yes, because any change in citizenship before trial controls.
choices.why_attractive: The student grabs the later Colorado move and treats any pretrial citizenship change as controlling. The breaker is the filing-day Gold Key; later citizenship changes do not create diversity missing at filing.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word any and the before-trial timing both fight the filing-day snapshot.
choices.future_cue: Circle the complaint-filing date and check citizenship there first.

choices.text: No, because Ruth and Daniel were both Arizona citizens when the complaint was filed.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. The answer locks the jurisdiction snapshot at the filing date. At that point, Ruth and Daniel were both Arizona citizens, so complete diversity was absent. Daniel’s later move to Colorado, even before his first answer, does not retroactively create diversity.

Gold Key: Diversity citizenship is measured when the complaint is filed. A later domicile change does not cure missing complete diversity.

Silver Key: When a Civ Pro jurisdiction stem gives both a filing-day citizenship fact and a later move, freeze the snapshot at filing before reading answer choices that try to move the measurement point.

choices.text: Yes, because diversity is measured when Daniel first answers.

subject: REAL_PROPERTY
tension_axis: actual knowledge of an express covenant versus implied/common-scheme or possible constructive-notice routes
stem: A businessman who owned Blackacre and Whiteacre, two adjoining parcels, conveyed Whiteacre to a gas company owner and covenanted in the deed to the gas company owner that when he, the businessman, sold Blackacre he would impose restrictive covenants to prohibit uses that would compete with the filling station that the gas company owner intended to construct and operate on Whiteacre. The deed was not recorded. The gas company owner constructed and operated a filling station on Whiteacre and then conveyed Whiteacre to his nephew, who continued the filling station use. The deed did not refer to the restrictive covenant and was promptly and properly recorded. The businessman then conveyed Blackacre to a man, who knew about the businessman's covenant prohibiting the filling station use but nonetheless completed the transaction when he noted that no such covenant was contained in the businessman's deed to him. The man began to construct a filling station on Blackacre. The nephew brought an appropriate action to enjoin the man from using Blackacre for filling station purposes. If the nephew prevails, it will be because
call: If the nephew prevails, it will be because
distilled_core_question: A successor buys burdened land knowing of an unrecorded land-use covenant and then violates it. Can the benefited successor enjoin the use?
review_truth: An equitable servitude may bind a successor with actual notice of a land-use restriction intended to run with the land.

choices.text: the man had actual knowledge of the covenant to impose restrictions.
choices.c3_signal: A uses the exact fact the stem gives: the man knew about the covenant before buying Blackacre.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: See the preserved right-answer explanation above.

choices.text: the man is bound by the covenant because of the doctrine of negative reciprocal covenants.
choices.c3_signal: B names a real nearby doctrine, but the stem is not a common-scheme subdivision or omitted-uniform-restriction case.
choices.why_attractive: It names a real property doctrine that sounds tailored to omitted restrictions. The breaker is that no common scheme or subdivision pattern appears.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This invokes a real common-scheme doctrine, but the stem gives an express covenant and actual knowledge rather than a subdivision/common-plan omission.
choices.future_cue: Use the express covenant and actual-knowledge route instead.

choices.text: business-related restrictive covenants are favored in the law.
choices.c3_signal: C does not give an element-based reason. It says the law favors this kind of covenant, which is not the servitude rule.
choices.why_attractive: It sounds like a policy reason for enforcing a commercial restriction. The breaker is that enforcement depends on servitude elements, not a general policy favoring business restrictions.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This policy statement is not the rule for enforcing a restrictive covenant against a successor.
choices.future_cue: Cut policy glosses that do not mention remedy, notice, intent, or land-use burden.

choices.text: the man has constructive notice of the possibility of the covenant resulting from circumstances.
choices.c3_signal: D uses a weaker and different notice story: constructive notice of a possible covenant from circumstances. The stem gives actual knowledge of the covenant.
choices.why_attractive: It stays in the notice neighborhood and sounds plausible because recording and circumstances are heavily featured. The breaker is that the stem gives actual knowledge, not merely constructive notice of a possible covenant.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This substitutes constructive notice of a possible covenant for the actual knowledge fact the stem gives.
choices.future_cue: When one choice says actual knowledge and the stem gives actual knowledge, do not choose a possible-notice theory.

remediation_card.title: Injunction + Land-Use Restriction = Equitable Servitude
remediation_card.signal: Successor tries to use land contrary to a restriction; plaintiff seeks an injunction.

remediation_card.tiny_rule: Actual knowledge satisfies the successor-notice requirement.
remediation_card.trap: Do not switch to common-scheme or constructive-possibility theories when the stem gives actual knowledge.

gold_keys.statement: When the plaintiff seeks an injunction enforcing a land-use restriction, think equitable servitude. The burden can bind a successor if the restriction concerns land use, was meant to run, and the successor had notice; actual knowledge is enough.
gold_keys.trigger: injunction to stop a successor's land use, plus actual knowledge of the covenant
gold_keys.authority: Equitable servitude / covenant running with land doctrine

gold_keys.statement: Negative reciprocal covenant doctrine is the common-plan / omitted-lot-restriction route. Do not use it when the stem gives an express covenant and actual knowledge instead.

gold_keys.authority: Common-scheme equitable servitude doctrine

silver_keys.statement: Read the remedy first. Injunction means equitable-servitude lane; damages would push toward real-covenant lane.
silver_keys.trigger: the call asks for an injunction enforcing a land-use restriction

silver_keys.statement: When the stem gives actual knowledge, do not trade it for a weaker possible-notice theory unless the answer must use that weaker route.

negative reciprocal covenant applies to any omitted restriction
constructive notice is always the right notice answer

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
topic: Relations Between Federal and State Governments
tension_axis: practical interference vs geography/formality
stem:
Under authority granted by Congress, the United States Department of Defense hired Barnabas Metalworks, a private Advent-themed shop owned by Lydia, to manufacture rugged rescue-beacon casings for military search teams. The contract required all casting and polishing to occur at Barnabas’s old rail-depot workshop beside Mercy Brook, and it allowed the shop to release no more than four ounces per day of a polishing solvent into the brook from that production.

While producing the beacon casings under the contract, Barnabas routinely released between three and four ounces per day of the solvent into Mercy Brook. The state later prosecuted Barnabas under a state clean-water statute that prohibits any person or business entity from releasing more than three ounces per day of that solvent into any creek located in the state.

Barnabas defended on the ground that, as a federal contractor, it was immune from state regulation. Which one of the following additional facts or inferences, if it were the only one true, would most effectively support the state’s argument?
call: Which additional fact or inference, if it were the only one true, would most effectively support the state's argument?
distilled_core_question: A federal contractor violates a stricter state discharge limit. Which fact best supports the state? The stricter limit does not increase federal production cost.
review_truth: For a federal contractor, the state’s best fact is the one showing the state rule does not interfere with the federal project.

choices.text: Congress has not expressly exempted Barnabas from complying with state clean-water statutes.
choices.c3_signal: It talks about express wording, not practical effect on the federal project.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells the formal idea that express congressional wording controls. The breaker is that express wording does not answer practical interference.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice focuses on express exemption instead of the interference axis.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the fact addresses practical burden on federal work.

choices.text: Mercy Brook is not navigable.
choices.c3_signal: Navigability belongs to a different jurisdictional frame.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells navigability as a legal-sounding jurisdiction fact. The breaker is that navigability is not the federal-contractor immunity axis.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice shifts to navigability, a different jurisdictional frame.
choices.future_cue: Return to the immunity call, not admiralty or river power.

choices.text: Keeping the releases at three ounces or less per day would not increase the cost of producing the rescue-beacon casings required by the contract.
choices.c3_signal: It is the only answer that speaks to the practical effect on the federal contract.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: After geography/formality traps are cut, C is the answer that matches the interference axis.

choices.text: Mercy Brook is located entirely within the state.
choices.c3_signal: The stem already gives federal authority; creek location does not answer immunity.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells the creek’s intrastate location as state-control proof. The breaker is that federal authority is already supplied by the stem.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice shifts to intrastate geography after federal authority is already given.
choices.future_cue: Accept the stem’s federal-authority premise and look for interference.

remediation_card.signal: state regulation of a private federal contractor
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the state rule burdens the federal job.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No interference, no immunity win.
remediation_card.trap: geography or express-exemption formalism

subject: TORTS
subtopic: Standard of Due Care / Contributory Negligence / Causation
tension_axis: defendant no-breach versus plaintiff avoidability versus other-cause blame
stem:
Original row used: BARMATRIX Q# 20649, Torts, official key A. The source row asks which added fact would most likely produce judgment for an independent contractor in an all-or-nothing contributory-negligence jurisdiction. 

Chosen variation title: *The Christmas Pageant Platform*

Naomi worked for Lydia’s private pageant-production company, which was staging a Christian Christmas pageant. The company hired Barnabas, an independent contractor, to adjust the idle setting on a motorized rolling platform that carried a large manger prop. Barnabas adjusted the idle setting too high. Later, Naomi stood beside the platform and pressed the start switch to move it; because the platform lacked a roll-stop interlock, it lurched and injured her.

Naomi asserted a negligence claim against Barnabas. Which one of the following additional facts or inferences, if it were the only one true, would be most likely to result in a judgment for Barnabas in a jurisdiction that applies the all-or-nothing rule of contributory negligence?
call:
Prediction: pick the fact that attacks Barnabas’s own negligence. Best target: unforeseeable risk or no breach.

Adjacent-call traps:

A and D answer “who else is at fault?”

B answers “could Naomi have avoided injury?”

The real call asks “what fact helps Barnabas win?”
distilled_core_question: A contractor adjusted equipment in a way that caused injury only because a safety device was missing. Which added fact most helps the contractor win: normal safety-device custom, plaintiff avoidability, product defect, or another party's notice failure?
review_truth: A defendant wins a negligence claim by breaking the plaintiff's proof of the defendant's own unreasonable foreseeable-risk conduct, not by merely pointing to avoidability or another possible cause.

choices.text: The company that previously rented the platform failed to notify Lydia’s company that the platform needed a roll-stop interlock.
choices.why_attractive: Choice A looks useful because it blames a different business in the equipment chain. The breaker is that another actor's lapse does not answer whether Barnabas's own foreseeable-risk breach is defeated.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice blames a different company instead of attacking Barnabas's own negligence.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the fact defeats Barnabas's own negligence.

choices.text: If Naomi had been standing on the operator step when she started the platform, she would not have been injured.
choices.why_attractive: Choice B looks powerful because the call mentions contributory negligence and the fact says Naomi could have avoided injury. The breaker is that avoidability is not the same as negligent plaintiff conduct.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice proves a safer hypothetical, not negligent plaintiff conduct.
choices.future_cue: Demand a fact saying Naomi acted unreasonably.

choices.text: Rolling pageant platforms of this type are usually equipped with roll-stop interlocks.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. The call asks for the added fact most likely to produce judgment for Barnabas. If platforms of this type usually have roll-stop interlocks, then Barnabas may reasonably have expected the interlock to prevent the platform from lurching even after an idle adjustment. That fact attacks Barnabas’s own negligence: it weakens foreseeability of the risk created by the idle adjustment.

Gold Key: Negligence turns on unreasonable conduct in light of foreseeable risk. A fact that makes the particular risk not foreseeable can defeat breach.

Silver Key: In a “which added fact helps the defendant win” array, prefer the fact that breaks an element of the plaintiff’s claim over facts that merely blame someone else or describe a safer hypothetical.

choices.text: The absence of a roll-stop interlock was a manufacturing defect in the platform.
choices.why_attractive: Choice D looks powerful because a manufacturing defect feels like a complete alternate explanation. The breaker is that another cause does not automatically defeat Barnabas's own negligence.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice points to product-defect liability, not a defense to Barnabas's own negligence.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the fact negates Barnabas's foreseeable risk.

remediation_card.title: Avoidability is not contributory negligence
remediation_card.signal: The answer says the plaintiff would not have been injured if she had acted differently.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the actual conduct is described as unreasonable.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Contributory negligence needs plaintiff negligence, not mere avoidability.
remediation_card.trap: Safer hypothetical sold as all-or-nothing plaintiff fault.

gold_keys.statement: Negligence turns on unreasonable conduct in light of a foreseeable risk. A fact that makes the specific risk not foreseeable can defeat breach.
gold_keys.trigger: The added fact says the missing safety device is usually present.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 3.

gold_keys.statement: Contributory negligence requires negligent plaintiff conduct that contributed to the harm. A fact that the plaintiff would have avoided injury by doing something else is not enough by itself.
gold_keys.trigger: The answer says the plaintiff would not have been hurt from another position.
gold_keys.authority: Common-law contributory negligence rule.

silver_keys.statement: In an added-fact defense question, sort each option by what it attacks: defendant breach, plaintiff negligence, other cause, or other party.
silver_keys.trigger: Choices point in four different blame directions.

drill_seeds.prompt: A plaintiff would not have been injured if she had used a safer position. Does that alone prove contributory negligence?
drill_seeds.answer: No. It shows avoidability, not negligent conduct.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two answers survive: one says the device is usually present; one says the plaintiff could have stood elsewhere. Name the axis.
drill_seeds.answer: Defendant no-breach / unforeseeable risk versus plaintiff avoidability.

drill_seeds.prompt: In an added-fact defense call, which fact is stronger: one blaming a manufacturer, or one making the defendant's risk unforeseeable?
drill_seeds.answer: The unforeseeable-risk fact, because it attacks the plaintiff's claim against this defendant.

drill_seeds.prompt: What must the added fact show before contributory negligence bars recovery?
drill_seeds.answer: Plaintiff negligence that contributed to the harm.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: cognition vs volition
stem:
Stem / Fact Pattern

Lydia has a severe compulsion disorder that psychiatrists recognize as a legitimate mental disease. She has been examined and found to understand fully that damaging another person’s property is illegal and wrong. Even so, whenever she visits a privately run Christian craft market and sees ceramic nativity ornaments for sale, she experiences overwhelming uncontrollable urges to snap the shepherd staffs off the ornaments. She does this on repeated visits and is charged with multiple counts of criminal mischief.

The jurisdiction uses both M’Naghten and the irresistible-impulse supplement. Lydia’s expert testifies that, because of her mental disease, her urges were genuinely uncontrollable and she could not conform her conduct to the law.

Call of Question

Which of the following best states Lydia’s insanity claim?
call: Which of the following best states Lydia's insanity claim?
distilled_core_question: A defendant knows the act is wrong but, due to mental disease, cannot conform conduct in a M'Naghten-plus-irresistible-impulse jurisdiction. Which insanity test may apply?
review_truth: Knowing wrongfulness kills only the M'Naghten cognitive route; irresistible impulse can still matter when mental disease prevents control.

choices.text: Lydia has an insanity defense because she has a recognized mental disease.
choices.c3_signal: The choice grabs the threshold fact but does not answer which legal incapacity applies.
choices.why_attractive: This choice grabs the mental-disease fact and treats it as enough. The breaker is that the call needs a legal incapacity, not a diagnosis alone.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice proves a threshold diagnosis but does not state the legal incapacity that answers the call.
choices.future_cue: Mark diagnosis as threshold only, then look for cognition or volition.

choices.text: Lydia may have an insanity defense under the irresistible-impulse supplement because she could not conform her conduct to the law despite knowing the damage was wrong.
choices.c3_signal: This choice matches the jurisdiction trigger and the volition fact.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. Lydia’s strongest insanity claim is not that she failed to know the act was wrong. The stem says she did know that. Her claim is that, because of a recognized mental disease, she could not conform her conduct to the law.

Gold Key: M’Naghten is the cognition lane: knowing the nature or wrongfulness of the act. Irresistible impulse is the volition lane: knowing wrong but unable to control or conform conduct.
Silver Key: In this answer array, sort every choice into one of three buckets: cognition, volition, or diagnosis alone. The stem gives “knows wrong” and “cannot conform,” so the volition bucket wins.

choices.text: Lydia has no insanity defense because she knew breaking the ornaments was wrong.
choices.c3_signal: The choice answers only the M'Naghten lane and ignores the supplement named in the stem.
choices.why_attractive: This choice correctly notices that Lydia knew the damage was wrong. The breaker is that knowledge defeats only M'Naghten, not the irresistible-impulse supplement.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice answers the cognition lane only and ignores the volitional supplement named in the stem.
choices.future_cue: Use the Gold Key: cognition fails, volition may survive.

choices.text: Lydia has an insanity defense under M'Naghten because the impulse overrides her cognition.
choices.c3_signal: The choice puts the impulse fact under the cognition test label.
choices.why_attractive: This choice hears the impulse fact and tries to use it. The breaker is that impulse belongs to the irresistible-impulse lane, not the M'Naghten lane.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice places the impulse-control fact under M'Naghten, which is the wrong test label.
choices.future_cue: Attach impulse-control facts to irresistible impulse, not M'Naghten.

remediation_card.title: Insanity tests: cognition vs volition
remediation_card.signal: Stem gives M'Naghten plus irresistible impulse.
remediation_card.student_move: Match facts to lanes before picking.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Know-wrong = cognition; cannot-conform = volition.
remediation_card.trap: Treating one lane as the whole insanity defense.

gold_keys.statement: M'Naghten is cognition: did the defendant know the nature or wrongfulness of the act? Irresistible impulse is volition: the defendant may know wrong but still be excused if mental disease prevents control.
gold_keys.trigger: The stem says the jurisdiction uses M'Naghten plus irresistible impulse and gives both knowledge-of-wrongfulness and inability-to-conform facts.
gold_keys.authority: M'Naghten's Case; Model Penal Code section 4.01 conform-conduct analogue; Cornell Wex summaries.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
stem: Mary runs a private Christmas-market design studio in State A. She sued Daniel, a State B drone-show contractor, in federal court after Daniel's 'Bethlehem Star' drone display failed during a paid rehearsal for Mary's Advent market. Daniel served an answer that did not object to personal jurisdiction, although he already knew every fact supporting that objection. Seven weeks later, Mary amended the complaint against Daniel only to add a lost-profit damages theory from the same failed drone display. Daniel then moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction.
call: How should the court rule?
distilled_core_question: A defendant knew all facts supporting a personal-jurisdiction objection, answered without raising it, then faced a same-defendant amended complaint adding only a new damages theory from the same transaction. Should the later personal-jurisdiction motion be granted?
review_truth: Personal jurisdiction is waivable; a same-defendant amended complaint does not automatically revive an available personal-jurisdiction defense omitted from the first answer.

choices.text: Deny the motion only if Mary establishes supplemental jurisdiction over the amended damages theory.
choices.c3_signal: The call says personal jurisdiction; the choice answers supplemental jurisdiction.
choices.why_attractive: This choice borrows a jurisdiction word that sounds like a threshold requirement. The breaker is that supplemental jurisdiction answers subject-matter power over claims, while the call asks whether this defendant lost a personal-jurisdiction objection.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice answers supplemental jurisdiction, while the call asks personal-jurisdiction waiver.
choices.future_cue: Circle the jurisdiction word in the call and in the answer; cut if they do not match.

choices.text: Deny the motion because Daniel waived the available personal-jurisdiction defense by leaving it out of his first answer.
choices.c3_signal: This is the only answer that matches the call, the first-answer fact, and the no-new-defect amendment fact.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Only B is true and responsive to the late personal-jurisdiction motion.

choices.text: Grant the motion because lack of personal jurisdiction can never be waived.
choices.c3_signal: The word never is too absolute; the Gold Key supplies the exception.
choices.why_attractive: This choice exploits the student myth that all jurisdiction defects are never-waivable. The breaker is the personal-versus-subject-matter distinction: personal jurisdiction can be waived.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice overclaims with never; personal jurisdiction can be waived.
choices.future_cue: Separate subject-matter jurisdiction from personal jurisdiction before choosing.

choices.text: Grant the motion because every amended complaint gives a defendant a fresh chance to assert all Rule 12 defenses.
choices.c3_signal: Every and all overstate the effect of an amended complaint.
choices.why_attractive: This choice turns a new pleading response moment into a full procedural reset. The breaker is that a same-defendant amendment does not automatically revive Rule 12 defenses that were available and waived earlier.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice invents an automatic fresh-start rule for every amended complaint and all Rule 12 defenses.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the amended complaint first created the defense; same transaction and same defendant usually means no.

remediation_card.title: First response freezes waivable Rule 12 defenses
remediation_card.signal: Known personal-jurisdiction facts + answer or first Rule 12 motion without PJ objection.
remediation_card.student_move: Check whether the later pleading created a new defect. If not, cut fresh-start answers.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Available PJ objections are use-it-or-lose-it; same-defect amendments do not restart them.
remediation_card.trap: Amended complaint = fresh Rule 12 slate.

gold_keys.statement: Personal jurisdiction is a waivable Rule 12(b)(2) defense. If it was available and the defendant omitted it from the first answer or first Rule 12 motion, it is waived.
gold_keys.trigger: A defendant answers or files a Rule 12 motion without objecting to personal jurisdiction.

gold_keys.statement: An amended complaint does not automatically revive a Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defense that was available and waived earlier unless the amendment first creates the defense.
gold_keys.trigger: Plaintiff amends after defendant already failed to raise a known threshold defense.
gold_keys.authority: Gilmore v. Shearson/American Express, Inc.; State Auto Ins. Co. v. Thomas Landscaping & Constr., Inc.; Gnotec Reftele AB order.

silver_keys.statement: Match the jurisdiction word to the call before doing doctrine. Personal jurisdiction is defendant-court power; supplemental jurisdiction is subject-matter power over claims.
silver_keys.trigger: A choice switches from personal jurisdiction to supplemental jurisdiction.

drill_seeds.prompt: The call asks whether a late personal-jurisdiction motion should be granted. A choice says the plaintiff must establish supplemental jurisdiction. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: NOT_RESPONSIVE / misfit.

drill_seeds.prompt: A defendant knew all personal-jurisdiction facts and answered without raising PJ. What happens to the PJ defense?
drill_seeds.answer: Waived.

drill_seeds.prompt: Plaintiff later amends only to add damages from the same transaction against the same defendant. Does that automatically revive waived PJ?
drill_seeds.answer: No.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says every amended complaint restarts all Rule 12 defenses. What is the C3 tell?
drill_seeds.answer: Every/all overclaim plus fabricated Rule 12 reset.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
tension_axis: Is this a general taxpayer grievance, or the narrow spending-power/Establishment-Clause exception?
stem: After reports that teenagers at weekend robotics competitions are injuring themselves while soldering circuit boards, Congress enacts a provision distributing free soldering-safety kits to participants in public programs and private youth academies. The kits contain goggles, burn pads, and safety cards; they contain no prayer, worship material, or religious instruction. In many states, most private youth academies are church-affiliated. Lydia, a federal taxpayer, challenges the provision, arguing that it unconstitutionally supports religious entities.
call: Does Lydia have standing to make the challenge?
distilled_core_question: A federal taxpayer challenges a congressional spending program that gives neutral materials to public and church-affiliated private recipients, claiming an Establishment Clause violation. Does the taxpayer have standing?
review_truth: Federal taxpayers usually lack standing, but a challenge to congressional spending under the Establishment Clause fits the narrow Flast exception.

choices.text: No, because Lydia has not shown the required nexus between her taxpayer status and the safety-kit expenditures.
choices.c3_signal: After the Gold Key, the required connection is supplied rather than missing.
choices.why_attractive: The choice uses technical standing language, so it feels precise. The breaker is that the Gold Key says this spending-limit connection is supplied, not missing.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice says the standing nexus is missing, but the Gold Key shows the congressional spending and Establishment Clause facts supply the narrow exception.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the challenge is to congressional spending and alleges an Establishment Clause limit.

choices.text: Yes, because any federal taxpayer may challenge a congressional spending authorization.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'any' makes the taxpayer-standing rule too broad.
choices.why_attractive: The choice turns taxpayer status into a simple open door. The breaker is the absolute word 'any,' because taxpayer standing is narrow.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word 'any' overstates federal taxpayer standing.
choices.future_cue: Mark 'any' and replace it with 'only if the narrow exception applies.'

choices.text: No, because there is no proof that any money freed up by the free kits will be used for religious purposes.
choices.student_label: Merits-proof answer on a standing call.
choices.c3_signal: The choice asks how recipients will use saved money; the call asks whether Lydia may sue.
choices.why_attractive: The choice feels like it tests whether religious support has been proved. The breaker is that proof of religious use is a merits question, while the call asks standing.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice addresses proof of religious use, not taxpayer standing.
choices.future_cue: Separate entry-to-court from proving the Establishment Clause violation.

choices.text: Yes, because the challenge alleges a possible violation of a specific constitutional limit on Congress’s spending power.
choices.c3_signal: Congressional spending plus a specific Establishment Clause limit is the narrow taxpayer-standing exception.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
D is correct. Lydia is not relying on a general taxpayer grievance. She is challenging a congressional spending provision and claiming that the spending violates a specific constitutional limit on that spending power.

Gold Key: Federal taxpayers generally cannot sue just because tax money is being spent, but the Flast exception allows standing for a challenge to congressional taxing-and-spending action when the claim invokes a specific constitutional limit on that spending power. The Establishment Clause is the classic trigger.

Silver Key: Lock the call as standing, not merits. Do not ask whether the robotics kits are actually unconstitutional; ask whether this taxpayer is allowed into court to make that claim.

remediation_card.title: Taxpayer Standing: Narrow Door, Not Open Gate
remediation_card.signal: Federal taxpayer challenges religious spending.
remediation_card.student_move: Cut 'any taxpayer' overclaims, then check the narrow spending-power/Establishment trigger.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: General no standing; Flast exception for congressional spending plus Establishment Clause.
remediation_card.trap: Treating all taxpayer challenges as allowed, or treating merits proof as standing proof.

gold_keys.statement: Federal taxpayers generally lack standing, but they may challenge a congressional taxing-and-spending enactment when the claim alleges violation of a specific constitutional limit on that spending power; the Establishment Clause is the classic trigger.
gold_keys.trigger: Federal taxpayer + congressional spending + Establishment Clause claim.
gold_keys.authority: Flast v. Cohen, 392 U.S. 83 (1968).

silver_keys.statement: On a taxpayer-standing call, separate entry-to-court from whether the aid is unconstitutional.
silver_keys.trigger: The call asks whether the taxpayer has standing.

drill_seeds.prompt: Federal taxpayer challenges a congressional spending program as violating the Establishment Clause. Standing?
drill_seeds.answer: Yes, under the narrow Flast exception.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says: 'Any federal taxpayer may challenge any congressional spending.' Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: overclaim.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice denies standing because no religious use has been proved. What is the skipped move?
drill_seeds.answer: The choice answers merits proof, not standing.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: breach evidence vs breach-caused-injury evidence
stem:
Final Christian variation — `20717_ruths_hymn_recording_procedure`

Ruth, an adult soprano preparing a private Christmas hymns recording, had been treated by an allergist for severe medication sensitivities for four years before undergoing an elective outpatient vocal-cord procedure performed by Dr. Peter, a throat surgeon. Three days after the procedure, Ruth suffered respiratory collapse from a delayed drug reaction that developed after the procedure. The collapse put her in a coma. When doctors concluded that she was in a permanent vegetative state with no hope of recovery, the ventilator and feeding support were withdrawn at her family’s request after court approval, and Ruth died later that evening. Dr. Peter was not involved in that decision or its execution.

Ruth’s estate filed a wrongful death action against Dr. Peter, alleging that he was negligent in failing to consult an allergist before the procedure. At trial, the estate offered evidence that accepted medical practice required an allergist to examine a patient before this type of procedure.

In this action, the estate should
call:
Call: Should the estate prevail?

Prediction: No. The estate has breach evidence. It lacks causation evidence.

Adjacent-call trap: Did the doctor violate accepted practice? That is not the whole question.
distilled_core_question: A malpractice plaintiff proves a required specialist consult was omitted but offers no evidence that the consult would have changed the outcome. Should the plaintiff prevail?
review_truth: Breach evidence does not win malpractice unless the plaintiff also links that breach to the injury.

choices.text: not prevail, because there is no evidence that an allergist would have provided advice that would have changed the outcome if one had examined Ruth before the procedure.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
A is correct. The estate has evidence on the breach side: accepted medical practice required an allergist examination before this type of procedure. But the estate still needs evidence connecting that missed consult to Ruth’s respiratory collapse and death. Nothing in the facts shows that an allergist would have recommended different medication, different precautions, postponement, or cancellation.

Gold Key: In malpractice, breach evidence is not enough; the plaintiff must connect the specific breach to the injury.

Silver Key: Do not ask whether the procedure led to death. Ask whether the *missed consult* led to death.

choices.text: prevail, because the respiratory collapse that caused Ruth’s death was caused by the procedure that Dr. Peter performed.
choices.why_attractive: A student sees a complete medical timeline from procedure to collapse to death. The breaker is that the alleged breach is the missed consult, not the procedure in general.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice proves the procedure was in the causal chain, but the alleged breach is the missed allergist consult.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the missed allergist consult caused the collapse.

choices.text: not prevail, because Dr. Peter had nothing to do with the withdrawal of life support, which was the cause of Ruth’s death.
choices.why_attractive: A student sees that Dr. Peter did not withdraw support and treats that later decision as a clean causal break. The breaker is the life-support Gold Key: if the breach caused the need for support, withdrawal normally does not supersede causation.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice treats life-support withdrawal as the cause that defeats liability, but that move fails if the breach caused the condition requiring support.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the alleged breach created the condition requiring support.

choices.text: prevail, because Dr. Peter was negligent in failing to have Ruth examined by an allergist before the procedure.
choices.why_attractive: A student grabs the strongest plaintiff fact, the accepted-practice violation. The breaker is that breach is not enough without evidence that the breach caused the injury.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice proves breach but omits proof that the breach caused Ruth's collapse.
choices.future_cue: Require evidence that the breach changed the outcome.

remediation_card.title: Breach is not causation
remediation_card.signal: The stem proves what the doctor should have done but not what would have happened if the doctor had done it.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask what evidence links this specific missed step to this specific injury.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No link, no negligence win.
remediation_card.trap: Choosing the answer that proves breach or the answer that proves the procedure caused harm.

gold_keys.statement: In malpractice, proof that the doctor broke a professional rule is not enough; the plaintiff must prove that the broken rule caused the injury.
gold_keys.trigger: standard-of-care evidence but no evidence the missed consult would change the outcome
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts §§ 26, 29

gold_keys.statement: When the alleged tort creates the condition requiring life support, later withdrawal of support normally does not cut off causation.
gold_keys.trigger: family/court withdrawal after permanent vegetative state
gold_keys.authority: State v. Pelham; State v. Patterson

silver_keys.statement: Track the alleged breach, not the whole medical timeline. The question is not procedure-to-death; it is missed-consult-to-injury.
silver_keys.trigger: procedure-caused-harm answer competes with missed-consult answer

drill_seeds.prompt: A malpractice stem proves accepted practice required a specialist consult. No evidence says the consult would have changed the outcome. Cut the breach-only answer.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut as wrong_element: breach without causation.

drill_seeds.prompt: One answer says the doctor was negligent for omitting a consult. Another says no proof shows the consult would change the result. Name the axis.
drill_seeds.answer: Breach evidence vs breach-caused-injury evidence.

drill_seeds.prompt: The injury causes a vegetative state; family and court approve withdrawal of support. Does that usually break causation?
drill_seeds.answer: No, if the original breach caused the condition requiring support.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: plaintiff class boundary
stem:
Paul owned a small private company, Emmaus Games, that made Bible-themed board games. To decide whether to buy a used industrial laser cutter from Paul, Ruth asked for an inspection report. Paul hired Daniel, a professional equipment inspector, and told him that the report would be sent to Ruth for that purchase. Daniel prepared a report stating that the laser cutter had no major functional defects, but he carelessly failed to include that its control board was failing. Ruth reasonably relied on the report, bought the cutter, and lost money when it broke down soon after.

Call: Is Ruth likely to prevail on a negligent misrepresentation claim against Daniel?

Source row: the original item is BARMATRIX Q#20725, Torts, negligent misrepresentation, with official answer B and the rule reference that negligent misrepresentation may impose liability on a professional information supplier to a known limited class expected to rely on the information.
call:
Call: liability on negligent misrepresentation.
Prediction: yes, if the known-recipient rule applies.
Adjacent traps: contract privity, unlimited foreseeability, fraud-level knowledge.
distilled_core_question: A professional supplies careless false information for a specifically known person's reliance in a business transaction. The known person relies and loses money. Can that person recover for negligent misrepresentation?
review_truth: Known recipient is enough; every foreseeable reader is too many; knowledge of falsity is fraud territory, not negligence.

choices.text: Yes, because negligent misrepresentation reaches every foreseeable purchaser who might later read the inspection report.
choices.why_attractive: The choice flatters broad foreseeability: if anyone could be expected to read the report, liability feels fair. The word every makes the class too wide and the known-recipient Gold Key narrows the answer.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice over-expands the class with every foreseeable purchaser.
choices.future_cue: Bracket the class: not every foreseeable reader, only the named recipient or limited known group.

choices.text: No, because Ruth was not in contract with Daniel.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sells the familiar contract boundary: Ruth never hired Daniel. The Gold Key cuts it because the known-recipient duty does not require contract privity.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice invents a contract-privity requirement for a known-recipient professional-information case.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the professional knew this plaintiff or limited group would rely in the transaction.

choices.text: No, because negligent misrepresentation requires Daniel to have known the control-board statement was false.
choices.why_attractive: The choice imports a fraud mental state, making the mistake feel more serious before liability attaches. The call says negligent misrepresentation and the facts say careless, so knowledge of falsity is the wrong mental state.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice imports a knowledge-of-falsity requirement into a negligent/careless frame.
choices.future_cue: Use the stem's word careless and the call's word negligent to reject knowledge as the required mental state.

choices.text: Yes, because Daniel supplied false information for a known buyer’s reliance in a business transaction.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
D is correct. Daniel is a professional information supplier. He prepared an inspection report for a business transaction, knew that Ruth was the named person who would receive and rely on it, carelessly supplied false information, and Ruth suffered a reliance loss.

Gold Key: In negligent misrepresentation, contract privity is not required when the plaintiff is the known person, or one of a limited known group, expected to rely on professional business information.

Silver Key: Bracket the answer array. “No contract” is too narrow. “Every foreseeable purchaser” is too broad. The named-recipient answer is the middle lane.

remediation_card.title: Known recipient, not no one and not everyone
remediation_card.signal: Professional report prepared for a named recipient's business reliance.
remediation_card.student_move: Cut the extremes: no-contract is too narrow; every-foreseeable is too broad.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Known recipient or limited known group can recover for careless false business information.
remediation_card.trap: Students choose either strict privity or unlimited foreseeability.

gold_keys.statement: For negligent misrepresentation by a professional information supplier, no contract privity is required when the plaintiff is the known person, or one of a limited known group, expected to rely on the information in the transaction.
gold_keys.trigger: professional report + named recipient or limited known group + business reliance
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §552; Private Mortgage Investment Services, Inc. v. Hotel & Club Associates, Inc.

silver_keys.statement: When the array swings from no contract to every foreseeable reader, bracket both extremes and look for the named-recipient middle lane.
silver_keys.trigger: choices include no contract, every foreseeable, and named-recipient reliance

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says negligent misrepresentation reaches every foreseeable reader of a professional report. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: tiered_absolute / too broad.

drill_seeds.prompt: Professional knows a named buyer will rely on a careless report. Buyer is not in contract with professional. Does no contract alone defeat the claim?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Use the known-recipient Gold Key.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says negligent misrepresentation requires knowledge of falsity. Stem says carelessly false information. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: flat_misstatement / wrong mental state.

drill_seeds.prompt: Array contains no contract, every foreseeable reader, and known recipient. Which lane is structurally favored after the Gold Key?
drill_seeds.answer: Known recipient.

subject: TORTS
subtopic: Abnormally dangerous activities - harms outside abnormal risk
tension_axis: special-risk injury link vs shortcut reason
splitting_fact: The injury came from a folding costume rack, not blasting danger.
stem:
Final variation — `20727_easter_garden_blast_hose`

Esther owned a private hillside garden where she planned to stage a Bible-themed outdoor drama. She hired Daniel’s blasting company to use explosives to carve a stone backdrop for the “empty tomb” scene. While the crew was checking the perimeter and before any explosive charge had been set, Lydia arrived to drop off palm-branch props. Near the refreshment tent, an ordinary folding costume rack tipped over and fractured Lydia’s ankle.

Lydia sues Daniel’s company for strict liability based on the blasting. Is the company strictly liable?
call:
The call is not “was blasting dangerous?” It is not “was Lydia at the site?” It asks whether the company is strictly liable based on the blasting.

Prediction: No, because the injury came from the falling costume rack, not the blasting risk.
distilled_core_question: A plaintiff is hurt by an ordinary site hazard during preparation for blasting. The injury does not come from blasting danger. Is the blaster strictly liable?
review_truth: Strict liability for an abnormally dangerous activity covers only injuries caused by the special danger that makes the activity abnormal.

choices.text: No, because the injury did not result from an explosion, flying rock, ground shock, or other special risk of the blasting.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A is correct. The answer does not stop at the dangerous label. It links the injury to the risk that makes blasting abnormal. Gold Key: Strict liability for an abnormally dangerous activity follows the special danger, not every accident near the activity. Silver Key: In a 2-yes / 2-no array, do not pick the outcome first; pick the reason that matches the injury source.

choices.text: No, because strict liability never applies before blasting begins.
choices.why_attractive: The stem gives a timing fact, so this answer feels like a clean no-liability rule. The breaker is the absolute word 'never,' which overstates timing and ignores the injury-source rule.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word 'never' makes timing an absolute rule. The item turns on special-risk causation, not timing alone.
choices.future_cue: Cut the absolute and ask whether the harm fell inside or outside the special risk.

choices.text: Yes, because the injury occurred at the blasting site.
choices.why_attractive: The injury did occur at the blasting site, so the answer uses a true fact. The breaker is that location does not prove the injury came from the special blasting risk.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The site fact is true but not enough. It does not connect Lydia's injury to the special danger of blasting.
choices.future_cue: Separate location from injury source.

choices.text: Yes, because blasting with explosives is abnormally dangerous.
choices.why_attractive: Blasting with explosives sounds like the whole strict-liability trigger. The breaker is that the activity label omits the required link between the abnormal risk and this injury.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The dangerous-activity label is true but incomplete. It omits the injury-source link.
choices.future_cue: Ask what made the activity abnormal and whether that danger caused this injury.

remediation_card.title: Strict Liability Needs the Risk Link
remediation_card.signal: Dangerous activity plus ordinary injury.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask what hurt the plaintiff before choosing a strict-liability answer.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Activity label is not enough; injury must flow from the abnormal risk.
remediation_card.trap: Picking the dangerous-activity label or site connection.

gold_keys.statement: Strict liability for an abnormally dangerous activity follows the special danger, not every accident near the activity. The injury must be the kind of harm that made the activity abnormal.
gold_keys.trigger: The stem gives an abnormally dangerous activity plus an ordinary injury mechanism.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §519(2)

silver_keys.statement: In a 2-yes / 2-no strict-liability array, do not pick the outcome first. Pick the reason that links this injury to the risk named in the answer.
silver_keys.trigger: Two answers say yes, two say no, and only one answer talks about the injury source.

drill_seeds.prompt: A fireworks company is preparing a show. Before any fireworks are armed, a visitor is hurt by a collapsing picnic table. Strict liability?
drill_seeds.answer: No, unless the injury came from the special fireworks risk.

drill_seeds.prompt: Strict liability never applies before the dangerous activity begins.
drill_seeds.answer: Cut the absolute; timing alone is not the scope rule.

drill_seeds.prompt: Two answers say yes, two say no. One yes proves activity danger; one no proves no special-risk injury. Which reason controls?
drill_seeds.answer: The injury-source reason controls.

drill_seeds.prompt: State the tiny rule for abnormally dangerous activity strict liability.
drill_seeds.answer: Liability covers only the kind of harm that makes the activity abnormally dangerous.

subject: REAL_PROPERTY
subtopic: Landlord and Tenant - Assignments and subletting
stem:
Lydia owns a privately run Christmas craft hall called Star & Stable Market. For the season, she leased Stall 7 to Timothy to sell handmade Nativity candles. After Peter mailed a rent check for Stall 7 in his own name, Lydia deposited the check and said nothing. Timothy had assigned the remaining stall lease to Peter the week before. The lease said Timothy could not assign or sublease the stall without Lydia’s consent. When Lydia later decided she did not want Peter operating the booth, she declared the stall lease terminated.

May Lydia do so?
call:
Call lock: This is not asking whether the assignment was originally prohibited. It asks whether Lydia may terminate after what she did.

Prediction: No. The rent acceptance plus silence triggers waiver.
distilled_core_question: A landlord accepts rent from a known unauthorized assignee without protest, then tries to terminate the lease for the assignment. May the landlord terminate?
review_truth: Accepting rent from a known unauthorized assignee without prompt objection may waive the right to terminate for that assignment.

choices.text: Yes, because Lydia’s ownership interest in the market hall was superior to Timothy’s and Peter’s leasehold interests.
choices.why_attractive: The student reaches for the simple idea that the property owner has the stronger interest. The breaker is that ownership hierarchy does not answer whether Lydia's later conduct waived termination.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice answers a property-hierarchy question rather than the waiver-by-conduct question.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer explains the rent acceptance and no-protest facts.

choices.text: No, because Lydia waived her right to terminate the lease.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is correct. Lydia accepted Peter’s rent check in his own name and made no objection before later trying to terminate the lease. Gold Key: A landlord who knows of an unauthorized assignment or sublease and accepts rent without promptly reserving rights generally waives the right to terminate for that transfer. Silver Key: When the answer set pits the original lease clause against later landlord conduct, do not stop at the clause; lock the later acceptance-with-no-protest fact.

choices.text: Yes, because Lydia objected within a reasonable time.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats Lydia's later declaration as an objection. The breaker is that the stem first gives rent acceptance and silence, not a prompt reservation.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice claims timely objection, but the stem first gives acceptance and silence.
choices.future_cue: Mark the earlier deposit-and-silence fact before evaluating the later termination.

choices.text: Yes, because the lease prohibited assignments without Lydia’s consent.
choices.why_attractive: The student stops at the lease clause because it cleanly prohibits assignment. The breaker is the later conduct fact: Lydia accepted rent from Peter without protest, which triggers the Gold Key.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice proves the original assignment restriction but does not answer the later waiver fact.
choices.future_cue: Say: original clause first, later acceptance second; later fact controls the termination call.

remediation_card.title: Original Clause vs Later Conduct
remediation_card.signal: Lease restricts assignment, but landlord accepts rent from the assignee.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not stop at the restriction. Check whether the landlord later acted like the transfer was accepted.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Known breach + rent accepted without objection can waive forfeiture.
remediation_card.trap: Choosing the original clause after the landlord's later conduct changes the result.

subject: REAL_PROPERTY
tension_axis: one-consequence answer versus combined-consequence answer
stem: Lydia leased an urban courtyard lot that she owned to Timothy for a seven-year term so Timothy could run evening Bible-verse calligraphy workshops there. In the third year of the term, the city condemned the entire courtyard lot by eminent domain for a public stormwater basin.
call: Which statement best describes Timothy's rights?
distilled_core_question: A tenant still has years left on a lease when the government condemns the entire leased parcel. Is the tenant still liable for future rent, and does the tenant receive part of the condemnation award?
review_truth: A total eminent-domain taking of leased land ends future rent and compensates the tenant for the leasehold value taken.

choices.text: Timothy is entitled to a share of the condemnation award based on the value of the unexpired term of the leasehold less the rent that would have become due during that term.
choices.c3_signal: This gives only one of the two rights in the array.
choices.why_attractive: This choice sells the constitutional-compensation half, which sounds like the whole eminent-domain answer. The breaker is that the tenant also stops owing future rent, so the award-only statement is incomplete.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Award-only answer. It omits the future-rent consequence.
choices.future_cue: When the array offers X-only, Y-only, and X-plus-Y, test both components before choosing.

choices.text: Timothy may continue to use the courtyard for the balance of the term unless his leasehold interest was specifically named in the condemnation award.
choices.c3_signal: The answer invents a formal naming condition.
choices.why_attractive: This choice sells a formal-document trap by making the condemnation award sound controlling. The breaker is the Gold Key: a total taking reaches the leasehold whether or not the award names it separately.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It invents a requirement that the leasehold be specifically named before the taking reaches the tenant.
choices.future_cue: Recall that total taking of the parcel includes the leasehold.

choices.text: Timothy is freed of the obligation to pay rent for the balance of the term and is also entitled to a share of the condemnation award based on the value of the unexpired term of the leasehold less the rent that would have become due during that term.
choices.c3_signal: This answer contains both true components.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Gold Key: when the government takes the entire leased parcel, the taking reaches the leasehold as well as the landlord’s interest. The tenant loses possession, so future rent stops, and the tenant also has a compensable leasehold interest measured by the value of the unexpired term minus the rent the tenant no longer has to pay.

Silver Key: the answer array splits the rule into two single-consequence answers and one combined answer. Once both consequences are true, the combined answer is the complete response.

choices.text: Timothy is freed of the obligation to pay rent for the balance of the term.
choices.c3_signal: This gives only one of the two rights in the array.
choices.why_attractive: This choice sells the intuitive landlord-tenant half, because no rent after total ouster feels complete. The breaker is that the leasehold itself is also compensable, so the rent-only statement is incomplete.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Rent-only answer. It omits the compensation consequence.
choices.future_cue: Add the leasehold-value compensation consequence when the entire leasehold is taken.

remediation_card.title: Whole taking of leased premises
remediation_card.signal: Entire leased parcel is condemned during an unexpired term.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask for both consequences: rent and award.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Whole taking = leasehold gone; future rent gone; leasehold value claim remains.
remediation_card.trap: Picking only the rent half or only the award half.

gold_keys.statement: A total eminent-domain taking of leased land reaches the tenant's leasehold: future rent stops, and the tenant may claim the value of the leasehold interest taken.
gold_keys.trigger: entire leased parcel taken by eminent domain during the lease term
gold_keys.authority: U.S. Const. amend. V; United States v. General Motors Corp.; Farr v. Williams; City of Vista v. Fielder

silver_keys.statement: When two choices each give one consequence and a third combines them, test each component. If both components are true, the combined choice is the complete answer.
silver_keys.trigger: one answer says X, one says Y, one says X plus Y

drill_seeds.prompt: A tenant has four years left when the entire leased parcel is condemned. Name the two tenant consequences.
drill_seeds.answer: Future rent stops; tenant may claim leasehold value in the award.

drill_seeds.prompt: One choice says X, one says Y, one says X and Y. What move do you run?
drill_seeds.answer: Test X and Y separately; if both are true, choose the combined answer.

drill_seeds.answer: fabricated_rule.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: contact intent vs injury/risk/motive mental-state distractors
stem: At a privately run Bible-story craft fair held in a rented community center, Mary brought her seven-year-old son Peter. When Lydia, a volunteer judge, gave the blue ribbon to another child's model of Noah's ark instead of Peter's painted shepherd-sling display, Peter shouted, ran across the aisle, and slammed his shoulder into Lydia. Lydia fell against a table and fractured her elbow.
call: In Lydia's battery action against Peter, which argument most strongly supports liability?
distilled_core_question: A child deliberately makes body contact with an adult, causing a fall and injury. In the adult's battery action against the child, which fact most strongly supports liability?
review_truth: For battery, aim intent at the contact, not the injury, risk, or motive.

choices.text: Peter was old enough to appreciate the riskiness of charging across the aisle.
choices.c3_signal: This answer talks like negligence: risk appreciation. The call says battery.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because risk appreciation sounds like the responsible mental-state inquiry for a child. The breaker is that the battery call asks for contact intent, not negligence-style risk awareness.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This imports a risk-appreciation frame. The battery call is answered by contact intent.
choices.future_cue: Ask which choice targets contact rather than risk.

choices.text: Peter was old enough to appreciate that knocking Lydia into a table could inflict serious injury.
choices.c3_signal: This answer aims at injury appreciation. The stem's best battery fact is deliberate contact.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because serious injury sounds more legally important than mere contact. The breaker is that battery liability does not require injury appreciation when intentional harmful or offensive contact is shown.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This targets injury appreciation. The credited answer targets intentional contact.
choices.future_cue: Apply the Gold Key: battery does not require intent to injure.

choices.text: Peter's anger over the ribbon decision was not justified.
choices.c3_signal: This answer explains why Peter was angry. It does not give the contact element.
choices.why_attractive: A student picks this because unjustified anger feels like a moral reason to impose liability. The breaker is that motive does not supply the battery element; deliberate contact does.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This targets motive and moral justification. The call needs the battery-contact element.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer supplies the battery element or only explains why Peter acted.

choices.text: Peter intended to slam his shoulder into Lydia.
choices.student_label: True and responsive after Gold Key.
choices.c3_signal: This answer repeats the deliberate-contact fact that matches the battery call.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: D is the only choice that supplies the contact-level intent required by the battery call.

remediation_card.title: Battery mental-state target
remediation_card.signal: Battery answer set offers contact, injury, risk, and motive.
remediation_card.student_move: Lock the call, then pick the answer that targets contact.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Contact intent beats injury/risk/motive.
remediation_card.trap: Choosing the more serious-sounding injury or risk answer.

gold_keys.statement: Battery intent points at harmful/offensive contact or apprehension of that contact. It does not require intent to injure, appreciation of risk, or bad motive; a child can be liable if the child formed that contact-level intent.
gold_keys.trigger: Battery call plus choices that talk about injury, risk, age, or anger.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 13, 18; Garratt v. Dailey.

silver_keys.statement: When the answer array gives four mental states, choose the one aimed at the tort named in the call. For battery, the contact-target answer beats injury, risk, and motive answers.
silver_keys.trigger: Battery call with choices about contact, injury, risk, and anger.

drill_seeds.prompt: Battery call: one choice says contact intent, one says injury intent, one says risk appreciation, one says bad motive. Which target belongs to battery?
drill_seeds.answer: Contact intent.

drill_seeds.answer: No. It requires intent to cause harmful/offensive contact or apprehension.

drill_seeds.prompt: A child is old enough to appreciate risk. Is that the strongest battery argument?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Risk appreciation is a negligence-style frame; battery turns on contact intent.

drill_seeds.prompt: The defendant was unjustifiably angry before making contact. Is that the battery element?
drill_seeds.answer: No. It may explain motive, but the element is intentional contact.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: special erroneous-death-notice category vs ordinary NIED physical-danger default
stem: Galilee Trails, a private company that runs paid Christian wilderness retreats, required each participant to list an emergency contact. During a dawn prayer hike, Lydia became separated from her group. Peter, the company’s trip coordinator, mixed up two radio reports and sent Lydia’s husband, Timothy, an emergency text saying that Lydia had been found dead near the overlook. Lydia was actually alive and waiting in a ranger cabin with Ruth, a first-aid volunteer. Timothy suffered severe emotional distress from the death notice. The jurisdiction recognizes negligent erroneous death notice as a special NIED category.
call: If Timothy sues Galilee Trails, how should a court likely rule on the emotional-distress claim?
distilled_core_question: A spouse receives a negligent false death notice, suffers severe emotional distress, and the jurisdiction recognizes erroneous death notice as a special NIED category. Is the claim viable?
review_truth: A recognized negligent erroneous-death-notice category can support NIED without ordinary physical-danger limits.

choices.text: Yes, because any careless emergency message that causes grief creates emotional-distress liability.
choices.c3_signal: The word any turns a special category into a universal rule.
choices.why_attractive: A picks up the real idea that the message caused grief and then broadens it into a universal rule. The breaker is the word any: the stem gives a special category, not general liability for every careless message.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word any converts a special category into a universal misinformation-liability rule.
choices.future_cue: Circle absolute words and ask whether the stem supplies a narrower rule.

choices.text: No, because Lydia was alive, so Timothy cannot have legally cognizable distress from the message.
choices.student_label: CUT: uses the error as the denial
choices.c3_signal: The fact that Lydia was alive makes the death notice erroneous; it does not erase Timothy’s distress.
choices.why_attractive: B feels concrete because Lydia was alive, so the report was factually false. The breaker is that the false death notice is the very event the special category is built to address.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The fact that Lydia was alive makes the notice erroneous; it does not defeat the distress claim.
choices.future_cue: Ask what fact made the notice wrongful and what fact caused Timothy’s distress.

choices.text: Yes, under the jurisdiction’s special category for negligent erroneous death notice.
choices.c3_signal: This choice matches the call and the stem’s special-category trigger.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. The stem gives the key gate: this jurisdiction recognizes negligent erroneous death notice as a special NIED category. Timothy received a negligent false death notice about Lydia, and the stem states that he suffered severe emotional distress from that notice.

Gold Key: Erroneous death notice is a special NIED category when the jurisdiction recognizes it; do not import the ordinary physical-danger or bystander screens.

Silver Key: When the stem says “special category,” cut answers that answer the ordinary default rule instead of the special-category rule.

choices.text: No, because Timothy was never in physical danger from the retreat company’s mistake.
choices.c3_signal: The choice answers ordinary physical-danger NIED, not the special death-notice category.
choices.why_attractive: D imports the ordinary zone-of-danger screen and treats physical danger as the gate. The breaker is the Gold Key: a recognized erroneous-death-notice category does not depend on Timothy being physically endangered.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice imports ordinary physical-danger NIED into a stem-given special category.
choices.future_cue: When the stem says special category, test whether the choice is answering the default rule instead.

remediation_card.title: Special category beats ordinary NIED gate
remediation_card.signal: Stem gives a recognized emotional-distress category.
remediation_card.student_move: Do not import zone-of-danger or bystander requirements unless the call asks for the ordinary rule.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Recognized erroneous death notice is its own NIED lane.
remediation_card.trap: Physical danger sounds like the default NIED screen.

gold_keys.statement: When a jurisdiction recognizes negligent erroneous death notice, the claim does not fail merely because the plaintiff was outside physical danger or because the reported death was false.
gold_keys.trigger: False death notice to close family + severe distress + jurisdiction recognizes the category.
gold_keys.authority: Johnson v. State of New York, 37 N.Y.2d 378 (1975); Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 47(b).

silver_keys.statement: When the stem says the jurisdiction recognizes a special category, cut choices that answer the ordinary default lane instead of the special lane.
silver_keys.trigger: Stem phrase: jurisdiction recognizes negligent erroneous death notice as a special NIED category.

drill_seeds.answer: Special-category lane check.
