subject: TORTS
tension_axis: all-or-nothing remedies versus tailored abatement
splitting_fact: moderate-cost relocation and scrubber would end nearly all interference
stem:
Barnabas ran a private Christmas-nativity petting-zoo business on land next to Ruth’s small prayer-retreat cottages. To dry animal bedding overnight, Barnabas installed a compost-air blower behind the donkey shed. The blower pushed a sour odor and low rumble across Ruth’s cottages, and several guests lost sleep. Ruth sued for private nuisance and requested a permanent injunction closing the petting-zoo business entirely. Before the hearing, Barnabas proved that, for a moderate cost, he could move the blower into a sealed feed room and add a scrubber, which would end nearly all odor and vibration without closing the business. Ruth refused to discuss that change and demanded closure because the guests had been miserable for months.

What is the most likely remedy in Ruth’s private nuisance claim against Barnabas?
call:
Call lock: remedy, not liability.
Prediction: tailored abatement plus limited compensatory damages.
Adjacent-call trap: nuisance exists does not automatically mean shutdown.
distilled_core_question: A private nuisance can be mostly fixed by reasonable abatement at moderate cost. The plaintiff wants total closure and refused to discuss the fix. What remedy is most likely?
review_truth: A nuisance remedy is usually tailored to reasonable abatement; mitigation can limit damages, but it does not erase the nuisance or require total shutdown.

choices.text: No remedy, because Ruth refused to mitigate by accepting Barnabas’s proposed relocation.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees Ruth refuse the proposed fix and treats that as forfeiture of the whole claim. The breaker is that avoidable consequences limit damages, not all nuisance relief.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice pushes mitigation beyond its range by making Ruth's refusal erase all remedy.
choices.future_cue: Say: mitigation trims avoidable damages; it does not erase nuisance relief.

choices.text: Only punitive damages, because Barnabas kept operating after complaints.
choices.why_attractive: The student wants to punish Barnabas because he kept operating after complaints. The breaker is that the call asks for the likely nuisance remedy, and the stem points to abatement rather than punishment.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice answers a punishment frame instead of the remedy-fit call.
choices.future_cue: Return to the abatement fact.

choices.text: A permanent shutdown injunction, because any substantial nuisance requires the defendant to stop the activity.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees a substantial nuisance and jumps to shutting it down. The breaker is the word 'any,' which ignores the moderate-cost fix and makes equitable relief automatic.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The word 'any' turns nuisance into automatic shutdown and ignores the moderate-cost fix.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the stem gives a narrower fix.

choices.text: A tailored injunction requiring reasonable abatement, with damages limited to nonavoidable loss-of-use harms.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
D is correct. The facts point to a nuisance remedy that fixes the interference without overcorrecting. The blower’s odor and rumble substantially interfere with the cottages, so “no remedy” is too severe. But Barnabas has shown a moderate-cost fix that will end nearly all of the problem without shutting down the business, so total closure is too severe too.

Gold Key: In nuisance remedies, avoidable-consequences principles limit damages; they do not erase the nuisance or force an all-or-nothing remedy. Equity can tailor abatement to the reasonable fix.

Silver Key: When the answer array offers shutdown, no remedy, punitive-only, and tailored abatement, read the array as an oversteer screen. The credited answer is the one that tracks the stem’s moderate-cost abatement fact.

remediation_card.title: Nuisance Remedy Oversteer
remediation_card.signal: The answer says total shutdown, no remedy, or punitive-only.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask which remedy fits the abatement fact.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Tailor the fix; limit avoidable damages.
remediation_card.trap: All-or-nothing remedy language.

gold_keys.statement: In nuisance remedies, a court can tailor abatement to a reasonable fix. Avoidable-consequences principles can limit damages, but they do not erase the nuisance or require total closure.
gold_keys.trigger: The stem gives both a substantial interference and a moderate-cost abatement option.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 822, 826; Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co., 26 N.Y.2d 219 (1970).

silver_keys.statement: When the choices are shutdown, no remedy, punitive-only, and tailored abatement, treat the first three as remedy oversteers. Match the remedy to the stem’s reasonable-fix fact.
silver_keys.trigger: The stem says a moderate-cost change would end nearly all interference.

drill_seeds.prompt: A nuisance exists, so any substantial nuisance requires the defendant to stop the activity. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut: automatic-shutdown overclaim.

drill_seeds.prompt: No remedy because plaintiff refused mitigation vs tailored abatement with limited damages. Name the axis.
drill_seeds.answer: Whether mitigation erases the remedy or only limits avoidable damages.

drill_seeds.prompt: What does mitigation do in a nuisance-remedy question?
drill_seeds.answer: It can limit damages; it does not erase nuisance relief.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choices are shutdown, no remedy, punitive-only, tailored abatement. What should you look for?
drill_seeds.answer: The fact that supports a reasonable tailored fix.

subject: CONTRACTS
subtopic: Specific performance for unique or highly unusual goods
tension_axis: Which fact triggers specific performance?
stem: At a Bible-camp art fair, Lydia arrived on March 5 with $3,700 to collect a hand-carved olive-wood lyre shaped like Jonah’s whale. Two days earlier, Paul, who operated a booth selling Christian folk art, had agreed to sell that lyre to Lydia for that price. Paul refused to hand it over.
call: If Lydia sues Paul, is Lydia entitled to specific performance of the sale?
distilled_core_question: A buyer agreed to buy a highly unusual chattel, and the seller refused to deliver it. Can the buyer get specific performance?
review_truth: Specific performance for goods turns on uniqueness or high unusualness, not merchant status, ordinary personalty labels, or the seller’s hypothetical remedy.

choices.text: Yes, because Paul is a merchant with respect to the sale of Christian folk art.
choices.c3_signal: The choice points to Paul’s seller status, not to the unusual-object fact.
choices.why_attractive: It grabs the real-looking UCC status word merchant and treats it as the remedy trigger. The breaker is that the call is about specific performance, and the stem-trigger is unusual goods, not seller status.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Merchant status is not the buyer-specific-performance trigger.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer uses the highly unusual object.

choices.text: Yes, because the lyre is highly unusual.
choices.c3_signal: This is the only answer that uses the stem’s unusual-object fact.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It is true and responsive: the lyre’s highly unusual character is the remedy trigger.

choices.text: Yes, because Paul could have obtained specific performance if Lydia had breached.
choices.c3_signal: The choice answers a hypothetical question about Paul, not Lydia’s actual remedy.
choices.why_attractive: It makes reciprocity feel fair by asking what Paul could have obtained if Lydia had breached. The breaker is wrong party and wrong remedy; Lydia's entitlement does not depend on Paul’s hypothetical remedy.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Paul’s hypothetical remedy does not answer Lydia’s actual remedy call.
choices.future_cue: Restate the call as Lydia’s buyer remedy.

choices.text: No, because specific performance is not available as a remedy for breach of a contract for the sale of personalty.
choices.c3_signal: The choice says personalty never gets this remedy; the Gold Key supplies the exception.
choices.why_attractive: It starts from the normal damages default for ordinary personal property sales. The breaker is the exception for unique or highly unusual goods, which this object supplies.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The personalty-never statement omits the unique-goods exception.
choices.future_cue: Apply the Gold Key: unique or highly unusual goods can support specific performance.

remediation_card.title: Specific performance for goods: find the uniqueness trigger
remediation_card.signal: Buyer asks for specific performance of a chattel.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the object is unique or highly unusual; ignore merchant status and reciprocity.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Unique/highly unusual goods can support buyer specific performance.
remediation_card.trap: Ordinary personalty damages default overstated into a never rule.

gold_keys.statement: For goods, specific performance is exceptional but available to a buyer when the goods are unique or highly unusual.
gold_keys.trigger: The stem describes an unusual object and asks for specific performance.

silver_keys.statement: In a 3-Yes/1-No remedies array, do not accept the first Yes. Pick the answer tied to the stem’s remedy-trigger fact.
silver_keys.trigger: Multiple Yes answers give different reasons for specific performance.

drill_seeds.answer: Pick the Yes tied to the stem’s remedy-trigger fact.

subject: TORTS
tension_axis: foreseeability target
stem:
Christian variation — final locked version

During setup for a private Christmas Bible-pageant at a rented fairground, Timothy was pushing a handcart stacked with manger scenery when he clipped Lydia and hurried away, leaving her sprawled in a marked loading lane. A few minutes later, Stephen, drowsy after knowingly taking a strong sleep aid, drove a small electric forklift down the lane and ran over Lydia’s leg.

If Lydia brings a negligence action against Stephen for damages resulting from her fractured leg, Stephen’s liability will most probably turn on whether it was foreseeable that
call: Call first: this is not asking who was most morally blameworthy. It asks what fact must be foreseeable for Stephen’s liability. Prediction: the answer should point to the risk Stephen’s driving created—someone in the lane.
distilled_core_question: A vehicle operator injures a person already in the travel path. Which foreseeability target matters: a person in the path, the prior event that put the person there, the exact second accident, or the operator's own negligence?
review_truth: Foreseeability targets the plaintiff/risk created by the defendant's conduct, not the exact set-stage event and not the defendant's own negligence.

choices.text: a person clipped by a prop cart would be involved in another collision within a few minutes.
choices.why_attractive: A feels precise because it tracks the whole chain from the first collision to the second collision. The breaker is that the exact chain is not the target; the person-in-lane risk is.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A targets the exact follow-on accident chain instead of the general person-in-lane risk.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether this choice names a general person/risk or an exact chain.

choices.text: a person would be in the loading lane.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
B is correct. The clean foreseeability target is not the handcart accident, the precise chain of collisions, or Stephen’s own impaired driving. The target is whether a person might foreseeably be in the lane Stephen chose to drive through.

Gold Key: For negligence by an active operator, ask what person or class of persons was foreseeably put at risk by the defendant’s conduct. Do not require foreseeability of the exact prior event that placed the plaintiff there, and do not require foreseeability of the defendant’s own negligent breach.

Silver Key: In a “foreseeable that ___” answer array, compare the noun phrase after “that.” The credited answer usually names the general plaintiff/risk target, while the traps name the old set-stage event, the exact chain, or the defendant’s own wrongdoing.

choices.text: Stephen would operate the forklift while drowsy after taking a strong sleep aid.
choices.why_attractive: C feels compelling because Stephen's drowsy operation is the obvious bad act. The breaker is that the plaintiff need not show Stephen's negligence itself was foreseeable.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: C targets foreseeability of the defendant's own breach instead of the plaintiff/risk.
choices.future_cue: Mark drowsy operation as breach color and return to who or what was foreseeably endangered.

choices.text: Timothy would handle the prop cart carelessly and leave Lydia lying in the loading lane after clipping her.
choices.why_attractive: D feels natural because Timothy's cart accident explains why Lydia was on the ground. The breaker is that Timothy's prior conduct is set-stage, not Stephen's foreseeability target.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: D targets the prior set-stage actor's conduct instead of the risk created by Stephen's operation.
choices.future_cue: Treat facts that existed before Stephen acted as set-stage unless the call asks about the prior actor.

remediation_card.title: Foreseeability target scan
remediation_card.signal: All answers ask what had to be foreseeable.
remediation_card.student_move: Name the object after 'foreseeable that' before judging law.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Pick the plaintiff/risk target, not the old cause, exact chain, or defendant breach.
remediation_card.trap: Students pick the most dramatic fact instead of the legal target.

gold_keys.statement: For negligence by an active operator, the foreseeability target is the plaintiff/class/risk created by the defendant's conduct, not the exact prior event that put the plaintiff there and not whether the defendant's own careless act was foreseeable.
gold_keys.trigger: answer choices all complete 'foreseeable that ___'
gold_keys.authority: Palsgraf v. Long Island R.R.; Restatement (Third) of Torts §§ 7, 29

silver_keys.statement: When every choice starts from 'foreseeable that,' compare the object of foreseeability first. Set-stage cause, exact chain, defendant breach, and plaintiff risk are different targets.

subject: EVIDENCE
stem:
At Daniel’s federal mail-fraud trial over forged Bible-study supply invoices, the prosecutor offers a rubber stamp marked “PAID” that was found in a clearance bin at Lydia’s Christian Bookshop twenty miles from the post office used in the alleged scheme. No witness connects the stamp to Daniel, any invoice, or the charged mailing. Daniel objects.

How should the court rule?
call:
Call: Court ruling on objection.

Prediction: Exclude. The object has no bridge to the case.

Adjacent-call traps:

* “Could a stamp ever matter in fraud?” Yes, but not this one on these facts.
* “Could the stamp illustrate what stamps look like?” Maybe in another case, but that use is not offered.
* “Could it be prejudicial?” That is later. Start with connection.
distilled_core_question: At a federal trial, the prosecution offers a physical object with no connection to the defendant, the charged event, or any relevant issue. Should it be admitted?
review_truth: A physical object is not relevant just because it belongs to a category that could matter; it needs a connection to a fact that matters in this case.

choices.text: Admit the stamp only as demonstrative evidence of what rubber stamps generally look like.
choices.why_attractive: The choice gives the student a fallback use, so the stamp feels admissible even without a case link. The breaker is that the stem never offered the stamp for that demonstrative purpose.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice invents a demonstrative use not supplied by the stem.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the stem actually offered the object for that purpose.

choices.text: Exclude the stamp only because it is unfairly prejudicial as a matter of law.
choices.why_attractive: The choice reaches exclusion, so it feels close to the credited answer. The breaker is that it makes prejudice the exclusive legal reason and skips the more basic missing-connection problem.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice reaches the correct outcome but overclaims with 'only' and 'as a matter of law' while skipping the connection layer.
choices.future_cue: Cut 'only' / 'as a matter of law' when a more basic live layer is visible.

choices.text: Admit the stamp because all office stamps are relevant in a mail-fraud trial.
choices.why_attractive: The choice lets the crime label do the work: mail fraud sounds like it could involve a stamp. The breaker is the word 'all,' because an object category is not a connection to this case.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice treats all objects in a category as automatically relevant.
choices.future_cue: Treat 'all' category language as an overclaim unless the stem supplies a connection.

choices.text: Exclude the stamp because, without a connection to the charged mailing or another relevant issue, the object lacks probative value.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
D is correct. The stamp is a physical object, but the stem gives no link between the stamp and Daniel, any invoice, or the charged mailing. That means the object has no fact-path into the case. It is not enough that mail-fraud schemes can involve office supplies. The object must help prove something that matters.

Silver Key: Start with connection and purpose before object-category or prejudice. If the stem gives no bridge between the thing and the charged event, the “this kind of object fits this kind of crime” answer is bait.

remediation_card.title: Real object needs a bridge
remediation_card.signal: Physical object offered, but no fact connects it to the charged event or issue.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask: what fact does this object make more likely?
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Object category is not a bridge.
remediation_card.trap: The crime label makes the object feel relevant.

silver_keys.statement: In Evidence, start with the bridge: what fact does this item help prove in this case? If the stem gives no bridge, do not jump to object category, demonstrative use, or prejudice.
silver_keys.trigger: A physical object is offered, but the stem says no witness connects it to the defendant, document, event, or issue.

drill_seeds.prompt: A physical object is offered because all objects of that kind are relevant in this type of case. What is the C3 cut?
drill_seeds.answer: Tiered-absolute overclaim; category alone is not a case connection.

drill_seeds.prompt: The proponent offers an object as real evidence. A choice admits it as a demonstrative aid, but the stem gives no such purpose. What is the cut?
drill_seeds.answer: NOT_RESPONSIVE; bait_doctrine / offered_for_purpose.

drill_seeds.prompt: An object has no link to the charged event. One choice excludes under prejudice only; another excludes for no probative value. Which layer comes first?
drill_seeds.answer: Connection/relevance comes before prejudice.

subject: CONTRACTS
tension_axis: timely oral objection versus required written objection
stem: Martha and Timothy are both merchants who wholesale supplies for Christian camp stores. At a trade fair, Timothy orally agrees to buy 180 brass lanterns with Psalm-themed labels from Martha for $18,000. Later that week, Martha mails Timothy a signed written confirmation of the deal. On the eighth day after receiving it, Timothy leaves Martha a voicemail: “I object to your confirmation.” Timothy sends no written objection and later refuses the lanterns. Which statement best states the result?
call:
The call asks which statement best states the effect of Timothy’s voicemail.

Prediction after Gold Key: voicemail is not enough. The objection must be written.
distilled_core_question: Two merchants make an oral goods deal; the sender sends a signed confirmation; the recipient objects orally within 10 days but sends no writing. Does the confirmation still work against the recipient?
review_truth: Between merchants, a confirming writing is not defeated by an oral objection; the objection must be written within 10 days.

choices.text: The confirmation fails because Timothy did not sign it.
choices.why_attractive: The choice activates the normal Statute of Frauds signature instinct. The breaker is that the merchant-confirmation rule can operate against the recipient without the recipient’s signature.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice imports the ordinary signature instinct into a merchant-confirmation problem. The Gold Key shows recipient signature is not required if no written objection is sent in time.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the sender’s signed confirmation can substitute for recipient signature between merchants.

choices.text: The confirmation fails unless Martha proves Timothy actually read every word of it before leaving the voicemail.
choices.why_attractive: The choice sounds careful because actual reading feels like stronger notice. The breaker is that the rule uses reason to know contents, not proof of reading every word.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice invents an actual word-by-word reading requirement. The rule asks reason to know contents, not proof of reading every word.
choices.future_cue: Cut word-by-word reading requirements unless the Gold Key says they exist.

choices.text: Timothy’s voicemail does not prevent the merchant-confirmation rule from applying, because the objection must be written.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. Gold Key: in a UCC merchant-confirmation problem, the receiving merchant must give a written notice of objection within 10 days after receiving the confirmation. A voicemail objection is not the required objection.

Silver Key: do not let the “within 10 days” fact swallow the “written notice” requirement. Timing and form are separate boxes.

Here, Timothy received a signed written confirmation from Martha and objected only by voicemail. Because Timothy sent no written objection, his oral objection does not stop the merchant-confirmation rule from applying.

choices.text: Timothy’s voicemail prevents the confirmation from satisfying the Statute of Frauds because any objection within 10 days is enough.
choices.why_attractive: The choice grabs the most visible fact: Timothy objected within 10 days. The breaker is that the objection must be written, so timing alone is not enough.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice turns a timely oral objection into any sufficient objection. The Silver Key separates timing from required form, and the Gold Key supplies the written-objection rule.
choices.future_cue: Use the Silver Key: timing and form are separate boxes.

remediation_card.title: Merchant confirmation: oral objection trap
remediation_card.signal: Two merchants, oral goods deal, signed confirmation, oral objection.
remediation_card.student_move: Check whether the recipient sent written notice of objection within 10 days.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Written objection required; oral objection is not enough.
remediation_card.trap: Treating any timely objection as enough.

gold_keys.statement: Between merchants, a signed written confirmation sufficient against the sender can satisfy the UCC Statute of Frauds against the recipient if the recipient has reason to know its contents and does not give written notice of objection within 10 days. Oral objection is not enough.
gold_keys.trigger: two merchants + oral goods deal + signed written confirmation + oral/no written objection

silver_keys.statement: When a choice says the objection was within 10 days, ask a second question: was it in the required form? Timing does not cure the wrong method of objection.
silver_keys.trigger: oral objection inside a time window

drill_seeds.prompt: Two merchants make an oral goods deal. Seller sends a signed confirmation. Buyer calls within 10 days to object but sends no writing. Does the call defeat the confirmation?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Written objection is required.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says: 'Any objection within 10 days defeats the confirmation.' Name the trap.
drill_seeds.answer: Timing-swallows-form trap; objection must be written.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says the sender must prove the recipient read every word of a merchant confirmation. Mold?
drill_seeds.answer: fabricated_rule.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says the confirmation fails because the recipient merchant did not sign it. Why cut?
drill_seeds.answer: The merchant-confirmation rule can work without recipient signature if no timely written objection is sent.

subject: CONTRACTS
tension_axis: new legal detriment vs preexisting duty
splitting_fact: Lydia had already agreed that Timothy could use the press whenever he wished.
stem:
Hannah owned a vintage hand-cranked letterpress called the “Jericho Press,” which Timothy liked to use to print private Bible-verse cards. Hannah transferred title to the press to Lydia, but only after Lydia agreed that Timothy could use the press whenever he wished. Lydia agreed but did not tell Timothy about that promise.

Mary lived in a coastal town and had long wanted Timothy to move there for the town’s private Scripture-calligraphy fairs. Mary wrote Timothy a letter saying that, if he moved to the town, she would leave him her estate when she died.

Timothy knew that Lydia now owned the Jericho Press. He told Lydia that, if she would let him use the press until Mary died, he would give Lydia half of whatever he received from Mary. Lydia agreed, and Timothy moved to the town and used the press.

Mary died shortly afterward. Her will left her entire estate to Timothy, but Timothy refused to share any of it with Lydia.
call: If Lydia asserts a claim against Timothy for a share of the estate that Timothy received from Mary, a court should find for:
distilled_core_question: A claimant promises to allow a use she already owed, in exchange for half of a later estate. Is the estate-sharing promise enforceable?
review_truth: A promise to do what you already legally must do is not consideration for a new promise.

choices.text: Lydia, because Timothy promised to share the estate with her if she promised to let him use the press until Mary’s death.
choices.student_label: surface bargain, missing new legal detriment
choices.c3_signal: This answers with the visible promise exchange but skips the element the call turns on: whether Lydia gave anything new.
choices.why_attractive: It sees the visible promise-for-promise exchange and stops there. The breaker is the Gold Key: Lydia gave only permission she already owed, so the exchange adds no legal detriment.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice identifies a visible promise exchange but skips whether Lydia gave new legal detriment.
choices.future_cue: Apply the Gold Key: already owed is not new consideration.

choices.text: Timothy, because his promise to Lydia was not supported by consideration.
choices.c3_signal: This directly answers the call and names the missing consideration problem.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A, C, and D each break one filter; B is the only true-and-responsive answer.

choices.text: Lydia, because Timothy is estopped from denying the existence of an enforceable contract between him and Lydia.
choices.c3_signal: This reaches for an exception path but the stem gives no new reliance by Lydia.
choices.why_attractive: It reaches for promissory estoppel as a fairness rescue. The breaker is the missing reliance move: Lydia did not change legal position because of Timothy’s promise.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice reaches for promissory estoppel but lacks a Lydia reliance fact.
choices.future_cue: Require an induced action or forbearance before using promissory estoppel.

choices.text: Timothy, because Lydia’s promise to Hannah created an implied condition precedent to Timothy’s obligation to share the estate with Lydia.
choices.c3_signal: This imports Hannah's earlier hidden condition into Timothy's later promise.
choices.why_attractive: It uses the hidden first-transfer condition to support the same winning party. The breaker is frame control: Timothy's later promise was not made subject to a condition he never knew.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice imports a hidden earlier condition into Timothy's later promise.
choices.future_cue: Cut answers that import someone else's hidden deal into the current call.

remediation_card.title: Existing duty is not new consideration
remediation_card.signal: A party promises to do the same thing already owed.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask what new legal detriment appears in the later exchange.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Already owed is not newly paid for.
remediation_card.trap: Promise-for-promise wording looks like consideration.

gold_keys.statement: A promise to do what the promisee is already legally obligated to do is not consideration for a new promise, unless the new performance is materially different or the old duty is honestly disputed.
gold_keys.trigger: A later promise is exchanged for permission or performance already owed under an earlier deal.
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 71, 73.

silver_keys.statement: When one answer says 'promise-for-promise' and the other says 'no consideration,' ask what new legal position the plaintiff gave up in the later deal.
silver_keys.trigger: A surface bargain repeats an earlier duty.

drill_seeds.prompt: A promises B to do the exact act A already owes B under an earlier contract. Is A's promise consideration for B's new promise?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Existing duty is not new consideration.

drill_seeds.target_skill: new legal detriment vs preexisting duty
drill_seeds.prompt: Choice 1 says promise-for-promise. Choice 2 says no consideration. What fact decides?
drill_seeds.answer: Whether the promisee gave up a new legal right or only repeated an existing duty.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice says estoppel applies, but the plaintiff did not change position because of the promise. Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut. Estoppel needs reliance.

drill_seeds.prompt: A choice uses a hidden earlier promise to make a condition in a later promise by another person. What is the C3 label?
drill_seeds.answer: Wrong-frame bait doctrine.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
tension_axis: defendant-created contacts vs plaintiff-side fairness/effects
stem:
Lydia, a Maine resident, paid to attend Barnabas’s private “Illuminated Psalms” calligraphy workshop in New Mexico. During the workshop, Barnabas handed students a solvent that he had prepared for the class. All instruction, materials use, and alleged negligent conduct occurred in New Mexico. After Lydia returned to Maine, her hands became inflamed and she missed several weeks of work on paid Advent-card commissions.

Lydia sued Barnabas in Maine. She argues that Maine is the fairest forum because she is recovering there, her family can help her there, and traveling back to New Mexico would be difficult. Barnabas has never taught workshops, advertised, shipped supplies, or taken commissions in Maine.
call: Can fairness considerations alone create specific jurisdiction in Maine?
distilled_core_question: A plaintiff travels to another state for a paid service, all defendant conduct occurs there, the harm is later felt at home, and the defendant has no home-state contacts. Can plaintiff hardship and forum fairness alone create specific jurisdiction?
review_truth: Fairness can make jurisdiction unreasonable after contacts exist, but it cannot create minimum contacts by itself.

choices.text: Yes, because Lydia's injury was felt in Maine.
choices.student_label: Plaintiff-side injury fact, not defendant-side contact.
choices.c3_signal: The answer points to where Lydia felt harm. The call needs Barnabas's Maine contacts.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees a real Maine fact: Lydia's injury was felt there. The breaker is that personal jurisdiction turns on Barnabas's forum contacts, not Lydia's forum effects.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer uses the location of Lydia's injury, but the call needs Barnabas's forum contacts.
choices.future_cue: Mark injury location as plaintiff-side and return to defendant contacts.

choices.text: No, because private workshop injury claims are excluded from federal courts.
choices.c3_signal: The answer talks about federal-court claim category. The call asks Maine personal jurisdiction.
choices.why_attractive: The student hears formal federal-court language and treats it as a threshold answer. The breaker is that the call asks specific jurisdiction in Maine, not a categorical federal-court exclusion.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer switches from personal jurisdiction to a federal-court category gate.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer addresses personal jurisdiction in Maine.

choices.text: Yes, because Lydia's hardship is enough to create minimum contacts.
choices.c3_signal: The answer puts the second-layer fairness idea in the first-layer contacts slot.
choices.why_attractive: The student sympathizes with Lydia and wants the fair forum to win. The breaker is that fairness is second-layer and cannot create the first-layer minimum contacts.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer treats hardship and fairness as if they create minimum contacts.
choices.future_cue: Say: contacts first, fairness second.

choices.text: No, because fairness cannot create minimum contacts absent purposeful Maine-directed conduct by Barnabas.
choices.c3_signal: It answers the call directly and tracks the missing forum-directed conduct.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: D is the only answer that both answers the fairness-alone call and preserves the contacts-before-fairness threshold.

remediation_card.title: Contacts First, Fairness Second
remediation_card.signal: Plaintiff argues home forum is fairest, but defendant did all conduct elsewhere.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask for defendant-created forum contacts before weighing fairness.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Fairness can defeat jurisdiction; it cannot create minimum contacts.
remediation_card.trap: Letting sympathy for plaintiff hardship substitute for purposeful availment.

gold_keys.statement: Specific jurisdiction starts with defendant-created forum contacts. Fairness or convenience can defeat jurisdiction after contacts exist, but it cannot create contacts by itself.
gold_keys.trigger: The plaintiff felt harm at home or argues the home forum is fair, while the defendant's conduct all occurred elsewhere.
gold_keys.authority: International Shoe; World-Wide Volkswagen; Walden; Ford.

silver_keys.statement: In a specific-jurisdiction array, sort contacts first and fairness second. A plaintiff-side hardship fact cannot do the work of a defendant-side contact fact.
silver_keys.trigger: Choices mention hardship, injury felt in the forum, and no forum-directed defendant conduct.

drill_seeds.prompt: A defendant did all conduct in State X; plaintiff feels injury in State Y. Is injury felt in State Y the defendant contact?
drill_seeds.answer: No. It is a plaintiff-side effects fact.

drill_seeds.prompt: The call asks personal jurisdiction; an answer discusses federal-court exclusion. What is the cut?
drill_seeds.answer: Misfit: wrong procedural gate.

drill_seeds.prompt: A personal-jurisdiction answer relies on fairness before defendant contacts. What is the ordered move?
drill_seeds.answer: Contacts first, fairness second.

drill_seeds.prompt: Plaintiff is ill and travel is hard. Defendant has no forum contacts. Can hardship create contacts?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Fairness cannot create minimum contacts.

subject: CIVIL_PROCEDURE
tension_axis: court power over defendant vs plaintiff/property/collection lures
splitting_fact: The State B property is unrelated to the State A injury claim, and Daniel has no other State B contacts.
stem: At a privately rented Bible-story obstacle-course party in State A, Lydia and Daniel, both State A citizens, are helping set up a giant foam whale prop. Daniel negligently bumps the prop, which falls and injures Lydia. Daniel owns a hand-carved olive-wood Nativity set stored in a private storage locker in State B, but Daniel has no other contacts with State B. Lydia sues Daniel in a State B court for the prop injury and attaches the Nativity set, arguing that the property gives State B power to decide the whole injury claim.
call: What is the best analysis?
distilled_core_question: Defendant has unrelated property in State B and no other State B contacts. Plaintiff sues there on a State A injury claim and attaches the property. Does State B have personal jurisdiction over the whole claim?
review_truth: Unrelated forum property is not a magic key to personal jurisdiction over an unrelated claim.

choices.text: State B may decide the claim because Lydia was injured, and plaintiffs choose the forum.
choices.c3_signal: The answer talks about Lydia's injury and forum choice, but the call asks whether State B has power over Daniel.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees Lydia as the injured party and treats plaintiff choice as enough to pick a court. The breaker is that personal jurisdiction asks about State B's power over Daniel, not Lydia's preference.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer focuses on plaintiff injury and forum choice rather than State B power over Daniel.
choices.future_cue: Ask which party's connection to State B matters.

choices.text: State B likely lacks personal jurisdiction over the unrelated prop-injury claim despite the attached Nativity set.
choices.c3_signal: It answers the exact court-power question and uses the property/claim mismatch.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: B is the best analysis. Gold Key: Attaching a defendant’s forum property does not itself let the forum decide an unrelated personal claim; after *Shaffer*, the property must supply a jurisdictional connection among the defendant, the forum, and the litigation, or other minimum contacts must exist. Silver Key: Lock the call as court power, not collection. The attached asset is only a lure unless it connects to the claim.

choices.text: State B has jurisdiction only if the Nativity set is valuable enough to satisfy the whole judgment.
choices.c3_signal: Value of the attached item answers collection, not court power.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats a valuable attached item as practically sufficient because it could pay the judgment. The breaker is that value answers collection after a valid judgment, not the court's power to enter one.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer focuses on the value of the attached asset, which answers collection rather than jurisdiction.
choices.future_cue: Decide jurisdiction before thinking about judgment satisfaction.

choices.text: State B may decide the entire injury claim because any property in the forum creates personal jurisdiction.
choices.c3_signal: The word any turns property presence into an unlimited court-power rule.
choices.why_attractive: The student remembers that property in the forum can matter and upgrades that memory into an any-property shortcut. The breaker is the Gold Key: unrelated property alone does not create jurisdiction over the whole unrelated claim.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer uses an overbroad any-property rule that the Gold Key defeats.
choices.future_cue: Check whether the property connects the defendant, forum, and litigation.

remediation_card.title: Unrelated property is not forum power.
remediation_card.signal: Plaintiff attaches defendant's forum property for a claim arising elsewhere.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the property connects the defendant, forum, and litigation.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Unrelated property alone does not create jurisdiction over the personal claim.
remediation_card.trap: Any-property / asset-value shortcut.

gold_keys.statement: Forum property is not a magic key. If the claim is unrelated to the attached property, the forum still needs a defendant-forum-litigation connection.
gold_keys.trigger: A plaintiff attaches a defendant's forum property to sue on an unrelated personal claim.
gold_keys.authority: Shaffer v. Heitner, 433 U.S. 186; International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310.

silver_keys.statement: Separate court power from collection. An asset's value may matter after a valid judgment, but it does not answer whether this court can decide the claim.
silver_keys.trigger: An answer asks whether the attached property can satisfy the whole judgment.

drill_seeds.prompt: A plaintiff sues in State B because she was injured and prefers that forum. What is the C3 break?
drill_seeds.answer: NOT_RESPONSIVE: plaintiff preference is not defendant-forum power.

drill_seeds.prompt: An answer says the attached property is valuable enough to satisfy the judgment. What is the trap?
drill_seeds.answer: It answers collection, not jurisdiction.

drill_seeds.prompt: A defendant's unrelated property is attached in the forum for a claim arising elsewhere. Does the property alone support jurisdiction?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Unrelated property alone is not enough.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says any property in the forum creates personal jurisdiction. What word should ring?
drill_seeds.answer: Any.

subject: TORTS
stem:
Lydia operates a private, for-profit Bible-themed candle-dipping studio called Lampstand Studio. A statute requires businesses that invite the public into hands-on workshops to keep their customer walkway reasonably safe. Before opening for a paid “Psalms and Candles” class, Lydia hires Barnabas, an outside floor-care contractor, to cover and clean a slick olive-oil spill on the only ramp customers use to enter the studio. Barnabas negligently leaves the slick oil on the ramp, and Peter slips and falls while entering.

Call: What is Peter’s best argument against Lampstand Studio?
call:
Call lock: best argument against the business.
Prediction: the best argument is not employee status. It is that the statutory walkway-safety duty could not be escaped by hiring Barnabas.
distilled_core_question: A public-facing business has a statutory duty to keep its customer walkway reasonably safe, hires an outside contractor to make the walkway safe, the contractor negligently leaves a hazard, and a customer falls. What is the customer's best argument against the business?
review_truth: A hirer may remain liable for an independent contractor's negligence when the breached duty is nondelegable.

choices.text: Lampstand Studio is liable only if Lydia or one of her employees personally poured the oil on the ramp.
choices.why_attractive: Students try to make the business liable only through its own hands. The Gold Key breaks that frame because a nondelegable safety duty can stay with the business even when the contractor created the hazard.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer invents a personal-creation prerequisite for business liability.
choices.future_cue: When a duty is statutory or public-safety based, ask whether the duty stays with the hirer.

choices.text: Lampstand Studio has no possible liability because it hired an outside company to make the ramp safe.
choices.why_attractive: Students remember that hirers usually are not liable for independent contractors. The word 'possible' overextends that default past the nondelegable-duty exception.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer pushes the independent-contractor default into a complete shield.
choices.future_cue: Treat independent-contractor status as a default, then check for nondelegable duty.

choices.text: Lampstand Studio may be liable because the public-walkway safety duty is nondelegable.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: C is the best answer. It ties the claim to the fact that the business had the walkway-safety duty in the first place. Gold Key: when the law imposes a nondelegable safety duty on a hirer, the hirer may remain responsible even though an independent contractor performed the negligent work. Silver Key: do not turn this array into “contractor equals employee” or “contractor means no liability.” Look for the middle route: the duty stays with the business.

choices.text: Lampstand Studio is liable because every outside company that works at a public business is treated as the business’s employee.
choices.why_attractive: Students see a business premise and convert outside workers into employees. The word 'every' is the overclaim; nondelegable duty is a narrower route than employee status.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer says every outside company is treated as an employee.
choices.future_cue: Cut 'every' and look for the narrower liability route.

remediation_card.title: Independent contractor is not the end of the story
remediation_card.signal: Hirer has a statutory/public safety duty and hires someone else to perform it.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the duty itself can be delegated.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Nondelegable duty can keep liability with the hirer.
remediation_card.trap: Contractor status as total shield.

gold_keys.statement: A statutory or otherwise nondelegable safety duty stays with the hirer even when the negligent work is done by an independent contractor.
gold_keys.trigger: statutory/public safety duty plus outside contractor
gold_keys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 409, 424

silver_keys.statement: When the stem gives a legal safety duty and an outside contractor, do not choose the all-or-nothing contractor answers; look for the duty-stays-with-the-hirer route.
silver_keys.trigger: statutory duty + hired contractor + injured public entrant

drill_seeds.prompt: A business has a statutory duty to keep an entrance safe and hires an independent contractor to clear it. The contractor is negligent. What argument keeps the business in the case?
drill_seeds.answer: The duty may be nondelegable.

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut this answer: 'Every outside contractor working at a business is treated as the business's employee.'
drill_seeds.answer: Cut as tiered_absolute; nondelegable duty is narrower than employee status.

drill_seeds.prompt: Stem signal: statutory safety duty + independent contractor + public entrant injured. What trap should you expect?
drill_seeds.answer: The trap is treating contractor status as a total shield.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
tension_axis: family-integrity route vs ordinary zoning route
stem: In the city of New Capernaum, the One Hearth residential code permits a one-unit rowhouse to be occupied by a parent and that parent’s children, but it does not allow an adult aunt to live in that same rowhouse with her niece and the niece’s children. Naomi, Lydia, Timothy, and Ruth share a privately owned rowhouse they call Manna House. The city orders Naomi to move out under the code. The household challenges the code as a direct interference with their family living arrangement.
call: What is the best constitutional route?
distilled_core_question: A city directly excludes a close relative from living with family in one home. What constitutional route should the family use?
review_truth: Direct government exclusion of close relatives from a shared household routes to substantive due process family integrity, not generic zoning or commerce.

choices.text: Resolve the case only under the Dormant Commerce Clause.
choices.c3_signal: No commerce fact appears. The call is family living arrangement, not interstate commerce.
choices.why_attractive: The choice offers a familiar constitutional clause, which can feel safe on a route question. The breaker is that the stem has no commerce facts.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: No commerce facts appear; the answer routes to a constitutional home outside the stem.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the stem contains commerce facts.

choices.text: Uphold the code automatically because aunts are never family for constitutional purposes.

choices.why_attractive: The choice gives a clean categorical cutoff and avoids hard family-liberty analysis. The breaker is the absolute word 'never,' defeated by the family-integrity Gold Key.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The absolute 'never' overclaims the family category; the Gold Key supplies the close-family household anchor.
choices.future_cue: Mark 'never' and trigger the close-family household Gold Key.

choices.text: Analyze the code as a substantive due process burden on family integrity.
choices.c3_signal: It answers the route call and uses the family-household trigger.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It is the only choice that is both true and responsive to the route call.

choices.text: Treat the code as ordinary residential zoning subject only to rational basis, with no family-liberty concern.
choices.c3_signal: Generic zoning is a real frame, but the Gold Key says this family-household fact changes the route.
choices.why_attractive: The choice borrows the real ordinary-zoning frame and pairs it with rational basis. The breaker is that a direct close-family household exclusion changes the constitutional route.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: Ordinary zoning is a real neighboring frame, but the family-household trigger routes the item to substantive due process.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the ordinance regulates unrelated occupants or directly excludes close relatives.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: misdemeanor label vs cause link
stem: At a Christian homeschool co-op fair in a rented convention hall, Peter ran a paid Bible-verse puzzle booth without the required county amusement permit, a misdemeanor. Ruth bought a ticket, completed the puzzle, collected a bookmark, and left. Later that afternoon, while helping Stephen hang a banner at a bakery for a separate youth-group fundraiser, Ruth stood on a defective stepstool, fell, and died. Peter was charged with involuntary manslaughter based on operating the booth without the permit. Is Peter guilty of misdemeanor manslaughter?
call: Is Peter guilty of misdemeanor manslaughter?
distilled_core_question: A person commits a misdemeanor by running an unpermitted paid booth. The customer later dies in a separate accident. Is that misdemeanor enough for misdemeanor manslaughter?
review_truth: Misdemeanor manslaughter needs a cause link; a misdemeanor that merely came first is not enough.

choices.text: No, because operating the unpermitted puzzle booth did not actually or proximately cause Ruth’s fall from the stepstool.
choices.c3_signal: This choice connects the charged misdemeanor to the death mechanism and says the link is missing.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A is correct. The charged theory is misdemeanor manslaughter based on the unpermitted puzzle booth. The booth did not produce, set up, or increase the risk of Ruth’s later fall from a defective stepstool at a different location. Gold Key: misdemeanor manslaughter still needs actual and proximate causation; a misdemeanor that merely happened earlier is not enough. Silver Key: when one answer links the misdemeanor to the death and another only names the misdemeanor, choose the cause-link answer.

choices.text: Yes, because Peter was committing a misdemeanor when he operated the puzzle booth.
choices.c3_signal: It proves the unlawful act but does not connect that act to Ruth’s death.
choices.why_attractive: The student sees a real misdemeanor and feels the unlawful-act box is checked. The breaker is that the answer never links the misdemeanor to Ruth’s death.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It proves the misdemeanor predicate but skips the cause link to the death.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the misdemeanor produced the death.

choices.text: No, because misdemeanor manslaughter applies only to violent misdemeanors.
choices.c3_signal: It ignores the cause-link fact and substitutes a violent-only rule.
choices.why_attractive: The student reaches for a narrower category because violent-only sounds like a sophisticated limitation. The breaker is that the case turns on causation, not a violent-only threshold.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It substitutes a violent-only threshold for the causation problem.
choices.future_cue: Prefer the answer that uses the actual death mechanism.

choices.text: Yes, because any death after a misdemeanor is involuntary manslaughter.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'any' turns a cause rule into a pure timeline rule.
choices.why_attractive: The student treats sequence as enough because a misdemeanor came before a death. The breaker is the absolute word any, which erases the cause requirement.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It says any death after a misdemeanor is enough, which erases causation.
choices.future_cue: Cut absolute chronology language unless the law is truly categorical.

remediation_card.title: Misdemeanor label is not a death cause
remediation_card.signal: A misdemeanor is followed by a death from a separate event.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the misdemeanor produced the death, not merely whether it came first.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: No cause link, no misdemeanor manslaughter.
remediation_card.trap: Counting chronology as causation.

gold_keys.statement: Misdemeanor manslaughter still needs actual and proximate causation. A misdemeanor that merely happens before a death is not enough.
gold_keys.trigger: unlawful act followed by a separate death mechanism
gold_keys.authority: MPC §2.03; People v. Penny; Logan/Ceasar line reflected in Oklahoma jury-instruction commentary

silver_keys.statement: When the array gives you a misdemeanor-label answer and a cause-link answer, lock the cause link before debating the label.
silver_keys.trigger: one choice says the misdemeanor happened; another choice says the misdemeanor did not cause the death

drill_seeds.prompt: A defendant commits a permit misdemeanor. The victim later dies in an unrelated accident. Is the misdemeanor label enough?
drill_seeds.answer: No; check actual and proximate cause.

drill_seeds.answer: tiered_absolute; NOT_TRUE.

drill_seeds.prompt: State the Gold Key for misdemeanor manslaughter.
drill_seeds.answer: The misdemeanor must actually and proximately cause the death.

drill_seeds.answer: The cause-link answer.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
stem:
Final Christian variation — “Tiny-House Hymn-Sheet Night”

At Lydia’s tiny house, a private psalm-singing rehearsal has turned into a hymn-sheet stapling contest. Police, holding an arrest warrant for Timothy, get a tip that Timothy is helping there. They have no search warrant for Lydia’s home, no consent, and no emergency. They enter the tiny house and arrest Timothy in the prayer nook.

Call: Was the entry lawful?
call:
Call: was the entry into the home lawful?

Prediction: No. The home belongs to Lydia. The warrant names Timothy. No search warrant, consent, or emergency appears.
distilled_core_question: Police have an arrest warrant for a suspect but enter someone else’s home to arrest him without a search warrant, consent, or exigency. Was the entry lawful?
review_truth: An arrest warrant is not a search warrant for someone else’s home.

choices.text: Yes, because the tip gave officers reasonable suspicion that Timothy was inside.
choices.why_attractive: The tip makes the police seem specifically focused rather than fishing. The breaker is that suspicion level is not the authority needed to enter a third party’s home.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The choice uses reasonable suspicion as the authority for entering a third party's home. The Gold Key requires a search warrant for that home or a valid exception.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the answer supplies a warrant or valid exception for the home entered.

choices.text: Yes, because an arrest warrant travels with the suspect into any private home.
choices.why_attractive: The answer treats an arrest warrant as portable authority that follows Timothy wherever he goes. The breaker is the Gold Key: a person warrant does not become a place warrant for Lydia’s home.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The phrase 'any private home' overextends the arrest warrant. The Gold Key separates a person warrant from a place warrant.
choices.future_cue: Mark 'any private home' as the overclaim and apply the Gold Key.

choices.text: No, but only because Timothy was seized in the prayer nook rather than at the front door.
choices.why_attractive: The prayer nook is a vivid concrete fact, so it feels legally operative. The breaker is the Silver Key: entry authority is decided at the door, not by the room where the arrest happens.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The prayer-nook fact concerns where Timothy was found after entry. The call asks whether entry was lawful.
choices.future_cue: Resolve the door before the room.

choices.text: No, because officers needed a search warrant for Lydia’s home or a valid exception.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: D is correct. The entry was into Lydia’s home, not Timothy’s. Gold Key: an arrest warrant authorizes seizure of the named person; it does not itself authorize officers to enter and search a third party’s home for that person. The officers needed a search warrant for Lydia’s home or a valid exception such as consent or exigency. Silver Key: resolve the door before the room. The question asks about crossing Lydia’s threshold, so the prayer-nook detail comes too late to supply entry authority.

remediation_card.title: Person warrant vs place warrant
remediation_card.signal: Arrest warrant for suspect + suspect inside someone else's home.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whose home the police entered.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Third-party home requires a search warrant for that home or a valid exception.
remediation_card.trap: Arrest warrant portability.

gold_keys.statement: An arrest warrant lets police seize the named suspect; it does not by itself authorize entry into someone else’s home. For a third party’s home, look for a search warrant for that home, consent, or exigency.
gold_keys.trigger: arrest warrant + suspect located in a third party's home
gold_keys.authority: Steagald v. United States, 451 U.S. 204 (1981); Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573 (1980)

silver_keys.statement: When the call asks whether entry into a home was lawful, decide the door before the room. A bedroom, prayer nook, or living room fact cannot supply authority to cross the threshold.
silver_keys.trigger: answer turns on where the suspect was found after entry

drill_seeds.answer: No. Third-party home requires a search warrant or valid exception.

subject: CONSTITUTIONAL_LAW
tension_axis: in-state sales condition vs out-of-state price control
stem: Ruth’s Workshop, Inc., a private company founded by Ruth, makes ScriptureQuest, a Bible-trivia board game sold through ordinary retail stores around the country. A state allows board-game makers to sell games in the state only if each month they certify that the price charged for the same game in every other state during that month is not lower than the in-state price. The state insists that it is regulating only sales inside its borders.
call: What is the company's strongest dormant Commerce Clause objection?
distilled_core_question: A state says: sell here only if your out-of-state prices this month are not lower than your in-state price. What is the strongest DCC objection?
review_truth: A state cannot condition in-state sales on the seller’s promise not to charge lower prices in other states.

choices.text: The law is valid because price rules never affect commerce.
choices.c3_signal: The word 'never' overclaims; the stem is about prices, which are commercial.
choices.why_attractive: The choice flatters the belief that price regulation is local housekeeping. The breaker is the word never: prices are the substance of commerce.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer says price rules never affect commerce, which overclaims from the answer text itself.
choices.future_cue: Mark 'never' and ask whether the stem itself is about commerce.

choices.text: Article IV privileges and immunities is the only relevant doctrine.
choices.c3_signal: The call says dormant Commerce Clause; this answer exits into a different doctrine.
choices.why_attractive: The choice reaches for a familiar state-discrimination clause and tries to end the search there. The breaker is the call itself: the item asks for a dormant Commerce Clause objection, and this price gate is commercial regulation.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The call asks for a dormant Commerce Clause objection; Article IV privileges and immunities is a different doctrine home.
choices.future_cue: Return to the call: it asks for a dormant Commerce Clause objection.

choices.text: The law directly controls prices charged in other states and risks impermissible extraterritorial regulation.
choices.c3_signal: This answer tracks the stem's lever: sell here only if prices elsewhere meet the state's condition.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct:
C is correct. The statute does not merely set the price for sales inside the state. It makes access to the in-state market depend on what the seller charges in every other state during the same month.

Gold Key: A state may not condition in-state sales on a seller’s out-of-state prices. When the in-state sales gate is tied to prices charged elsewhere, the strongest dormant Commerce Clause objection is extraterritorial price control.

Silver Key: Follow the pricing lever, not the state’s label. The state says “inside our borders,” but the certification forces the seller to account for prices outside the state.

choices.text: The law is valid because a state may control all nationwide prices once a seller enters its market.
choices.c3_signal: The true kernel is local sales power; the bad move is stretching it to all nationwide prices.
choices.why_attractive: The choice starts from a true-sounding local-power idea: the state can regulate sales inside its own market. The breaker is the jump to all nationwide prices, which is the overreach the Gold Key forbids.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The answer stretches in-state sales power into control over all nationwide prices.
choices.future_cue: Separate in-state sales regulation from out-of-state price control.

remediation_card.title: Price Gate Across State Lines
remediation_card.signal: Sell here only if prices elsewhere satisfy this state’s rule.
remediation_card.student_move: Follow the price lever across the border.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: In-state access tied to out-of-state prices points to DCC extraterritorial price control.
remediation_card.trap: Accepting the state’s in-state label.

gold_keys.statement: A state may not condition in-state sales on a seller’s prices charged wholly outside the state. Price-affirmation laws tying in-state access to out-of-state prices are classic dormant Commerce Clause danger zones.
gold_keys.trigger: in-state sales permission depends on prices in other states

silver_keys.statement: Ignore the state’s label and follow the lever. If the in-state sales gate moves when out-of-state prices move, the DCC objection is extraterritorial control.
silver_keys.trigger: certify prices in every other state

drill_seeds.prompt: Cut the choice: 'The state may control all nationwide prices once the seller enters its market.'
drill_seeds.answer: extreme_of_range; local sales power is being pushed to nationwide prices.

drill_seeds.answer: Cut: misfit / wrong doctrine home.

drill_seeds.answer: Extraterritorial price control / price affirmation.

drill_seeds.answer: The certification lever tied to prices in every other state.

subject: CONTRACTS
tension_axis: offer vs acceptance by required performance
stem:
Final Christian variation — QID `21879_noahs_ark_puppet_set`

On April 3, after hearing that Lydia was organizing a neighborhood Bible-story night, Peter sent Lydia a note offering to sell his handmade Noah’s Ark puppet set. Lydia wrote back on April 10 and told Peter that she would buy the puppet set for $175 if Peter delivered it to her courtyard studio on May 6. On May 5, Lydia decided that she would borrow puppets from Naomi instead and wrote Peter a note telling him that she was no longer interested in buying the puppet set. She was about to take the note to the mail drop when Peter knocked at her door. As soon as Lydia opened the door, Peter said, “I’ll bring you that puppet set tomorrow. I’ll just have to borrow Barnabas’s cargo tricycle to carry it.” Lydia said, “Never mind. I don’t want it,” and handed Peter the note she had written but not mailed.

Peter’s statement on May 5 that “I’ll bring you that puppet set tomorrow” was probably:
call: The call is classification. Predict the label for Peter’s words. The sentence expresses willingness to go forward, but no delivery has happened. Prediction: offer.
distilled_core_question: Buyer says she will buy only if seller delivers on a date; seller says the day before that he will bring it tomorrow. What is seller’s statement?
review_truth: A promise to deliver later is not delivery; if delivery is the required acceptance, the promise is best labeled an offer.

choices.text: a ratification of Lydia’s earlier acceptance of Peter’s sale offer.
choices.why_attractive: The word ratification sounds like a sophisticated way to validate the earlier exchange. The breaker is that no earlier acceptance existed to ratify.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: It assumes an earlier acceptance existed, but the earlier letter required delivery.
choices.future_cue: Mark the earlier letter as delivery-conditioned before labeling Peter’s later statement.

choices.text: commencement of performance.
choices.why_attractive: Peter talks about the transport step, so the answer feels tied to action. The breaker is that he has not delivered, tendered, or begun delivering yet.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: A future promise to bring the goods is not present commencement of performance.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether the goods were delivered, tendered, or physically being brought.

choices.text: an offer.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: C is correct. Peter’s statement shows willingness to go forward with a sale on the known price-and-delivery terms. Gold Key: When the earlier buyer letter makes delivery the required way to accept, a later statement that “I’ll bring it tomorrow” is not itself the invited delivery; it is best treated as a new offer to complete the deal. Silver Key: Read the answer array as four legal labels for the same sentence. Cut the labels that require an act already completed, then keep the label that fits a future-tense commitment.

choices.text: an acceptance.
choices.why_attractive: Peter’s words sound like agreement, so students call them acceptance. The breaker is that the invited acceptance was delivery, not a promise to deliver later.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: The statement promises later delivery; it is not the delivery-conditioned acceptance.
choices.future_cue: Ask what the buyer invited as the accepting act.

remediation_card.title: Mode-of-Acceptance Label Drill
remediation_card.signal: One party says “I will buy if you deliver,” and the other says “I will deliver.”
remediation_card.student_move: Ask what act the first statement required and whether that act has happened.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Words promising future delivery are not the delivery itself.
remediation_card.trap: Calling the future promise an acceptance or commencement.

gold_keys.statement: If an offer requires acceptance by a specified performance or tender, a later promise to perform is not the invited acceptance; it is at most a new offer or counteroffer.

silver_keys.statement: Classify the sentence before debating doctrine: future-tense words are not performance already begun.

drill_seeds.prompt: Buyer: “I will buy if you deliver Friday.” Seller Thursday: “I will deliver Friday.” Classify seller’s words.
drill_seeds.answer: Offer, not acceptance, if delivery was the required acceptance.

drill_seeds.prompt: Choice says “commencement of performance.” Stem says “I will bring it tomorrow.” Cut or keep?
drill_seeds.answer: Cut; future words are not present performance.

drill_seeds.prompt: Can a party ratify an acceptance that never legally occurred?
drill_seeds.answer: No.

subject: CRIMINAL_LAW
tension_axis: private search/state action versus privacy-in-container analysis
splitting_fact: The man, not the police officer, searched the house and opened the wooden box; the officer gave non-directive advice earlier and came only after the man called.
stem: A man went to stay with his brother for a few weeks. While staying at his brother’s house, the man started worrying that his brother was dealing drugs. A few days later, the man met a police officer at a party. The man asked the police officer about what kinds of signs he should look for to determine whether his brother was dealing drugs. The police officer told him the best thing to do would be to ask his brother flat out if he was dealing drugs. If not that, maybe the man should look around and see if he finds any hidden drugs or paraphernalia somewhere in his brother’s house. The next day, the brother left to be with friends and the man searched the house. In a closed wooden box, he found a significant amount of methamphetamine. The man called the police officer from the party, and the officer came and confiscated the drugs. The brother was charged with methamphetamine possession. The brother filed a motion to exclude the methamphetamine from evidence.
call: Should the court grant the brother's motion to exclude the methamphetamine?
distilled_core_question: A houseguest searched his brother’s closed box after a police officer suggested he might look around, found drugs, and called the officer. Should the drugs be excluded?
review_truth: The Fourth Amendment suppression remedy normally requires government action; a private person’s search does not trigger exclusion unless the private person acted as a government agent.

choices.text: No, because the brother left the man alone in the house.
choices.c3_signal: The choice talks about why the man had a chance to search, not whether the search was governmental.
choices.why_attractive: The answer feels practical because being left alone in the house sounds like permission or access. The breaker is that permission/access is not the suppression threshold when the searcher is private.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice points to the brother leaving the man alone in the house. That fact does not answer the suppression threshold: whether the search was governmental or private.
choices.future_cue: Ask whether consent/access matters if the searcher was not a government actor.

choices.text: No, because the man found the methamphetamine.
choices.c3_signal: The choice points to the decisive actor fact: the man found the methamphetamine.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: See the preserved right-answer explanation above.

choices.text: Yes, because the police officer directed the man’s search.
choices.c3_signal: The stem gives advice and a maybe; the answer says directed.
choices.why_attractive: The police officer’s advice makes the search feel police-connected. The breaker is that the stem says the officer suggested possibilities, not that he directed the search.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice turns a suggestion into a directive. The stem gives advice and a possible course, not police direction of the search.
choices.future_cue: Underline the actual command words in the stem before crediting a police-direction answer.

choices.text: Yes, because the search violated the man’s right to privacy by opening the closed wooden box.
choices.c3_signal: The closed box is a privacy fact, but the threshold fact is who opened it.
choices.why_attractive: A closed wooden box sounds like a strong privacy fact. The breaker is that privacy matters only after the state-action threshold is crossed.
choices.why_wrong_or_correct: This choice focuses on privacy in a closed wooden box. The missing threshold is state action: a private person opened the box.
choices.future_cue: Run actor first, privacy second.

remediation_card.title: Actor Before Privacy
remediation_card.signal: A private person searches, finds evidence, and later calls police.
remediation_card.student_move: Ask whether the search was done by the government or its agent before analyzing privacy in the place searched.
remediation_card.tiny_rule: Purely private searches do not trigger Fourth Amendment exclusion.
remediation_card.trap: Closed-container privacy feels dispositive, but the actor threshold comes first.

gold_keys.statement: The Fourth Amendment limits government searches, not purely private searches. Evidence found by a private person is not suppressed unless the private person acted as a government agent or with meaningful government participation.
gold_keys.trigger: a private person searches first and police become involved only after the discovery, or before discovery only by giving non-directive advice
gold_keys.authority: United States v. Jacobsen, 466 U.S. 109 (1984); Burdeau v. McDowell, 256 U.S. 465 (1921)

silver_keys.statement: On a suppression call, identify who performed the search before asking whether the place searched was private. Actor first; privacy second.
silver_keys.trigger: the answer choices talk about privacy, consent, or police direction after a non-police person opened the container

drill_seeds.prompt: A roommate opens a closed drawer, finds drugs, and calls police. Suppression?
drill_seeds.answer: No suppression unless the roommate acted as a government agent.

drill_seeds.prompt: An officer says, 'Maybe look around if you are worried.' The private person later searches alone. Did the officer direct the search?
drill_seeds.answer: No. Suggesting a possibility is not directing the search.

drill_seeds.prompt: Closed box opened by private sibling. Which fact matters first: the box was closed or the sibling was private?
drill_seeds.answer: The sibling was private.
